I am pleased to see so many Liberal members in the House today taking an active interest in this very important debate.
I think it is important, in opening this debate, for all members to realize the importance of expenditure restraint. It is critical in our attempt to ensure that we can provide a climate that is conducive to economic growth and stability. The issue of expenditure restraint is a key element of federal government policy.
The provisions outlined in this bill will help to ensure that Canada continues its progress toward economic recovery this year, but just as important these measures will help ensure that we set in place the essential conditions for stable continuous growth, and permanent job creation, as well as real increases in national and individual prosperity throughout the decade.
The legislation before us proposes to change four specific acts of Parliament. The Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act will be amended to extend the two-year limitation introduced in the 1990 budget on the growth of established programs funding to the provinces for another three years. In conjunction with this we are also proposing to amend this act to permit the withholding of other federal payments to provinces in the event of a breach of the national health standards set out in the Canada Health Act.

What happened? By 1984-85, the annual deficit had tripled under their regime to over $38 billion in just four years. Interest charges on the debt were consuming a rapidly increasing proportion of revenues, revenues that could not be allocated to better the lives of Canadians.

In fact, it is the compounding interest on the national debt we inherited that now accounts for almost all of the growth in the debt that has occurred over the last six years. That is the truth.
If we had followed the Liberal way, that short-sighted political way that is even today suggested by some of our more learned critics across the way, we would then have embarked upon a course of spending and fiscal irresponsibility which would have aggravated all of the fundamental problems we now have. It would have deepened and complicated the problem of renewing our national prosperity.
For example, if we had followed the same track that the Liberals were on, today instead of having a $30 billion deficit we would have had a $99 billion deficit. That is really the fact of the matter. It is a stark comparison of the difference in approaches and the difference in attitudes.
Instead of restoring the government's ability to assist Canadians in need, we would be weakening that capability. Instead of building greater confidence in Canada's ability to deal with its problems, we would be sending a message of indecision, uncertainty and probably incapacity.
We cannot spend our way out of difficult times with money that we have to borrow. The philosophy behind

our program for economic renewal is clear and very concrete. We have to pay our way at home and earn our prosperity in the international marketplace. That is why we have embarked upon a course that places less reliance upon government and taxpayers' pocketbooks and more on personal initiative and enterprise.
Government spending in the end comes only from one source: the taxpayer. It is not government that creates jobs, prosperity and provides higher real incomes. It is the private sector through its enterprise, its initiative and its production. It is that production which produces the wealth that not only services governments and the important services that governments provide, but indeed provides the wealth for Canadians. It is not government that creates jobs and provides higher real incomes. Prosperity cannot be legislated, it must be gained in the marketplace. That is a very important philosophy. If we have that right, then it is pretty clear that we have to concentrate our efforts on attempting to put in place the kind of economic environment that is conducive to providing ways in which the enterprise spirit will prevail. speechtext:
I am asking hon. members across the way to shoulder their share of the burden and the responsibility because they created it and are probably more responsible for it than any other government in this country.
It is in keeping with this philosophy that our government has given a priority to the two key aspects of this renewal: structural reforms, such as deregulation and privatization, and removing the obstacles and barriers to innovation and enterprise and growth, whether it be interprovincial trade barriers, over-regulation, or various kinds of burdens and impediments to growth and economic activity. Second, we have devoted our attention to sound macro-economic policies.
As I indicated, we recognize the pressures and hardships that are facing many Canadians. Economic recovery is this government's fundamental goal, but we have to get the fundamentals right. Our policies, reflected in the measures in this bill, are establishing the sound fiscal plan on which recovery must be based.
It will be a recovery that is not borrowed from tomorrow's account. Instead, it will be a recovery that gives lasting promise and opportunities to young Canadians entering the work force, one that protects those on fixed incomes, the poor and the elderly and those who save and invest, from the ravages of inflation. That is important, Madam Speaker. The members opposite scoff at the inflationary targets. At the same time they want to ensure that elderly Canadians will not see their incomes eroded. I think we can all agree on that and in order to preserve that capacity we must ensure that we fight inflation and maintain realistic inflationary targets.
As well, we will be basing our recovery program on a philosophy that allows working Canadians and employees to plan for the future in confidence, knowing that economic growth reflects real strength rather than being based on the artificial and transitory prop of government.
At this time in a globalized economy there is no way that we can hide our inefficiencies or our lack of competitiveness. We cannot hide those inefficiencies through government subsidies or the creation of Crown
corporations. It is all out there. We live in a day and age of globalization where national boundaries are becoming increasingly irrelevant. As a nation which relies on world trade for about one-third of its GDP we obviously have to address that as one of the most important priorities. That is what we are doing both in the budget and in the commitment undertaken in the Speech from the Throne.
Meeting these goals cannot be done without restraint, co-operation, some sacrifice and hard work. We must all share the burden.
Having set forth the reasons for this legislation I want to elaborate on some of the specific measures involved.
The current limitations to the growth of Established Programs Financing, or EPF, will be extended through to 1994-1995. This measure will reduce federal cash expenditures by about $340 million in 1992-1993, $465 million in 1993-1994, and about $750 million in the third year.
It is important to put this measure in context. While it is an important step for government, it is not the drastic and destructive burden on the provinces that some have suggested.
The savings that we will achieve represent only about one-half of 1 per cent of the total provincial revenues in 1992-1993. Even with the measures proposed in the bill, EPF transfers in 1992-1993 will exceed $20 billion.
These transfers will continue to grow with provincial populations. I trust that hon. members will remember as well that in addition to the EPF transfers, the federal government also provides substantial assistance to lower income provinces through the equalization program, to help them provide a level of service that is consistent across the country. This support provides for health care and post-secondary education as well.
Equalization transfers have grown significantly-

The hon. member says that they have been cut significantly and that is absolutely, categorically false. The fact of the matter is that equalization transfers have grown significantly over the last few years, from over $5 billion in 1984-85 to over $8 billion in the current fiscal year. These transfers are not affected, and I repeat, these transfers are not affected by the budget.
June 11, 1991

They will continue to grow in line with the nominal rate of growth of the economy.
The government recognizes as well that limiting the growth of transfers under EPF raises concerns about the ability of the federal government to continue enforcing national medicare principles. Therefore, the legislation under consideration will also amend the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act. This will allow the government to withhold other payments to provinces in the event there are insufficient EPF cash transfers against which to apply financial penalties for a breach of national medicare principles, as set out in the Canada Health Act.
At the same time that we are asking the provinces to share the burden of fiscal restraint, we are also calling on this government and members of Parliament to do their part. The February budget announced our intent to freeze the salaries of cabinet ministers for the coming year. As well, the bill before us will amend the Parliament of Canada Act to limit annual increases in sessional allowances for members of both Houses to the average wage increases within the Public Service of Canada for the years 1992, 1993 and 1994.
Any increases in salaries and allowances for office holders of the Senate and the House of Commons and expense allowances for all MPs in these years will be held to these same levels.
Such measures ensure that the burden of financial restraint is not limited to the Public Service alone. It also means that all of us in government must learn to live with the resources that we have available, a discipline that the private sector cannot avoid and that we must learn to share.
As another element of the expenditure restraint program is the legislation before us. It extends the freeze on the transfer payments to provinces under the Public Utilities Income Transfer Act, commonly referred to as PUITTA, for an additional four years until 1995. Under the terms of the 1990 budget, these payments were frozen at 1989 levels of $280 million. As a member from Alberta I want to suggest that our action here is much less drastic than the actions taken by the provincial government. In its 1990 budget, Alberta decided to eliminate completely its rebates of provincial income taxes paid to privately owned utility companies.
Government Orders
These tax revenues are now retained in full by the provinces, but our measure continues to return most of the federal income tax from these utilities to the provinces. That provides a level playing field with Crown corporations which do not pay taxes and operate in other provinces. It is for that reason that PUITTA was put in place in the first place.
Finally, the government proposes to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act to increase premium rates. Effective July 1, 1991, employee premiums will be increased to $2.80 per $100 of insurable earnings, from the current $2.25. Premiums for employers will rise to $3.92 per $100 of insurable earnings from the current level of $3.15. These measures work to assist the important restructuring of the unemployment insurance program that was undertaken last year, along with measures to provide more training and fewer disincentives to work. The program was placed on a sound financial footing with the costs financed through employee-employer contributions.
Since then, the deteriorating labour market conditions have led to higher than anticipated benefit payments. Consequently the program's account is projected to go sharply out of balance. This would seriously jeopardize the financial integrity of this self-financed program and further damage the government's fiscal position.
Since the UI account is consolidated in budgetary transactions, the changes in the rate will reduce the deficit by $2 billion in 1991-92 and by $2.4 billion in 1992-93.
The measures that we are proposing here today are not easy and not painless. They are the consequence of too many years of government overspending and overborrowing.
We worked hard to reverse that trend and reverse that record, but to make further progress on behalf of all Canadians we have to ask Canadians everywhere-individuals, other levels of government and businesses-to share in the burden of fiscal restraint.
I said earlier that our policies and programs are already having a positive effect on the economy. It is worth highlighting just a few of the recent indicators that show we are on track for recovery in the second half of this year.

June 11, 1991
Government Orders
For example, short-term interest rates have dropped by more than five percentage points in just over a year. The Bank of Canada dropped its rate again last Thursday to the lowest level since April 1988, and I am sure that all hon. members will agree that that is good news.
As well, I think it is important that the differential between Canada and U.S. interest rates has narrowed significantly. From a high of about 560 basis points a year ago, it has dropped to well below 300 basis points. I believe 2.59 per cent was the last figure I saw and that was for a three-month commercial paper.
If we compare the Canadian prime rate at nine and three-quarters per cent to the U.S. prime rate at eight and a half per cent, that is a differential of about one and a quarter per cent. Those wide spreads that were a legitimate complaint in the previous 12 months have narrowed significantly, and I believe that it is a clear expression of confidence in the measures we have taken. It is a clear measure of confidence in our bid to engage in fiscal consolidation that we have demonstrated a resolve and a commitment to deal with the deficit and to deal with the underlying causes of inflation.
I think the underlying causes of inflation and the inflationary expectations and pressures are key elements to interest rates now and in the future, and it is important for us to maintain that course.
In turn, the reduced interest rates are fuelling a significant rebound in the housing sector as both housing starts and resale transactions surged in April.
Also, last week Statistics Canada announced that manufactured shipments, due to the strength in the automobile sector, increased a half a per cent in March to $22.6 billion, the first rise in five months. A recent Conference Board of Canada index of business confidence showed a dramatic gain in the first quarter.
These are all positive signs and positive indicators, but we are not suggesting that we should get over-ecstatic about it. We think the recovery will be slow, but we hope that it will be a durable one.
I think it is a clear fact that the course we are on is proving to be the right one, and I think that is shown by the indicators that we see.
If we waver and let the deficit begin to surge again, we will significantly undercut the renewed business confidence in the mid-term prospects that will help generate
new investment and new jobs. We will also be encouraging Canadians in every sector to return to the inflationary behaviour and expectations that are the driving force behind higher interest rates.
We simply do not intend to let this happen. The national interest, the prospect for all Canadians to enjoy renewed growth and prosperity, demands that our commitment must not flag just at the point where we are beginning to get back on track. By persevering we will not only be able to bring the deficit under control but will also, in the not too distant future, begin removing this burden from the backs of the Canadian people and particularly the backs of future generations. Only in this way can we build the Canada that we want for ourselves and for our children.
I am presenting this bill for second reading. I urge the hon. members to support it, to support the motives and the inspiration that underlie the bill. It is certainly in keeping with the trend and the direction that we must take in terms of fostering a solid foundation for economic growth and prosperity in the future.

Madam Speaker, my congratulations to the Minister of Finance. I believe it is his first major speech in the House since taking over this portfolio. I would also like to thank the minister for having his staff brief the opposition parties and give us an opportunity to review some of the technicalities of this very important piece of legislation. When I was listening to the minister, I was thinking that it is unfortunate that the sins of the father have to be visited upon the son. I am sure the hon. member for Gander-Grand Falls is a man better equipped than myself with images for these situations. I was thinking about the change in the government and how it always tries to make things seem like a relay race, a smooth transition of handing things off. But if we look at this government since it changed portfolios, it is more like a hot potato race. Immigration is over here and external is over there and finance is there, and all are throwing hot potatoes into the air hoping someone else will catch them. The minister is being caught with a hot potato and the first move he has to make is with Bill C-20.
The reason why this party will not be supporting Bill C-20 is that we disagree fundamentally with the strategy behind this legislation. It is a strategy of social policy by stealth. It is a strategy of undermining the fundamental programs in this country by using technical measures
June 11, 1991

rather than by dealing with them in a straightforward way.
The harsh battle that we saw with Bill C-69 is about to be repeated with Bill C-20. We must show Canadians that this government is seeking to undermine the Canada Assistance Plan, to undermine the equalization programs, and to undermine medicare and post-secondary education. They are doing this not by dealing with them directly, not by telling Canadians they are no longer interested in those programs, but by using fiscal measures through the back door that Canadians have a difficult time understanding and following.
It is at this quiet moment in the House at 10.30 on a Tuesday morning that an important piece of legislation is being introduced without people really understanding what the future holds for them.
I would like to spend the time during my speech to go over some of these measures and to explain, as best as I can on behalf of my party, why this legislation is in fact dangerous.
A well-known Canadian, Grattan Gray, has written in Policy Options, a very well respected magazine, that he would describe the strategy of this government as social policy by stealth. I would like to quote, to set up this particular analysis, from Mr. Gray.
In brief, (he Tory style of restraint has become what can only be characterized as "social policy by stealth".
It relies heavily on technical amendments to taxes and transfers that are as difficult to explain as they are to understand and thus largely escape media scrutiny and public attention. It camouflages regressive changes in their rhetoric of equity in an attempt to convince Canadians that tax increases are tax cuts and that benefit cuts are benefit increases. By further complicating an already complex labyrinth of taxes and social programs, the stealth style of policy making confuses 1he electorate and so insulates itself from criticism. The Conservative's record on social and tax policy constitutes a variation on Newton's Third Law of Motion. For every positive action there is an equal and opposite negative change. As a result, the goal of a fairer, simpler and more rational system of taxes and transfers remains as distant as ever.
In other words, the language is there: the language of fairness, the language of concern, the language of good management. The government knows the language. The government does not have a clue as to how to carry this out fairly, on behalf of all Canadians.
Government Orders
The minister is fond of referring to the past. Anyone who watches the House of Commons during Question Period sees that this government refers constantly to what the bad guys did, what the Liberals did in the 1970s and the 1980s. They do not mention of course the introduction of medicare and old age security. They do not mention the amount of money that was put into post-secondary education so that this whole generation could be educated. They seem somehow to forget that.
Perhaps we should go back and ask: "What were they thinking in those years?" Let us take the former Minister of Finance, for example. He said as reported on March 23, 1982 at page 15758 of the Commons Debates:
In past years, the federal government has used its taxing power and the financial strength of its position to exert its influence and to establish national standards and programs-
National standards and programs, these are words that we hear all the time now. he continued:
This is acceptable and I think we can understand the use of that power.
Here we have the future Minister of Finance staking out the turf that he is in favour of national standards and in favour of the use of the federal powers to follow up.
He continued in the same debate:
The only sign the current government shows of cutting spending is by shifting the burden of the established programs funding on to the provincial governments. The provinces are now moving into a deficit position, a position which will make it more difficult for them to finance this shift in spending. This is particularly true in Ontario and in the eastern provinces which do not have the substantial energy revenues of most of the western provinces. That is not co-operative federalism. That is a predatory federalism, and it will not and cannot work in this country.
Let us read those words again and think about them: predatory federalism on provinces that cannot afford it. What do we see this government doing? We see it undertaking and participating in predatory federalism to the extent that the only road that these governments have nowadays is to go to the courts. We have federalism by court action. We have the provincial governments taking the federal government to court on basic constitutional issues such as the cap on the Canada Assistance Program.

June 11, 1991
Government Orders
Can we imagine a future Minister of Finance standing up in the House to speak in a debate like this and laying out a position that it is fundamental to his understanding of the country that we do not terrorize provinces?
Then in February this year he stands up and says, without any warning at all: "We will extend the existing 5 per cent cap on the growth of Canada Assistance Plan payments to the fiscally stronger provinces of Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta for three additional years". This is while they are already in court on another issue.
Second, the existing freeze on total per capita cash and tax transfers to the provinces, under Established Programs Financing, will also continue through 1994-95.
So there you go. On the one hand you stand in opposition and worry about the terrorism created by a government dealing with the recession. Then you come into power and say that the first people you are going to knock over are the provinces. You are going to make them pay for the programs even though you know most of them cannot afford to. In addition, it is fundamental to their fiscal security to have a strong central government. You take the language, you make people look this way, and while they are looking this way you take the cash and run.
Bill C-20 is all about taking the cash and running. It is done in a veiy quiet way where, if it is not pointed out, people will think that this is just a burden that we have to carry.
I listened very carefully to the Minister of Finance and I want him to remember his words when he said there was only one taxpayer. The great mythology in this country is that there is only one taxpayer, you and me. Well there may only be one taxpayer in this country, but there are distinctions among that so-called one taxpayer that this government refuses to admit.
Recent research has shown very clearly that the middle-class taxpayer is a special person as compared to the corporate taxpayer under this government. The rises in taxes paid by the average Canadian, which we estimate to be 34 taxes at last count, has doubled the rate of tax increases to the corporate sector. Now that is not to go on, as the NDP would, to a great anti-corporate diatribe. It is simply to point out to the government not to give us this thought that there is only one taxpayer when it has
made a distinction. If there is only one taxpayer, why do the taxes go up a high percentage for the middle-class family and only a small amount for the corporate taxpayer? The government itself is saying just the opposite, that there are two classes of taxpayers and that it favours the corporate taxpayer and is going to protect them.
The guilt that people try to bring out in this deficit reduction dialogue has to be stopped. There is a deficit, it is important for us to get rid of it, and this Liberal Party will participate in any reasonable debt reduction scheme. As part of that package we not only want to see deficit reduction but real tax reform from this government and some wealth creation. We do not have wealth creation in this country right now. We have the loss of 275,000 jobs in the manufacturing sector which is just one indicator as to how little we have.
We would then like to see some real policy directions and the reform of social policies in this country. You cannot just single out deficit reduction and then drive everything by that when you have no idea how to govern the country in a reasonable way. No wonder so many Canadians are turning elsewhere and are becoming introspective by wanting to set up their own countries and move away from the centre.
The centre cannot hold if you do not have any ideas. This government lacks ideas. As commentators have said, it moves by stealth.
Yesterday, we heard the ministers of finance in Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island talk about what it is like trying to set a budget when the government takes money away at every opportunity.
This is not to say that the provinces are not positioning or that they do not have their own axes to grind. None of us are naive about provincial ministers of finance, but I would just like to point out that federalism requires co-operation.
The government cannot on one hand be trying to set out a new constitutional regime and perhaps even be talking about a new economic regime while at the same time saying to the 10 colleagues around the table: "We are going to try to squeeze every ounce of cash out of the system, and we really do not care how much you scream".
June 11, 1991

The provinces are there under the Constitution to deliver services which are close to people. That includes welfare, education, looking after municipalities and a number of functions. If you ask who matters more to average Canadians, whether it be the backbenchers in the House of Commons, city councillors, local administrators or provincial people delivering education, they will tell you we count for less every time.
Our job here is to design a federal regime which protects and supports those people. We do not do it by undermining them at every opportunity.
Bill C-20 is designed to carry on the battle begun by this government in 1984 to undermine the social fabric and the current constitutional arrangement in this country. Each federal-provincial meeting whether in health, social policy or fiscal arrangements with the finance ministers, including the first ministers' meetings dealing with the Constitution, has been designed to shift the direction of this country.
Direction is not shifted by directly saying "this is the new Canada", but by saying "free trade will have no negative impacts on the country. Bill C-69 will have no impact on the country. The constitutional arrangement will really have no impact on your lives".
Suddenly people are turning around and saying: "Where is my country? Where is the place my parents built up? Where is the place I moved to? Where is the place that opened its arms and welcomed me?" It is depressed because the underpinnings have been removed by people who do not understand how it was put together in the first place.
The fight over Bill C-20 is a fight to get this government to recognize the significance of legislation which undermines the activities that people take pride in. The bill is a piece of legislation which comes out of the budget.
In the Canadian parliamentary system, when the budget statement is made the government presents a number of items to see it through. There is no new news in here, but we see the details under which the government hopes to continue its Draconian measures to destroy this country.
In the first section it deals with federal-provincial fiscal arrangements, federal post-secondary education and the Health Contributions Act. It repeals a number of
Government Orders
the sections and sets out a low growth strategy in the transfer payments to the provinces. I would like to deal with what that means to somebody in any one of our Canadian cities who is trying to get proper services.
What does it mean when the federal government says: "We are no longer going to sponsor post-secondary education the way we did in the past"? What does it mean to somebody 18 or 19 who is thinking of their education? It means they better begin to prepare and save if they can for very high tuition increases.
It is not out of line to think that tuition will hit $3,000 in the very near future. People say: "Why are we paying so much for education?" When people in this House went to university, they probably paid somewhere between $400 to $900 for tuition depending on the province.
Now we are saying to the next generation: "Three thousand dollars a year is not much. Don't worry about being $20,000 in debt". Then we will have to tell them: "You have to go back to Bill C-69 and Bill C-20 to understand how the federal government began to grab the cash out of the system". This can be very obscure and difficult to understand for a student in high school right now.
We stand in the House of Commons today and say to the government: "Rethink your fiscal arrangement strategy. Don't squeeze the universities. Find another way of financing this country. Find another way through tax reform. Find another way through economic growth. Don't be driven by the deficit to the point of distraction".
The act also continues on to outline the strategy, first noted in the budget, that the government is going to extend its powers under the Canada Health Act.
The Canada Health Act was designed by the last Liberal government to give the Minister of Health and Welfare fiscal authority and financial powers to limit payments to provinces which do not conform to the standards of the medicare program. The medicare program, of course, has five principles attached to it and with those five principles we protect our medicare system. If it is found to be sufficient, and as long as everyone stays committed to those five principles, then the need to actually use the Canada Health Act is very limited.

June 11, 1991
Government Orders
Members of this government are anxious to protect medicare because they understand that people out there fear them, they fear for medicare, they fear for its future. At the meetings of the ministers of finance yesterday in Charlottetown the story was: "You guys in the federal government are destroying medicare; we cannot finance it under the present program, let alone under future cuts".
This government understands that that message is out there in Canada. It has two choices. It can either recognize the concern that medicare is fundamental to the way Canadians think about themselves and do something about it, or take away medicare cash and force the provinces to find cash in other ways. This government pretends to be protecting the system, but in reality it pulls cash out of the rest of the system in order to play this charade. This is a charade and it is going to be called a charade and it is going to be fought as a charade.
The Government of Canada could protect medicare through the Canada Health Act and through proper funding of the provincial arrangements that now exist. It does not need to pull cash out of the rest of the system or threaten the provinces.
The act is somewhat obscure as to what measures are available. Perhaps for the public record this will be the opportunity to lay out exactly what is meant by other measures.
The federal government transfers funds to the provinces under several different programs. In reviewing these programs you have to remember that the federal government, if this gets through, will be able to pull money out of any of these programs. This sounds like a good idea, protecting medicare. Again, the way to protect medicare is to fund it, not to take money from elsewhere.
For example, under the Canada Assistance Plan the federal government shares the cost of each province's income maintenance and social services programs on a 50-50 basis. Cash expenditures for 1991-92 are forecast to be $5.7 billion. If the federal government decided that a province was not spending its medicare money properly, it could hold back the transfers under CAP which is meant for welfare. This is, in fact, an attack on poverty. Day care is paid for under the Canada Assistance Plan. If the federal government is not happy with the way medicare is working out, because public opinion polls tell
it to be careful in medicare, it could take money from day care. It is right here in the legislation.
Crop insurance, now here is a hoot. Farmers could be forced to pay for money lacking in medicare. It has the right to take away from crop insurance. The federal government shares administrative costs and premiums for crop insurance programs with the provinces and farmers. Federal contributions for the current year are estimated to be over $200 million.
This government could take money away from official languages and education. These formula payments to provinces under the Official Languages and Education Program provide enhanced opportunities for Canadians to learn a second official language. The cost is estimated to be about $263 million for the current fiscal year. That too can be pulled away.
There is a number of programs dealing with disabled persons under miscellaneous health and welfare to the extent of $170 million. Let us think about it. They want the authority to put into this legislation that if they want some money they can pull back $170 million from disabled persons.

We are going to be out there telling Canadians that we will do anything, anything except put up the cash, anything but tax reform, anything but turning this country around". This is just not the way to govern the country.
Tlirning to young offenders services, the federal government has agreements with the provinces and territories to share the costs incurred delivering justice services under the Young Offenders Act. The contribution is estimated currently to be $158 million.
Let us go over the list. They can take money from farmers. They can take money from young people. They can take money from the disabled. They can take money from welfare, from poor people. Is this the strategy for protecting medicare?
Let us continue. They can take money from justice. One of the great concerns of people is with safe cities. The federal assistance to provinces for legal aid programs related to criminal law and for programs that compensate victims of violent crime, $77 million. Again,

June 11, 1991

people who have been subject to violent crime could have their money taken away from them.
Transportation includes federal transfers to provinces and municipalities for coastal marine transportation services, the establishment and operation of airports, and rail grade separations. Another $69 million is made vulnerable.
Equalization, which the government puts at $8.4 billion, is a big pocket to get into. Territorial financing for the territorial governments, another $1 billion is not going to be available to the federal government.
Perhaps the one that I enjoy the most-and I am sure my hon. friend from Kingston and the Islands will be happy to discover it-is that this government wants to put into this package grants in lieu of property taxes. The federal government makes grants to provincial and municipal governments instead of paying the property taxes levied on federal and diplomatic property. The grants to municipalities right now is estimated at $344 million.
In other words, if there is a hospital in Ontario which for some reason the government does not like the way it is operating, perhaps with user fees or whatever, it can turn around and say to the city of Kingston: "We are withholding all your money". It could say to the city of Ottawa: "We are just going to withhold your money, that is it; get the province in order".
What kind of terrorism are they setting in motion? They have the legislative authority to turn municipalities against the province and against the federal government. Is that co-operative federalism the former Minister of Finance waxed on eloquently when he had the luxury of being in opposition? Perhaps he never thought he would be government and have to take responsibility for this country. Perhaps some of the good news is that he no longer is responsible for the financing of this country and we will find a better way of doing things.
We consider that this new weapon in the arsenal of the federal government in its attack on this country is totally unsuitable. We will work as hard as we can to make
Government Orders
Canadians familiar with this particular component of the legislation and to fight hard against it.
If that were all the bad news we would be saddened, but there is no end to the bad news from this government. The bill continues on to deal with the UI. It quietly announces a 30 per cent premium increase of $2.25 to about $2.85. We have to stop and think: this follows the legislation they are so happy about, Bill C-21, not two years ago in this House, after a long, bitter and acrimonious fight in which the government withdrew from the unemployment insurance and left it up to individuals and companies.
Now we find out that the premiums have to be raised because in the absence of government support the fund is in a great deal of debt. Is there any mention in this legislation or in the minister's speech about training? Did he say anything about training? No.
So here we have on the one hand the Prime Minister traipsing about the country, balloons going up about how interested the Department of Finance is in training issues and how incompetent the provincial governments are in education. What do we find in the legislation the government presents to the House. We find that it is capping the moneys and withdrawing moneys from post-secondary education.
The government talks about the unemployment insurance fund. Does it mention training? No. How do people get themselves back into the system if this government cannot even remember to mention it in a speech, let alone care to do something? It cannot even remember that it made a commitment.
The Conservatives come into this House and talk about the need for deficit cuts and so forth, and then they turn around and attack the working people of this country in a way which totally destroys their confidence that they will have a secure and full life in this country.
Until these attacks stop, the depression in this country and the uncertainty will continue. It is up to this Minister of Finance to show some leadership and to understand how a piece of legislation such as this is so destructive.
Recently this legislation and the budget were reviewed by the National Council of Welfare. This is an advisory group to the federal government. It published a report

Government Orders
entitled Funding Health and Higher Education-Danger Looming. This has been a subject of much discussion in the last 10 days. It is an excellent report. It comes from an organization which has been researching in this area for 20 years. It has managed to do the fine balancing act of being a critic of the government and a creature of the government at the same time and of being a spokesperson for Canada's poor at the same time as being responsible in its judgments.
I have over the years used many of its documents as a researcher and can attest to the seriousness of it work. It became the centre of a controversy last week when it indicated that the cash payments being made to the provinces were about to disappear.
As the government well knows, there are two components to the transfers that it makes under, for example, the health programs. It makes a tax point transfer, most of it settled under the 1977 EPF arrangement, Established Programs Financing arrangement, but it also transfers cash. In the analysis done by the National Council of Welfare, those cash payments begin to disappear from the provinces. Those cash payments are first to disappear in Quebec within five years, and in the rest of the provinces and the territories within 15 years.
When we look at this analysis we begin to understand the dilemma of the federal government. It refuses to tax properly, and therefore it is cash short. It does not have a gross strategy for this country and therefore revenues are shrinking. It has a deficit that is mind-boggling, three-quarters of which has been created by its own stupidity. When we take those components we realize what the National Council of Welfare is warning us about. Then we go back and look at Bill C-20 and all of a sudden realize what this is all about.
The government is trying to move out of its traditional domain. While it talks of national standards and tries to introduce into the constitutional debate a discussion on national standards, it pulls its cash off the table. As it pulls its cash off the table, particularly in medicare, the provinces say: "Well, listen, we need this cash for medicare. We are having trouble. We are having to choose between education and medicare". The government shrugs and says: "Medicare is protected under the Canada Health Act and by the way under Bill C-20, if you mess around with that, we have all these other weapons and we will go after you there".
The National Council of Welfare points out the following in its remarks, which I think are vety good: "Health care and post-secondary education are undertakings vital to the well-being of Canadians". That should not have to be restated, but it does in this country right now because people are losing sight that that is one of the reasons we got together in the first place. It warns that people in poorer provinces will have to make due with health care services inferior to the services enjoyed by Canadians who happen to live in richer provinces if these measures go through.
Again, let us think about it. Let us think about my colleague from Gander-Grand Falls having to go back to his constituency and saying: "No matter how difficult life is in the province and no matter how much you struggle, the only news I have for you after this spring is higher UI premiums and the likelihood that your medicare system is not going to be as good. By the way, if you want to go on to post-secondary education, you can try the university in this province, you can pay your $3,000, but really it is getting to be better elsewhere in the country".
We cannot deal with families on that basis. We have to tell them they are there as fishermen, as loggers, as miners and as farmers. Sometimes there are good years; sometimes there are bad years. Sometime there have been bad years in the west. What are they supposed to do if medicare gets undermined? Do they live for three months in the farms of Manitoba and then go to Toronto for medicare during the winter?
What are the Conservatives thinking about? The National Council of Welfare is saying: "Be careful, this is the system you are setting in motion. We want you to pay attention to it because, if you let them put this into legislation, in 10 years you will wake up with no cash from the federal government". The federal government says that it does not have cash, that it will squeeze somewhere else, and that, by the way, it is trying to make a good constitutional deal for everybody to make them feel like this is a fair country.
That is why this government has no credibility and that is why the sooner it is gone the happier Canada will be.
There are some very specific recommendations coming from the national council report which are worth while presenting to the House. As this legislation moves to committee, I would like to see the committee consider
June 11, 1991

some of them and make sure that the legislation conforms to these important points.
First, the federal government should continue to play a significant financial role in both health care and post-secondary education.
Second, any changes in the financing of health and higher education should result from federal-provincial negotiations rather than being imposed by Ottawa. What a message.
After years of co-operative federalism beginning under Lester B. Pearson in the 1960s, after special deals made by Mackenzie King to ensure that UI became a national program, after the leadership shown by Paul Martin, Senior, in ensuring the medicare came into Canada despite federal-provincial problems, the development of regional development programs in the 1970s within the atmosphere of federal-provincial agreements, the extension of economic development ERDA agreements, the Economic and Regional Development Agreements in the early 1980s, we are all of a sudden starting the 1990s with an advisory group having to make the most elementary statement that Ottawa should not impose new agreements.
Why does that have to be stated? It has to be stated because nobody trusts this government any more, particularly the people concerned about social policy in this country.
Third, any new arrangements negotiated for financing health and higher education should focus on federal cash payments. A cliche in business, particularly small business, is: after a deal has been made, who has the cash? Maybe we should remember this in dealing with the federal government: Who has the cash?
They do not have it because they will not collect it and, because they do not have anything, they will not give it to the provinces. We know that the individual taxpayer in Canada has no cash, their provinces have no cash, and the feds say they have no cash. The big question right now is: Who has the cash?
The Minister of Finance went over the problem and said: "Oh, I don't have any cash, Mr. Opposition Party. You should know that". This country has cash, so who has the cash? If the biggest tax collector in the country is telling us that he does not have cash, where is it? Is it
Government Orders
because they have wasted it and therefore should not be governing any more? Is it because they do not know how to collect it fairly? Why do they not have the cash? I ask the minister that question. Perhaps he can return to this point later on in his discussions.
Finally, federal funding for health care should be distinct from funding for post-secondary education. Federal legislation should stipulate that the cash received by a province for health and higher education is to be spent as intended.
I want to deal with one of the most subtle and dangerous changes in the fiscal arrangements in this country, by focusing attention on medicare which we can take for granted is one of the most important if not the most important programs we have, because when everything is said and done health is essential to life, and by building a corral around medicare we have to stop and think about what has been excluded. If we do not have cash for medicare, where do we find it? That is the question provincial ministers of finance have. You find it in post-secondary education. So many provinces have been guilty of stealing moneys from the post-secondary field to cover up other fields.
It is stealing from their future. It is stealing from students who need a first class education. I do not mean 50, 60 students in a political science class whose books are four years old. That is kidding ourselves. People who have language skills, people who you can trade with- how can you have a world trading system, as these ministers talk about, if you do not have people who can speak many languages? How can you speak many languages if you do not get trained?
You talk about going into Asia. Who are you talking about going into Asia and what skills are they going to have?
You talk about selling our wheat to new markets or developing new products in the wheat markets. Where is that research going to be done? You do not do that by reading a four year old book at a university library. You do it in first class facilities.
The National Council on Welfare is absolutely correct to say: "stop the stealing from education because nobody notices it today or yesterday". All of a sudden down the line everybody is going to notice it, everybody is going to

June 11, 1991
Government Orders
be in a panic and then it may be too late because you cannot create a new student. You cannot create a new university library. You cannot create a new community college by going "presto, it's here". This takes time and a lot of effort and if we do not start now, it will take us 20 years to catch up.
These are the comments on Bill C-20. As you can see, we have serious reservations about it. We are very concerned about the ongoing cutbacks to the transfer payments to the provinces. We think it is a strategy not developed in a realistic way in the context of program development, of tax reform, of deficit reduction.
We are as concerned as the government about the debt that it has created, and let the records show that it is their debt and no one else's debt. It had a finance minister there for seven years. He knew what the debt was. He projected every year that he would be doing a better job. He failed. It was turned over to a new minister. It is too late for them, but the country is saddled with $400 billion worth of errors.
This party is very sensitive to the need to reduce that deficit, but it is also, as I have indicated in my speech, it is something that is not done on the backs of farmers-and this is documented-of municipalities, of provinces, of people who are vulnerable in the society. You do not build strength by attacking the weakest.
This attack on the weak should not go unchallenged and, thus, our party opposes this legislation and will continue to challenge it.

precisely the problem. This government is taking the money from peoples' pockets which would otherwise be spent on goods and services and keeping people at work in this country.
The minister says positive indicators. He did not happen to mention the unemployment rate on Friday, which went up from the previous month to 10.3 per cent, an unemployment rate increase which includes a loss of jobs for our young people in this country, a loss of jobs for young men for a total of 13,000.
The seasonally adjusted figures for unemployment itself indicated that 15,000 more people were unemployed in this country last month. Is that a positive indicator? If we compare the unemployment figures that were just announced Friday with last year, what is the reality?
The reality is that full-time employment in this country of ours decreased by 330,000 jobs since April of last year. Surely it is not possible for this government to say that these are positive signs for the future of our country.
This decrease is not just in the goods producing area, the manufacturing sector which has been hit so hard. There were 174,000 jobs lost there, but 65,000 jobs were also lost in the service producing sector.
We have seen, brought home to us in these kinds of statistics, that this is not a country enjoying a durable recovery. This is a country still experiencing recession. When we move into recovery-eventually we will have to move into recovery because that is how business cycles work-what sort of recovery is it going to be?
Again, let me quote from the Bank of Montreal which is usually on the government's side. It does not say that it is going to be a durable recovery. No. It says that it is going to be a weak recovery. To quote:
Weak income growth is expected to be one of the main
impediments preventing a more robust recovery.
Expansion is expected to be sluggish. Maybe this government is satisfied with a sluggish, weak recovery. Let me tell you that you have lost 330,000 jobs in a year. To see a sluggish recovery and be satisfied with it is surely shameful. In my view, there is no question that this government is far too smug about what is happening.
Interest rates in this country are still far too high. The gap between us and the United States of 3 percentage points is far higher than anything that we had historically

Government Orders
between Canada and the United States in the past. We have never had that 3 per cent rate.
The dollar's value now is consistently over 87 cents American. Every single institution that you speak to in this country, from the government's own Economic Council to the Canadian Exporter's Association and the trade union groups that are being hit so hard in terms of jobs by this recession, says one thing with a single voice. The government succeeded in bring labour and business together on the one single, dominant point that the dollar in this country is far too high and that we have to reduce interest rates further so that we get a competitive level of dollar. The Economic Council, the government's own body, has suggested 78 or 80 cents.
We have a government that has changed the unemployment insurance system so that there are far more people being forced into the destructive experience of having to receive welfare payments to keep their families together.
We have seen the destruction of our manufacturing base. We need investment in the future, in training, in research and development, in new institutions to channel capital into the rebuilding of our manufacturing sector.
This government is giving us none of that kind of leadership. Instead, it gives us the bill that is in front of us this morning. This legislation is as mean-minded, penny-pinching and as non-creative as any of its previous legislation in the last seven years.
What we have in front of us is a piece of legislation which takes, at a time of a national unity crisis, the present level of support to the provincial governments and it says "we are going to cut that level of support even more in the future". It breaks its promises to the provinces with this piece of legislation, and assumes that somehow that is going to contribute to national unity.
Anybody who has any sensitivity, any sense of concern about the future unity of our country, has surely got to say to these people "for the sake of a united Canada, don't do this; don't destroy the promises that have been made in the past". These promises were broken last year, and this year the government has gone on to break them for a further three years, to 1994-95.
You cannot expect, if it continues in this way, to see medicare, which the people of this country care about so much, survive. You cannot squeeze a good system, a system which is performing so much better than its equivalent in the United States. The United States has a system where Americans spend over $2,200 U.S. per year per person for their coverage while Canadians spend under $1,600 per year per person. It costs on average for Americans $360 per day to stay in American hospitals, compared to $210 in Canada.
Here is a system that is helping our competitiveness, helping our capacity to deal effectively with competition from the United States, by giving us a much more effective, much more human, much more accessible program and the government is attacking it by cutting back the funds that are going to it.
My colleague, our health critic, is going to be talking more about this as this debate goes forward because this is one of the most dangerous parts of this piece of legislation. The government says it is going to be able to withhold other cash transfers. All that will do is increase the squeeze on the provinces, increase the conflicts with the provinces.

As we struggle with unity problems, is it wise to cut back transfer payments to the provinces? I do not think so, Madam Speaker.

There are other parts to this legislation too. There are amendments which reduce the ease with which members' salaries will increase. We have no problem with that. There are amendments to the Public Utilities Income Tkx Transfer Act. Some of my colleagues will be talking to that. There are amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. Some of my colleagues will be focusing on that. Over-all, what we have here in front of us is another example of the constipated, devastating approach that this government has been taking to management of our economy. People across this country are hurting and hurting badly as a result.
All I can hope is that this debate will bring this government to its senses, that it will somehow start to recognize that it must change direction for the future good of our country and of our people.
June 11, 1991

Madam Speaker, I would like to put a few words on the record with respect to the legislation which is before the House today, to amend certain acts in order to really enforce the budget that was brought in and, specifically, the federal transfers fiscal arrangements act, which really affects the money transferred to provincial governments from the federal treasury.
The Minister of Finance made a statement in this Chamber a few moments ago which I am going to disprove. I am going to lay on the Table of the House facts that are directly contrary to what this Minister of Finance said today and what the Government of Canada said in its budget. They said that although there were cuts to the provincial governments for education and health and equalization payments, the actual dollar figure was not cut. That is what the government is saying. It is saying that the rate of increase has been cut back, but that there is no actual dollar for dollar cut to the provincial treasuries.
I have with me the official charts given to me by officials from the Department of Finance. They show some interesting facts. They show that, for example, that the province of Newfoundland will receive for this year $16.9 million less than they received last year under equalization.
What is equalization? Equalization, as defined by the Minister of Finance, is, and I quote from a letter that he wrote to me.
-a formula set out in legislation that compares provincial governments in their abilities to raise revenues from the revenue sources typically used by all provincial governments.
In other words, a provincial government is sent every month a sum of money. The poorer provinces now, to make up for the revenues they could have received if they had the ability to raise money through taxes that the other provinces are able to raise through taxes, are given equalization.
That defines, then, what the poorer provinces are in Canada in total amounts of money. What are the poorer provinces in Canada, the top three?
The province that will receive the most money in equalization from the federal government is Quebec. Of the total equalization package of $8.4 billion this year, Quebec will receive about $4 billion, Manitoba about $1
Government Orders
billion, and Nova Scotia about $1 billion. Therefore, in total amounts of money being transferred to the provincial governments from the federal Treasury, the top three in total equalization to the poorer provinces are Quebec, Manitoba and Nova Scotia.
In looking at the figures year over year, here is the way they work out in equalization. The largest increase in equalization payments for this year will be to the province of Manitoba at $90 million more than it received last year. This is according to the federal Treasury. Then comes the Northwest Territories, which is is under what is called "territorial financing". It does not receive an equalization payment as a provincial government but will receive territorial financing of $90 million. Next comes Saskatchewan, which will receive an extra $70 million; then comes Quebec, which will receive an extra $60 million; then comes the territory of Yukon, which will receive an additional $36 million; and then there is New Brunswick; which will get an additional $25 million; Nova Scotia comes next and will receive an extra $23 million; then comes Prince Edward Island, which will get an additional $5 million.
Those are the increases in equalization for the year 1991-1992, as outlined by the Federal Department of Finance.
Madam Speaker, you will notice that I only read out nine provinces and two territories. I left out a province. I left out a province because that province is not receiving an increase. That province is receiving a decrease. It is not just a decrease of $1 million or $2 million or $3 million or $4 million or $5 million or even $10 million. No. It is a decrease of $20 million this year. Here it is on the official record, in French and English, if the Minister of Finance does not understand it. The province of Newfoundland will receive less money this year in federal equalization than it received last year.
Fet us not forget it is not just equalization payments we are talking about but the total transfers to the provinces. In other words, the federal government pays money to the poorer provinces to make up for the fact that they are poorer provinces and cannot raise the revenues from taxation that other provinces can raise. It is not only that. The transfers are also for health and education. They are for grants in lieu of property taxes, reciprocal taxation, public utilities, income tax transfers, statutory subsidies, youth allowance recovery, tax points for this and tax points for that. But if we add it all up, it is

called the total transfers to the provincial governments from the federal Treasury.
The total transfers to the provincial governments are interesting numbers. This upcoming year we will see total transfers of $36,472 billion, $36.4 billion. The provinces receiving the most in Canada are Quebec and Ontario at $10 billion apiece. It is then British Columbia at $3.2 billion, Alberta at $2.7 billion, Manitoba at $1.98 billion, Nova Scotia at $1.78 billion, New Brunswick at $1,623 billion, Saskatchewan at $1,453 billion, and down it goes to include the territories as well. Newfoundland is ninth. The big three in equalization payments, as I pointed out, are Quebec, Manitoba and Nova Scotia.
I mention all of that to show on the official record that the Minister of Finance is wrong. There is a province in Canada that is receiving less equalization this year than last year. There is a province in Canada that is receiving less in total transfers this year than last year, and that is the province of Newfoundland.
If that were not enough, another strange thing happened this year. You will notice that on these charts that I am going to table it says estimated federal transfers to the provinces, territories and municipalities for the fiscal year. The reason why it says estimated transfers is that these transfers are made prior to the federal government knowing how much is actually owed to the provincial governments.
In other words, at the beginning of every year the government makes an estimate for that year and sends a cheque in the mail toward the end of the month so that the provincial governments will get it at the end of the month. The total figure for the year is an estimate and at the end of the year the government then reassesses that estimate. After all of the figures are in, in 36 months hence, three years, it will determine the actual amount of money that should have gone to those provincial governments.
What happens from time to time under these fiscal arrangements is that provincial governments are either owed money or they sometimes have to pay back money to the federal Treasury.
Last March in the federal Department of Finance in Ottawa an audit was done on the fiscal transfers to the
provinces. They found out the amount of money that provinces get through taxation on cigarettes, booze, gasoline and all other taxes.
rrhey added it up and found the actual dollar figure that each province received, the amount the government paid them, the amount the provinces thought they were going to receive in equalization transfers and then the final accounting was done. At the end of March of last year the federal government found that there were four provinces in Canada who were overpaid, from three years ago. Those four provinces were Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland.
Do you know what that means? It means that now those provinces have to pay the money back. There is a formula for paying back the money and they have to pay it back at no more than $60 per head of population in any one year. Let us look at the figures. Who owes the money?
For all of Atlantic Canada in 1988 the Atlantic provinces owe $90 million to the federal Treasury. For 1989 they owe $85 million to the federal Treasury. What is interesting is that of the $90 million owed for the year 1988, the province of Newfoundland owes, according to the federal Department of Finance, $37 million. Thirty seven million dollars of the $90 million owed by the four Atlantic provinces was overpaid to the province of Newfoundland, according to the Department of Finance.
In 1989, of the $85 million that was overpaid to the four Atlantic provinces, it claims that Newfoundland was overpaid $34 million. As I explained a moment ago, the repayment schedule of limiting the amount of money to $60 per head of population per year, so as not to overburden a government every year, means that Newfoundland will be paying back that money for three fiscal years.
In other words, the only province in Canada that is paying back the federal treasury for money that the federal government claims was overpaid to them in 1988 and 1989, the only province that has to pay it back for this year and for a portion of next year, is the province of Newfoundland because the federal Treasury says: "You were paid too much money in 1988 and 1989".
June 11, 1991

Add those two facts together. Add together the fact that dollar for dollar the province of Newfoundland this year will receive far less than they got last year, and the fact that they now have to pay back millions of dollars. The cheques are sent out every two weeks, back to the federal government here in Ottawa for money that the federal government claims, and the books show the province was overpaid in 1988 and 1989.
If you were in a position to say: now, in which provincial government would I like to be the Minister of Finance? It certainly would not be the province of Newfoundland, would it? Here you are being cut back on your equalization payments, dollar for dollar, by the Government of Canada. You are being cut back on your transfer payments dollar for dollar and on top of that, you have to pay back money it claims was paid in this case to a previous government. Imagine that, a previous government. There was a Progressive Conservative government, a Tory government in power in the province of Newfoundland in 1988 and 1989.

and they are saying: "We are going to give you a lot less than you got last year, dollar for dollar". On top of that there is the federal government imposing a 7 per cent new tax that takes 7 per cent out of the economy of every provincial government in Canada.
I must say for the official record that I heard a newsman interview Premier Clyde Wells and ask him about the money owed. The premier said: "If Newfoundland owes it, then Newfoundland will pay it back. If we rightfully owe it on the books, in the accounting, then we will pay it back." Other leaders would have declared a day of mourning and had everybody in the province walking around with black arm bands, carrying coffins down the street. They would. Any other previous administration would have done that. But the premier of Newfoundland said that if we owe it we are going to pay it. You have to admire a man like that for his honesty and integrity, his apolitical approach to the entire question.
I think it is an outrageous thing for the Government of Canada to do and I ask them to do two things. First of all,forgive the overpayment. After all, we just forgave moneys that were owed to Canada by several foreign nations and several foreign banks. Secondly, and I will conclude with this, Madam Speaker, I know you are trying to get me to sit down; we should have a formula that says no province should actually lose money, dollar over dollar from last year, to ease the pain for those provincial administrations.

Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak at the second reading stage of Bill C-20.
It was not my intention to comment on federal payments to the province of Newfoundland, but after the hon. member's speech, I feel I should set the record straight.
First of all, federal transfer payments to the provinces, including Newfoundland, are statutory and subject to certain calculations, to ensure that annually, and I would

June 11, 1991
Government Orders
almost say in advance, the provinces receive the money to which they are entitled under a number of existing programs.
When I hear the hon. member complain that Newfoundland has to pay back money to the federal government, I may remind him that the amount Newfoundland received was more than the amount to which it was entitled after the final calculations were made. I will get back to this later.
So in this case, it is perfectly normal for Newfoundland to pay the money back to the federal government, as it would be for any other province, whether we are talking about Alberta or British Columbia or Quebec. All the provinces are governed by the same legislation. Madam Speaker, the hon. member also said-and I am not sure how he figured this out-that Newfoundland would receive less money this year or the year after. This is just not true. In 1991-92, Newfoundland will receive more money under all programs-I will elaborate on some of these later on-than it received in 1990-91. This applies to all programs, including equalization, established programs financing, and so forth.
I wanted to set the record straight because the hon. member got carried away by his subject, with figures that were probably inaccurate, but my point is, Newfoundland was not penalized in any way.
To get back to Bill C-20, the proposed legislation affects several areas. The two main ones are federal-provincial fiscal arrangements and the Parliament of Canada Act. When we talk about federal-provincial fiscal arrangements, we must be careful because there are several kinds. In Quebec, when we talk about federal money, the first word that comes to mind is equalization. This is one kind of transfer payment. There is also established programs financing.
Very briefly, established programs financing involves money that is distributed annually by the federal government to all provinces on an equal basis. Each province gets the same amount per capita, and whether I happen to live in Newfoundland, British Columbia or Quebec, the federal government sends the same amount.
Equalization-which is different-is a special program to help provinces who need more assistance in funding health care and education. Equalization payments are received annually by the four Atlantic provinces, Quebec and occasionally Manitoba.
And here is another distinction: federal money goes to the provinces in two forms: as tax points and as cash.
This year, the federal government will give Quebec about $11 billion. It does this through the equalization program and EPF, established programs financing. How does the government pay? That is indeed the question. There are two ways: tax points and cash. Mainly in Quebec, the amount paid in the form of tax points is much higher. Madam Speaker, perhaps you will remember that when you files your income tax return like all Quebecers, and I see it was a delightful experience, there was one line on the return for Quebec residents where it shows 16.5 per cent, because Quebec collects more income tax from its residents than the other provinces. This means that the amount on the cheque the federal government sends to the Province of Quebec is not as high, because the province has already collected the difference via the tax return you filed on April 30 like any good Quebecer.
So we have two programs under which Quebec receives money, and two ways in which the federal government pays the money to the province: income tax collected directly by the province from Quebec residents and the amount on the cheque sent by Ottawa.
Madam Speaker, recently there were reports and comments by various sources to the effect that in a few years, Quebec would no longer be receiving money from Ottawa. That is probably what will happen. It does not mean that the federal government gives the province less money. In fact-and I will quote the figures later on-the annual amount received by the Province of Quebec, like the amount received by the hon. member's Province of Ontario or by any other province, increases every year, but the amount on the cheque written by the federal government may go down because the province may be collecting more money directly in the form of income tax.
Madam Speaker, perhaps I may quote a few figures that are vital to this discussion and also to opposition members' understanding of Bill C-20 and that of the general public as well.
In 1984-85, Quebec received $8.1 billion from the federal government, which means $1,256 per capita. The federal government paid the province the equivalent of $1,256 per capita in 1984-85. For 1990-91, the amount is $10.1 billion, which means $1,503 per capita will be

received by Quebec in 1990-91, as money transferred by the federal government to the provinces.

What would it have been otherwise?
The hon. member says: what would it have been otherwise? That is not the point. The point is that annually, the federal government transfers more to the provinces percentage-wise that it spends on program spending. The federal government's expenditures are around 3 per cent per year, and we have maintained that so far, despite the fact that the opposition keeps telling us to reduce the deficit and at the same time spend more. We are working on the deficit, and we are maintaining increases in program spending at 3 per cent, the exception being transfers to the provinces that are now growing at a rate of almost 4 per cent per year.
So we have to keep these figures in mind. If we look at the provincial governments, Madam speaker, we see that the increase there is about 6 per cent. Well, the national debt is very national. It is the debt of all Canadians. Whether I live in British Columbia or Prince Edward Island, as a Canadian I have to cope with a problem that is called the national debt. Today, the national debt is more than $15,000 per individual, per Canadian. Each and everyone of us, from new born babies to senior citizens, is $15,000 in debt. Something must be done.
The measures taken by the federal government are in some cases draconian. I admit.
Last Friday, I took part in a lunchtime open line radio program at the CHLM radio station in Trois-Rivieres and the announcer, Michel Charland, was saying that Canadians feel they are paying a lot of taxes, if not too much. My reply was this: "It is true that we are heavily taxed, but we have many services and an enormous debt." This debt, Madam Speaker, has to be paid off; otherwise-if we keep increasing our spending by 6,7 or 8 per cent every year-the future generations will not be able to even dream of any new programs.
Just think, Madam Speaker, that 35 cents out of every tax dollar collected by the federal government is taken up to pay, not the capital, but the interest on this debt we inherited from the Liberal government. Let us call a spade a spade. When we came into office, the accumu-
Goverrvnent Orders
lated debt was $200 billion. Granted, it has increased. But, Madam Speaker, the national debt has grown by the amount of the interest payments we have had to make every year. Had it not been for this debt we inherited in 1984 and the interest to be paid on it, there would not be a annual deficit.
The Opposition gets angry, Madam Speaker, when we mention the debt they left us but it is the truth. There is a debt and we have to live with it.
But, I would like to come back to Bill C-20, if I may. The good thing about this, Madam Speaker, is that it wakes them up to hear me talk about their debt and our debt. I was just trying to explain to my colleague opposite that, had it not been for the interest we had to pay on these $200 billion, we would not have ended up with an annual deficit and, with no annual deficit, the debt would not have increased. It is as simple as that. So, 35 cents out of every tax dollar goes to pay the interest on our debt, the debt of all Canadians.
Madam Speaker, the federal government must continue on the course set out in 1984 and administer while recognizing, provincial needs regarding education, health, etc. Let me give you more figures, Madam Speaker. In 1992-93, Quebec will receive $10.8 billion from the federal government. That's $1,575 per capita. You will remember that I said that, this year, it is $1,503.
So, there is indeed an annual increase, and I could give the figures for all the provinces, Madam Speaker, because they will all get more next year that they got this year. Now, Bill C-20 calls for a reduction in this increase, so that the provinces can do their share and help us deal with the national debt and deficit problem we are faced with.
We could increase transfer payments further. That could be done, but the question would remain: where shall the money come from? If the national debt could be paid off tomorrow morning, which would mean no more deficit, we would not have to pay interest charges anymore. We would then have about $30 billion available every year to create programs to help Canadians, $30 billion to develop new programs, create jobs and make life yet easier for the people of Quebec and Canada. This is the amount we have to use right now to pay interest charges. The limit on the credit card has been reached,
