Madam Speaker, as it was in 1984. And what we have been trying to do ever since is precisely to pay off the interest on the debt and, by 1994, no longer have to borrow so that we can start paying back our debt the normal way, the way a country is normally administered. That is one of the aspects covered in Bill C-20.
As you know, Madam Speaker, in 1984, the federal government was spending $15 billion more, not $15 million but $15 billion-we are not talking peanuts here-every year than was coming in. The Canadian people were getting $15 billion more, in programs of all kinds, thant they were paying for in taxes. This contributed to the annual increase in the deficit and the national debt.
This year, we will be spending $10 billion less on programs than we will be collecting in taxes. Now, that's good management! That is what all the people who are watching us do, how the head of the family manages the household budget: they spend a little less than they earn and set some money aside. And that is what we have managed to do over the past five years. In just five years, we turned a $15 billion deficit in a $10 billion profit, a $25 billion improvement. It was no easy task. How did we do it? We made unpopular but necessary cuts and increased taxes a tad. But 70 percent of these $25 billion that have changed columns come from cuts within government, while 30 percent come from increased taxes. The tax increase was only 30 percent, not 100 percent, as the Opposition said. To achieve this turnaround, we brought government spending down by 70 percent, and more needs to be done, Madam Speaker. All is not well yet. There is one major outstanding problem.
There is nothing I would like better, Madam Speaker, than to hear the Opposition say they agree with Bill C-20. The time has come to work all together, the NDP and the Liberals along with the government, to settle the financial situation of the country. Among industrialized countries, Canada is the one with the largest debt. Every Canadian man and woman is $15,000 into debt without having received anything for it. I think that of members opposite for Bill C-20 the support.
There is another aspect of this legislation that I have heard hardly any comment about so far and that is the freeze on the salaries payable to the members of Parliament, including government members, opposition members, Cabinet members and the Prime Minister. Bill C-20 contains a provision whereby, next year, the percentage increase of the MPs and ministers' salaries would not exceed the average percentage in the public service of Canada. That is to say that, if federal civil servants do not get a raise, neither will the hon. members. And you are well aware that we are not necessarily planning on giving civil servants a raise.
So, I hope the opposition will support this piece of legislation to set an example for all Canadians. By voting against Bill C-20, they will be voting for a raise. I think that, in these difficult times, as they take such malicious pleasure to point out, the members opposite should join members of Cabinet and government members to show leadership and do what has to be done.
The other provision of Bill C-20 which did not get much publicity is the four-year freeze on the operating and capital budgets of all federal departments. This means that if next year a department wants to set up something new or increase its operations, it will not be able to get new money. It will not be able to knock on Treasury Board's door or ask the Minister of Finance or anyone else. It can't say: I need extra money for my budget because I have a special item. That won't work. All capital spending and operating budgets are frozen.
If they want to get around that, it will take another bill to allow department X to spend more than was provided in its budget for 1990-91. It would take another bill, so I imagine that frozen means frozen.
In concluding, Madam Speaker, and I see you are signalling that my time is almost up, I want to make it quite clear that all monies collected under the GST, as well as all revenue from privatization operations, will be used only to reduce our national debt. This money will not be used for new programs, new budgets or anything else. I think that is important, and that it will help improve our quality of life and the economic situation in this country.

Madam Speaker, I would like to make a few comments and perhaps pose a couple of questions to the hon. member in debating this bill.
June 11, 1991

I think the hon. member is trying to make a case that Canadians should be preoccupied with the deficit of money, but not the deficit of lives. In this bill there will be a cut in funding to provinces, a cut in education, a cut in health care. Many other complications are also emanating from this bill before us today.
In matters of education, I would like to indicate to the House that a consequence of cuts in funding to transfer payments to the provinces will be a cut to post-secondary education. We already know that over one million children are poor in this country and that one of the consequences of poverty is dropping out of school. We have heard Canadians tell us, and it has been debated in this House, that we should be competitive in the world. I ask the hon. member, if we do not have an educated citizenry how can we have a competitive citizenry?
In pursuing the economic argument, I wonder if the hon. member has read the Senate report on poverty released in January of this year. There is a beautiful analysis in the document telling us that if you spent $5 billion today for the poor of our country and for the poor children, you would reduce the number of school dropouts by 186,000. Over a period of 20 years there would be a net return of some $27 billion.
I would like to ask the hon. member if he disagrees with this well-researched analysis. Will he agree that it is not deficit spending to spend $5 billion today when you can, in return, get $27 million in productivity, in revenues, in payment to the unemployment insurance program, in reduced claims from the unemployment insurance program and in reduced claims from social assistance programs?
I would like to see the economics of this government.
While I am on my feet, I would just like to ask the hon. member: What is the distribution of the national debt? He alluded to our debt being equivalent to the debt of every single Canadian. I think that is a very simplistic analysis, and I think the hon. member must answer to Canadians. To whom do we owe money? I am told by the Library of Parliament that at least 20 per cent of the total national debt is owed to the Bank of Canada. Who owns the Bank of Canada? The Government of Canada.

Madam Speaker, I see I have very little time to answer the hon. member's question.
I would like to start by repeating a very important point which the hon. member does not seem to have understood. He says we are cutting amounts transferred to the provinces. I gave an example which shows we are not cutting, only reducing the annual increase in transfer payments. A cut-the people of Trois-Rivieres will understand-is when you earn $500 a week and your boss says: Well, now you will get $400 a week. That is a cut. However, if you earn $500 a week, and you were supposed to get $550 but your boss says: No, you won't

June 11, 1991
Government Orders
get more than $525, that is not a cut, because I am now earning more than I was earning before.
So transfer payments to the provinces are not being cut but the increase in those payments is being reduced. I hope the hon. member understands, because if we are not talking about the same thing, there is bound to be a problem, whether a person is asking or answering the question. So transfer payments to the provinces are not being cut but there is a reduction in the usual increase.
The hon. member also wanted to know to whom we owe all this money. We owe this debt partly to Canadians and partly to people outside Canada. But this is all part of the old Liberal philosophy, Madam Speaker, which maintains that the debt doesn't matter because we owe the money to Canadians. If I owe my brother $100,000 and my sister $200,000 and my father $300,000, and I have no money at all, when I go to the bank for a loan, can I tell them: No, I don't owe any money, I just owe money to my family? When I open my books for the bank, Madam Speaker, it doesn't matter who lent me the money. I still owe it!
The same is true here. Canada's debt which is partly owed to Canadians and partly to people outside the country is still a debt, whether we owe the money to Canadians or to non-Canadians. And internationally, when other countries look at Canada and its debt, they say: Canada, your debt is $400 billion. They don't care who lent us the money. It is still $400 billion.
I went to Japan recently, and we talked about this. They don't care who lent us the money. Their question is: Do you owe that much? Yes, we do.
Madam Speaker, I think we should get rid of this Liberal philosophy that it doesn't matter as long as we borrow from Canadians. Madam Speaker, this is very serious! And when I say that the federal government owes $400 billion, I am not talking about the money owed by the various provincial governments. If I happen to be an investor looking for a country to invest my money, and I look at Canada and I do some figuring, well, I don't think we have that much to offer, compared with other countries. And that is why we must deal with this problem.
Madam Speaker, my time has expired. Thank you for your patience.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to participate in debate of Bill C-20, an act to amend certain statutes to implement the budget tabled in Parliament February 26, 1991. It is debate on the values and ideals which are fundamental to our society and the institutions through which we maintain a national standard. These ideals and values are quickly being eliminated from the face of Canada.
The Minister of Finance, in this budget just as in the last budget, is continuing on course in passing the buck to the provinces of this country. The federal government has simply transferred their federal fiscal problems to other levels of government.
At this time I would like to draw attention to a statement made in the House, since we are great at going back 10 or so years, by the member of Parliament for Etobicoke Centre in March, 1982, in which he criticized the government of the day for shifting the financial burden to the provinces by reducing transfer payments. This is still true today.
The current five-year freeze on the EPF, Established Programs Financing, will substantially reduce the funds available to the provinces. By freezing transfers to the provinces, the government is clearly and systematically destroying Canada's health care and post-secondary educational systems at a time when the U.S.A. is trying and is hopefully going to find ways to implement a health care system in that country.
Each year as the population increases, students realize the necessity for higher education and the demand for classroom space escalates. While the number of instructors per students declines, the funding diminishes.
Students now face higher tuition fees. UPEI, opening in September, is predicting that tuition increases will be 15 per cent. Add that to the fact that there are not many jobs out there for students. There are higher tuition fees, overcrowded classrooms and the burden of other cost-maintenance measures which the smaller provinces are forced to administer.
Federal funding in post-secondary education is imperative to keep tuition fees from becoming unaffordable for most Canadians and to ensure better access to higher education for low-income people. This is a must.
**
June 11, 1991

We must not let our education system become a system for only the wealthy people in this country.
No wonder we have a problem with national unity. The federal government is forcing the provinces to compete with one another for insufficient funding.
Over the next two years Prince Edward Island will lose $12 million in transfer payments. This will spell higher taxes and fewer social programs, and most of all, it will sever Atlantic Canada's lifeline.
The writing is clearly on the wall. Social programs and medicare appear targeted as the first to go. Smaller provinces and territories will not be able to hold the system together or support the development of new or innovative health programs. How can the federal government expect a small province to maintain national health care standards when it slashes the EPF?
I again draw your attention to the member for Etobicoke Centre when in 1982 he stated that all Canadians will suffer from a cut in services for post-secondary education and health resulting from cuts to Established Programs Financing.
As our health care system advances, we find people living longer lives and the costs of high technology and medical equipment rising. With cuts to transfer payments, the provinces are forced either to slash essential services or impose higher taxes on the already overburdened taxpayer.
To cite again my hon. colleague for Etobicoke Centre, the government does not seem to realize that there is only one taxpayer who pays the taxes for the federal, provincial and municipal governments. The taxpayer does not care where services come from; what the taxpayer wants is to see service provided to meet his or her needs. As my hon. colleague stated almost 10 years ago, this government is showing utter contempt for that taxpayer.
At one time Canada maintained national standards for health care and other basic services, but no more. In the last budget the federal government vowed to maintain national standards through new legislation. Indeed, we now have a national standard, a national standard which is the slow death of medicare. It has become the standard in every province.
Government Orders
We need a strong federal presence in all social programs to ensure that Canadians will have access to similar services and similar benefits no matter where they live. A strong federal presence is impossible without a strong federal financial commitment. Without federal leverage, provinces can and probably will impose user fees for medical and hospital services. This is a backward step which will deter poor people from seeking the care they need and are entitled to.
On the other hand, it could be difficult for Canadians to have full medicare coverage when travelling outside their home provinces. Has the government forgotten that federal funding in the field of health was the incentive that lead to the development of medicare in all provinces and territories? Regional disparities have always been a problem throughout our history. Without substantial financial contributions from the federal government, regional disparities will continue to grow and affect our national standard of living.
There is no conceivable means whereby provinces like Prince Edward Island will be able to afford half of the meagre social programs existing today, unless there is strong federal financial commitment to uphold the national standard.
It will be difficult, much more difficult for poorer provinces to provide accessible and affordable programs to their residents.
In my riding of Hillsborough, a great many people are on fixed or low incomes or are seasonally employed. I strongly emphasize this is neither by choice nor by laziness. These people now have the added burden of paying the GST. The federal government will not even reimburse the rebate credit to those taxpayers under 19.
In the past, cash payments from the federal government have made it possible for Canadians to have highly developed systems of medicare and post-secondary education. Any cuts which threaten the integrity of these programs are a direct affront to the fundamental values and ideals of the Canadian people.
I would conclude by saying that Prince Edward Islanders are fully aware of the deficit problem that Canada is facing and are more than willing to pay their fair share. The federal government must realize that it cannot pass its fiscal mismanagement on to the provincial and municipal governments of this country.

Mr. Speaker, although it has been over a month since Canadian truckers, frustrated by this government's inaction, blockaded major highways in Ontario, the government has yet to deal or to act with the mess that deregulation has caused. Yet there is much it could do if it wanted to.
For example, deregulation has resulted in making $100 million worth of transport licences worthless. This has had a devastating impact on a trucking firm's equity base.
In the United States in 1980 when the trucking industry was deregulated, the American government gave its carriers a three-year accelerated write-off on these licences. I call on the government to do this in Canada for our tuckers and to offer loan guarantees for these authorities until that time at which the firm's equity base can be restored.
Truckers cannot afford to wait any longer for this government to act. As we saw a month ago, if this government does not act it could be a long, hot, slow summer on our nation's highways.

Mr. Speaker, a disconcerting new phrase has crept into Canada's national unity debate which frequently is used to misrepresent the values of our official languages legislation. That phrase is "enforced bilingualism". Those words tend to imply that bilingualism is a mandatory requirement which is imposed, perhaps unfairly or unjustly, upon individual Canadians.
In reality the reverse is true. Rather than imposing either or both official languages upon any citizen, the concept of bilingualism actually provides the freedom for each one of us to live completely in only one language in Canada if that may be our wish. Therein lies the basic value of bilingualism.
The Official Languages Act provides that Canadians can and must be served by the federal government in the language of their choice. The intent of that legislation is linguistic freedom, not linguistic imposition. To be sure, the concept of bilingualism does impose special linguistic capabilities upon government in order to serve the people. The fundamental purpose remains, however, to make individual Canadians free to be unilingual and to live fully in this country in either English or French.
To describe the concept as "enforced bilingualism" is to really miss the true values of linguistic freedom which must be inherent in a generous and tolerant Canadian society.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday we were reminded that the feminization of poverty is not an academic theory but rather an undisputed and acknowledged fact.
Jean Swanson of the National Anti-Poverty Organization, at the government's own symposium on women and the law, noted that many women today are forced by Canada's inadequate social support system to commit crimes of survival such as writing bad cheques, shoplifting and prostitution.
The federal government is retreating into the Middle Ages by cutting social programs. This government sees support for low income Canadians as charity, not as a right, not as an entitlement. It has cut unemployment insurance, capped the Canada Assistance Plan, and kept the minimum wage below a living wage.
All Canadians, and especially single parent women and their dependent children, are being sunk deeper into poverty. How much more evidence does this government need before it realizes that antiquated social policies are
*
June 11, 1991

forcing all Canadians, and especially women, to make impossible choices just to survive?
This is deplorable and Canadians should be outraged.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to bring to the attention of Canadians the efforts of the First Combat Engineer Regiment and its ongoing activities in the Persian Gulf.
The fighting in the Persian Gulf is over and the majority of the media has gone on to other issues, but the very important and extremely dangerous duties of our engineers continue. It is not a glamorous job, but it is an integral part of the United Nations effort to restore peace and safety to the border area between Kuwait and Iraq.
What is this onerous task that takes 250 members of our engineering regiment from their home at Canadian Forces Base Chilliwack? What is it that causes families to be separated and worry to be the order of the day? These very brave men and women are clearing unexploded ordinances from the Kuwait-Iraq border so that unsuspecting people will not get hurt. These people are finding and defusing bombs. They are laying their lives on the line every day, doing whatever it takes to ensure the safety of others.
I pay tribute to the brave Canadians of Chilliwack's First Combat Engineer Regiment. I wish them Godspeed and safety in their duties. I pay tribute to the families in Chilliwack who worry and wait for the return of their loved ones. I wish them strength. Canadians thank them for their service.

Mr. Speaker, English speaking Canadians who live in Quebec, Canada's French speaking province, a province of cultural plurality and diversity, also want their rights as Canadian citizens respected.
The English of Quebec believe it is time to reaffirm their place in a dynamic Quebec and a dynamic Canada
and want to stop the outflow of Quebecers, young Quebecers.
We are uncomfortable with the removal of our rights of presence and we want Bill 178 removed. It is disrespectful, offensive and neither reasonable nor justified. Removing Bill 178 would let all Canadians feel at home in Quebec and anywhere else in Canada for speaking and working in French or English is an economic, social and cultural asset.
Language itself is not the issue. It is rights and freedoms in a democracy that are at stake.
I sincerely hope the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs will remember in discussions with Premier Bourassa and other leaders the profound Canadian belief that you advance neither society nor its majority by diminishing the rights of any minority: English, French, aboriginal or any other minority group in our society.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian government's indebtedness is a serious problem, but it is not as disastrous as we describe it so often. In fact, it is a problem which Ottawa controls much better today than it did a few years back, in spite of accounting appearances and large figures.
In certain respects, we are doing the same thing as with the assessment of the Free Trade Agreement between Canada and the United States.
According to a recent study by the Bank of Canada, the Canadian economy has shown in 1990 a positive balance of $4.3 billion in foreign investments. It was the first time in 16 years that Canada had such a positive record. According to some economists, this positive balance is due only to the fact that Canadian investments abroad were lower last year. However the Bank of Canada believes that it is a positive effect of the Free Trade Agreement, which made Canada more attractive to foreign investors.
Mr. Speaker, one fact remains: Canada never had such a positive balance in 16 years.

Mr. Speaker, Georges Erasmus is retiring today as Chief of the AFN, that is, the Assembly of First Nations.
I have known Georges Erasmus from about 15 years ago when I was with the Berger commission up in the north. At that time Canada got its first view of an incredibly talented generation of native Canadian leaders. Georges Erasmus, a Dene from the Northwest Territories, is one of those leaders.
I wish to acknowledge in the House of Commons his work in the constitutional conferences, his administration of the AFN, and his energy and determination on behalf of Canada's first peoples. He is a tough and effective foe of government no matter what the stripe of that government, and he warned us of explosive grievances in the native communities.
I want to express the personal hope that Mr. Erasmus will spend a little time, perhaps in the Gray Lakes area of the Northwest Territories, will mellow out a bit, and will come back to serve the first nations and to serve Canada as he has done so effectively in the past.

Mr. Speaker, Alberta's Premier Getty says that we need greater decentralization but recent public hearings found that Albertans favour a stronger, not a weaker, federal government.
Quebec minister Remillard says that his province will not participate in a constituent assembly, but a recent poll says 57 per cent of Quebec residents favour holding a constituent assembly.
If the recommendations of a constituent assembly were subjected to ratification by a federally sponsored referendum tabulated on a province by province basis, the real feelings of the people of each province would be made abundantly clear to their federal and provincial representatives.
After all, Premier Getty and Mr. Remillard certainly would not be the first Canadian politicians whose views did not correspond to the wishes of the people they were elected to represent.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday a number of members of Parliament from both sides of this House met with the Drug Legislation and Enforcement Policy Committee of the Toronto Mayor's Thsk Force on Drugs. The municipal politicians need our help federally in two ways.
I want to know why this government, despite repeated requests, has done nothing? When will the Minister of Justice return the money used in undercover operations to the municipal police? Currently the police invest money for the undercover purchase of drugs. When the dealers are busted the money is kept by the federal government. It should be returned to the community to continue to fight against drugs.
Also, there must be a full review made of the Supreme Court Decision in the Duarte case. The police were told that the use of the audio and audio-visual taping equipment was not allowed, but they need that tool as undercover backup.
We are going to lose a whole generation of children unless we stop delaying and start to work to win the war against drugs.

Mr. Speaker, crossborder shopping is a form of tax revolt now being performed by thousands of Canadians. Let me point out that these Canadians believe they have every right to cross the border and shop in the U.S. despite the ruinous effects on Canadian business, but cross-border shoppers have no right to think they can be cross-border smugglers.
I want to rise today and praise the Minister of National Revenue. He has invested many hours in understanding the complexities of this problem and in listening to people living in border communities.
June 11, 1991

Now he has taken action. Soon cross-border smugglers will face additional personnel when they return to Canada and stiff new penalties on those goods they have tried to hide. Cross-border smugglers should no longer be above the law. They should not penalize the rest of Canadian taxpayers by tiying to avoid paying the taxes which support the great services in this country. Crossborder smugglers must be shown the way, and the minister has had the guts to stand up and do exactly that.

Mr. Speaker, today, June 11, marks Miners' Memorial Day in my riding of Cape Breton. Miners' Memorial Day, also known as Davis' Day, is a day to honour the many coal miners who have fallen victim to the hazards of coal mining.
The coal mines have been a part of our history on the Island and they have claimed many lives. The cold, dark, and dreary pit has taken many a father, a brother, an uncle and yes, many sons.
Today we honour those brave men and we give special thought to the families who remember this day with great sadness and loss.
Mining has changed through the years but yet the mines and the miners are still a pride for all of Cape Breton. We look at our coal mines with a sense of respect and yes, a sense of fear.
I would like to join with my constituents on this Miners' Memorial Day in remembering those who were lost and to pray for the safety of those who still carry on the great tradition of the Cape Breton coal miner.

Mr. Speaker, as we are all aware, the environment is an issue that affects us all. It transcends all boundaries, be they geographical, political or ideological.
Ensuring a healthy future for our environment demands a tremendous level of co-operation. The Fraser
River clean-up, announced June 1 in my riding of Delta, is the product of such co-operation.
Many groups, from environmentalists to industry, municipal, provincial and federal governments, have all played important roles in putting this clean-up program together.
The challenge now will be to build on the partnerships that have been established and to extend them to involve everyone who lives or works in the Fraser watershed. As the Minister for the Environment has said, the Fraser River is at a critical stage. By acting together and by acting now, we can save the Fraser for future generations to use and enjoy.
The headline in Vancouver Province reads: "Good news for fish". The $100 million clean-up plan is good news not just for fish, but for everyone in British Columbia.

Mr. Speaker, the blueberry industry of Nova Scotia has grown from a million pounds production in 1953 to about 20 million pounds production today. The value to the province each year is in the area of $30 million. Most of the blueberry crop is processed and exported, making it the most valuable exported horticultural crop in Atlantic Canada.
Considering this tremendous growth, the value to the economy, and that it is a major export competing with products from other countries, it was disappointing when the Department of Agriculture research station in Nap-pan, Nova Scotia discontinued research on blueberries a few years ago. The industry is now concerned that the remaining research being done at the Kentville research station is being threatened.
Research is being done on varieties, chemicals, production and harvesting. Research includes machinery and materials and in the past has resulted in significant strides ahead in blueberry production.
It is absolutely necessary that the Department of Agriculture continue this research if the industry is to continue to grow and be competitive.

Mr. Speaker, on Saturday in Halifax at the National Convention of the New Democratic Party, a resolution was passed that gives a clear indication that the Canadian shipbuilding industry will be taken seriously by a New Democratic government.
This resolution gives balanced support to all aspects of the industry-construction, supply of components, training, labour-and states that amendments will be made to the Canadian Shipping Act that will require Canadian ships to be built in Canadian shipyards by Canadian workers, then to be crewed by Canadians when carrying Canadian goods.
At the moment any ship built anywhere in the world can call itself Canadian as long as it flies the Canadian flag. This is wrong and is damaging the survival of the struggling Canadian shipbuilding and repair industry.
With the implementation of this resolution, that situation will change. For the first time the shipbuilding industry in this country has the assurance that a government of Canada will do what it can to protect the industry.

Mr. Speaker, it is very said to read the June Globe and Mail report of the environmental embarrassment that is the Barbara Weit River in western Prince Edward Island.
Choked by potato processing waste starch from the Irving owned Cavendish Farms plant and raw sewage from the town of Kensington, the river will not even grow seaweed.
Would it not have been nice during Environment Week to announce that federal and provincial governments would support and encourage those good corporate citizens, the Irvings, in building a fuel ethanol plant utilizing cull potatoes and this starch waste rather than putting up a $10 million sewage treatment plant.
The Irvings could then use this ethanol as a source of [DOT]octane for their gasoline operations while providing diversified employment for the Summerside region.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Minister of National Health and Welfare.
For months now, his government has been denying that transfer payments to the provinces for health care and education are being cut. We know now, following the tabling of documents by the Quebec Health Minister yesterday, that in six years transfer payments to Quebec will be reduced to nothing, zero, zilch.
Is the government now willing to admit that these cuts are threatening our universal medicare system?
Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health
and Welfare): Mr. Speaker, we will never point out enough how the hon. member for Hamilton East is ill informed and how much she is consistently distorting the facts.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member must know that transfer payments to the provinces in the health field come under two headings: cash transfers and tax point transfers.
In 1977, when her party was in power, the government of the day granted, to Quebec in particular, additional tax points to give, I presume, more responsibilities and more flexibility. This is why, starting in 1996, Mr. Speaker, all transfers from the federal government will come to Quebec as tax points that it will be able to manage as it pleases.
I wish the hon. member would tell the people from Quebec who are listening that she is against them managing their own health care system, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Prime Minister.
Canadian taxpayers want to send one message to the minister's finance meeting, one clear, unanimous message: We are paying too much tax to too many governments.
June 11, 1991

Can the government explain how increasing the number of tax collectors will make the system fairer for ordinary Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. Acting Leader of the Opposition would agree that we do have a serious fiscal problem in this country. I think all governments, federal and provincial, are addressing the fact that we must try to weed out any inefficiencies in the system and try to deliver our services as a government, as all governments, in a more effective and efficient way.
On that score, all governments agree with that fundamental philosophy. It is not a matter of cutting back services. It is a matter of trying to deliver the same standard of services but to do it in a more effective and efficient manner.

Mr. Speaker, according to the study released yesterday by the Quebec Minister of Finance, from 1990 to 1995 the federal share of health care costs will be reduced from 40 per cent to 32 per cent. It is on a downward, slippery slope that is causing a crisis in Canadian health care.
I want to ask the Minister of Finance: Is not his underlying agenda in fact to reduce transfer payments to the point where the federal government will no longer be responsible for universal health care? Does he not plan in fact to make the provinces responsible financially in that area as well?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member knows that in this fiscal year some $37 billion will be transferred to the provinces in the form of cash and tax points. That number is going to increase each yea,r not decrease.
As a matter of fact, for the next five years there will be increases in the order of 3.7 per cent per annum and that is built upon annualized increases of 4.7 per cent per year per capita for the have provinces and 5.5 per cent per year per capita for the have not provinces.
Not only has the growth been increasing over the last five years, but it will continue to increase over the next five years.
Oral questions

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Yesterday, Sidbec-Dosco announced 600 lay-offs, 275 of which are in my riding, in Ville Emard. The reason is obvious. I quote from the president of the company:
The dollar is killing us. It is the great culprit. American steel is
coming into Canada in full swing and at a very low price.
While this government is closing its eyes, companies are closing their doors. My question is as follows: How long will the government stick to its suicidal policies? How many more plants, Mr. Speaker, will have to close their doors before Canada knocks on St. Jude's door?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a lot of respect for the hon. member as a businessman and an entrepreneur. It would be nice to know what value he would place on the Canadian dollar and how he would go about sustaining that.
He knows very well that many factors contribute to the value of the dollar, namely the confidence within the Canadian economy both from an economic and a political point of view, the relative rate of interest, the relative rate of inflation, commodity prices, and the capital exchange market.
All those things have an effect upon the value of the dollar. Having regard to all those things, I would be interested in knowing how the hon. member would set the value of the dollar, what value he would set it at, and how he would sustain it.
Mr. Speaker, right after the next election we will answer those questions.
Hear, hear.

If you cannot answer them, then step down and let somebody else take the job who can.

June 11, 1991
Oral questions
That answer is absolute nonsense. It is wanton and callous. Since 1980, the U.S. government has funnelled over $30 billion a year to the U.S. steel industry while this government's only counter has been to hike our dollar to a suicidal 87 cents.
Let there be no mistake. The government can drop interest rates by a further two points. It can tell the world that enhancing our manufacturing base is as important as targeting a tax induced inflation.
There is only one issue. This government can provide our steel industry with a level playing field. Why won't it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to note that when I put the question to the hon. member all we saw was an absolute cop-out.
We know very well that consistent with the Liberal tradition we would end up with interest rates of 22 per cent and an inflation rate of 13 per cent.
I find it passing strange that the hon. member argues with the fact that there is confidence in the Canadian dollar, confidence in the Canadian economy and confidence in Canada as a political entity.
Why is he trying to downgrade and degrade the Canadian economy and the confidence that investors have in the country?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
Almost a year ago, I proposed on the floor of this House that we need to have a new process for building the Constitution. We need to have a process that we felt would succeed and that would have legitimacy and the faith of the Canadian people.
At the time I proposed that we should look at a process like a constituent assembly. At that time the Prime Minister said that he thought it was an idea worth consideration. Yet, in advance of the Beaudoin-Edwards report and in advance of the Spicer commission report, the government appears to have totally rejected that idea.
Why has the Prime Minister rejected the idea of having a more open process so that Canadians can be heard and listened to in the constitutional process?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (President of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada and Minister Responsible for Constitutional Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all of us in the House were interested in the quite constructive and complex discussions on national unity that occurred at the recent meeting of the New Democratic Party in Halifax.
I think that underlines the difficulty of the issues we are facing and also the importance of dealing with those in an innovative and a tolerant way. I personally want to congratulate the leader and her party on the way in which they approached those complex issues.
We have not at all ruled out a more open process. Quite the contrary. What we have done is taken the decision that at a time when we are seeking to restore confidence in this country it would be useful for us to draw the best from a parliamentary system that has served us by and large well, but also to add to that other elements that might ensure that people who feel excluded now will feel included in decisions affecting the Constitution and the future of our country.

Mr, Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs.
He is right that at my party's convention this weekend we were able to bring together people from very different parts of the country with disparate views, and it was tough. He is right, it is tough. However, after a whole day of talking about national unity and what we could come to agree on, I have renewed my faith and even strengthened my faith that everyday Canadians have something useful to say on the Constitution and that we have to look for a way to include them.
Yes, we have to include politicians as they were included in that discussion on the weekend. It is not a question of by-passing elected politicians at all. In fact what I am proposing is that we have a process that includes elected politicians from all three levels and adds to it the best of the other groups that have felt excluded so that we have one voice to look at the Constitution and the future of this country.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (President of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada and Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that the question has to do with whether the government is prepared to look at methods that can combine the elements that the leader of the New Democratic Party has just referred to, and the answer to that is yes.
June 11, 1991

I look forward to the opportunity to do two things: first, to discuss with her some of the ways in which that can be done in the proposal we are putting forward and, second, I look forward to reading the reports of the Beaudoin-Edwards committee which we expect will be before us on or before July 1.

Mr. Speaker, my point however is: if we are going to start a new process, let us start it in a new way right from the beginning.

At this point in time, the government is suggesting a committee made up of only politicians, including a large number of non-elected senators. That committee will simply have to study the government's proposals. Will the government consider replacing that totally inadequate process with a new one, and agree to consult other political parties and start that new process now, right from the beginning?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (President of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada and Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question here is if we are ready to abandon a process I have discussed in general terms with other parties, as well as native leaders, a committee representing women in Canada, the Canadian Ethnocultural Council, and the premiers.
No, we do not intend to abandon an approach based on our parliamentary institutions, but we are perfectly open to suggestions that would give our fellow Canadians the opportunity to get more involved and participate fully. I have already discussed such approaches with, for example, native leaders.
I am prepared to consider some other solutions, but in a country like ours, when you discuss the importance of our traditions, of our institutions, I think it would be best to use our parliamentary system as the basis for our approach.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to pose a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Oral questions
Yesterday when I asked the whereabouts of the secret memo that had been lost in the office of the former Secretary of State for External Affairs, the present minister said:
We are in the process of looking for the document within the
department-
The minister has had three months to look for that document. This is a document that goes to the very heart of the credibility and responsibility of this government.
How can the government and the minister be so cavalier and casual about a secret document that has been lost in the bowels of her department for over three months?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can only repeat what I said yesterday. I might say that because this memo did not come in the normal way and did not have the normal routing slip on it, it is a little harder to trace. We are looking for it. What can I say?

Mr. Speaker, if the minister was at all serious about this matter, she would know that this memo came in an envelope marked "Secret." Those of us on this side of the House take that seriously, even if the minister does not.
Considering how important it is to get to the truth of this matter, is the minister prepared, if she cannot find the document, to ask the RCMP to come in so that they could find the document and Canadians can know the truth?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member actually took his job as seriously as I take mine, he might have discovered that since the time I became minister other serious things are going on in the world, not one of which he has asked a question about.

Mr. Speaker, on May 16 the Secretary of State for External Affairs said she welcomed a parliamentary inquiry into the Al-Mashat affair. On the same day she said the government was prepared for full disclosure.

June 11, 1991
Oral questions
Yesterday the government House leader told the press that it was pointless for the parliamentary inquiry to continue and that the government would be moving to shut down the committee this afternoon.
My question is for the Prime Minister. Since Parliament has clearly yet to finish its inquiry into this matter, will the Prime Minister give an undertaking to the House that the government will stick to its promise of a full inquiry?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member has misinterpreted what I said to the press. I did not say the government would be closing down the committee, I said it was up to the committee. The facts are on the table. She knows it, everybody knows it. The committee will decide what to do.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is also for the Prime Minister. Given the fact that astounding new revelations are coming to light on the Al-Mashat case on a daily basis, we want to know what the government is trying to hide. Will the Prime Minister give his assurances that the inquiry will continue, and that the committee will be allowed to continue its work to get to the bottom of this affair.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: What is astounding is how they trivialize Parliament by these types of questions.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance with respect to cross-border shopping.
The Canadian Labour Marketing Productivity Centre has reported that the Canadian dollar is now worth 11 per cent more on purchases in the United States than it was in 1980.
Why does the government not cut interest rates more forcefully so as to reduce the value of the dollar and help Canadian border communities in that way.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows that in order to bring interest rates down and to
keep them down over the long term, you have to get the fundamentals right, that is attacking the inflationary pressures, inflationary psychology and expectations and that is what we are doing. As a result, interest rates have come down by over five percentage points since a year ago and the spread has narrowed between the United States and Canada from a high of about 5.5 per cent or
5.6	per cent to about 2.5 per cent. I am sure the hon. member would suggest that is a good track record. If we can keep on that track and continue to fight the root causes of inflation, hopefully we will see interest rates come down further still. That is the key to growth, that is the key to jobs and and that is the key to prosperity.

A supplementary, Mr. Speaker.
There is no doubt that the government has created a problem. Thanks to the GST, cross-border trips are up an incredible 22 per cent in the first four months of this year.
Why does this government rely on the big stick approach, which has been announced by the Minister of National Revenue? Why does it not change its economic policies so that people do not have to vote against its high tax, high dollar and high interest rate policy by cross-border shopping?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance just answered that question.
Since the member makes reference to my big stick approach, I had assumed that my announcement yesterday was going in the right direction until I read the following statement: "Those are all good steps. I welcome federal efforts to beef-up customs as part of a bid to deter cross-border shopping." That was Bob Rae, the Premier of Ontario.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to get back to the missing memo.
The government suggests that it is mere coincidence that a top secret memorandum in the Al-Mashat case has gone missing. The question is, if it was lost, who lost it? If it was stolen, who stole it? If it was shredded, who shredded it?
June 11, 1991

I would like to put a question to the Solicitor General. Why has the Solicitor General of Canada, responsible for national security, not called in the RCMP to track down the whereabouts of that particular memo?

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is because I have not been asked to.

Mr. Speaker, is the Solicitor General saying that he is waiting for a telephone call from the Prime Minister to investigate a missing top secret memo?
I put the question to the Solicitor General again. The credibility of the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs is at issue in terms of the whereabouts of this particular memo. The minister is responsible for matters of national security. Will the Solicitor General do his job and call in the RCMP to investigate the whereabouts of that particular memo, or is he going to continue to protect his cabinet colleagues?
The question was all right up until the end. An accusation that the Solicitor General is protecting a colleague is a completely improper allegation and I ask the hon. member to withdraw it.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to withdraw that and put the question to the Solicitor General. Will he not agree that he is responsible for matters of national security? Will he not agree that the RCMP should be called in to investigate the whereabouts of a top secret memo that went to the offices of the former minister of external affairs? Why is it that there is one standard of justice for ordinary Canadians and another standard for his cabinet colleagues?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what is perfectly clear is that all the information in this case has been coming forward to the committee. We have been very forthcoming. What the information has shown is that there were some errors made. There is no smoking gun anywhere, as the hon. member has not been able to prove through all these many months because we have been very forthcoming with information.
That is it, that is all, there is no more. I am sorry, John, but there is no more.
Oral questions

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. On May 14th, the minister said that Mr. Raymond Chretien had taken no action to make sure that his deputy minister would be informed of the Al-Mashat affair. Yet, documents made public yesterday, by the minister herself, clearly demonstrate that she was wrong. Indeed, according to those documents, Mr. Chretien took concrete action, as early as February 27th, to inform the deputy minister, Mr. Demontigny Mar-chand. Is the minister prepared today, in this House, to do the honourable thing, admit her mistake and put the record straight?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is a divergence of opinions between the official at the deputy minister's office and those at Mr. Chretien's office. All the information is before the committee. Everything is clear to the committee. It is up to the committee to determine which opinion is the correct one.

Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that the committee will face its responsibilities. What we are trying to do here, on this side of the House, is to make sure that ministers also take on their responsibilities.
According to documents made public yesterday by the minister herself, it is clear that Mr. Chretien is the only senior civil servant to have taken concrete action in order to inform both his minister and his deputy minister. So, in the light of this information, would the minister not be ready, in all fairness, to admit that she was wrong with regard to Mr. Raymond Chretien, and to apologize to him for having needlessly tarnished his reputation on May 14th?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we pledged to give all the information to the committee and to the public. That is what we have done and that is all we can do. What went on before the members of the committee is clear, and the decision is theirs.

June 11, 1991
Oral questions

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of the Environment.
Before the public ever had a chance to participate in an environmental assessment, the Rafferty-Alameda dam was built and the Oldman River dam was built. Before construction begins on any roads or dams, before any land is flooded, will the minister assure this House that there will be a single, comprehensive, environmental assessment review process on the James Bay II project, known as the Great Whale?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the member is probably aware that there have been discussions with the Government of Quebec and the Cree and the Inuit. The sense of those discussions was to try to explore whether there was a possibility of doing one single assessment. The Government of Quebec through its Minister of the Environment, Mr. Paradis, was willing to look at that question and get back to us. I expect that they will formally say whether or not they are ready to do that and we will take the matter from there.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is for the same minister. Four weeks ago the Federal Court of Canada wiped out the Kemano settlement agreement, struck down the Order in Council exemption of the project and ordered an environmental assessment review of Alcan's huge power export project in British Columbia.
Since the court concluded that time is of the essence and that environmental concerns should be dealt with in advance of construction, will the minister today undertake his legal obligations and appoint an EARP panel for Alcan's Kemano II project?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the member will know, the decision was rendered and is being actively reviewed by the government. There are legal and environmental considerations.
I do want to add one thing. The information I have is what the court suggested we do was not necessarily-and I stand to be corrected if it is not the case-to undertake an initial assessment that may or may not lead to an EARP panel. If I am wrong, I will correct myself. My
information, if I remember correctly, was that we undertake an initial assessment that may or may not lead to an EARP panel.

Mr. Speaker, there now appears to be a real human cost to the Senate stalling of the GST legislation. Delays in passing the bill have in turn caused delays in building the GST processing centre in Summerside, Prince Edward Island. This has caused great uncertainty in a community which has already suffered from government cutbacks when the Canadian forces base there was closed.
My question is for the Minister of National Revenue. Can he tell the House what steps he is going to take to fulfil his statement of last September when he said: "The welfare of the civilian employees of the base whose jobs will terminate in 1991 is uppermost in our minds".

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that statement stands. Because of the delays in the Senate last fall and winter, we were late out of the starting blocks in trying to begin preparations for the processing centre in Summerside. However, since then, with co-operation from other federal departments, we have caught up. We will begin training and hiring as early as next year and then phase in the operation.
I would like to advise the hon. member that I am meeting this afternoon with representatives of DND civilians from Summerside to assure them that this government continues to meet the commitments we made last year.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister is no doubt aware that a number of federal agencies, including the Bank of Canada, have embarked on a policy of preventive withdrawal from Quebec. Yesterday, we heard that as of July 1, the Bank of Canada will close its international division in Montreal and withdraw the position of foreign exchange
June 11, 1991

consultant which has existed for over 20 years to help financial institutions in Quebec.
My question to the Prime Minister is this: In the circumstances and considering that one-third of foreign exchange transactions take place in Quebec, will the Prime Minister ask the Bank of Canada to reconsider this decision which runs counter to the interests of Montreal and Quebec?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to reassure the hon. member who is often concerned for the wrong reasons. No service or position or person has been transferred from Montreal to Toronto by the Bank of Canada, as a result of the restructuring he mentioned.
What is happening, Mr. Speaker, is quite straightforward, and all government departments and agencies are having to cope with this. We have asked them to help reduce the deficit, and it is a fact that at its various offices, including those in Montreal, the Bank of Canada has cut certain positions. In Montreal, this amounts to about 2.5 person-years. The people in question were offered jobs in other positions in Montreal and elsewhere, but that is as far as it went, Mr. Speaker.

I have a supplementary for the Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker.
Another federally-controlled agency which has been partially privatized, and I am referring to Air Canada, has changed its mind about the training centre in Montreal and moved its flight simulators to Toronto, and I just heard that as a result of a restructuring of all Air Canada flight operations, out of 16 directors there will be only one Francophone and only three in Montreal, while the others will be posted in the rest of Canada.
Can the minister give a good reason why all this has to happen at the expense of Montreal, once more?

Mr. Speaker, as everybody knows, Air Canada was privatized several years ago and has become a commercial operation that is trying to restructure its operation like any commercial business, in order to survive as long as it can
Oral questions
and provide Canadians with an efficient transportation system.
I am surprised the hon. member opposite should be upset about the fact that a company tries to enhance its stability and thus be able to provide jobs for its employees for many more years to come.

Mr. Speaker, I have in my hand a booklet that I am sure the Prime Minister knows well. It is entitled Notes on the Responsibilities of Public Servants in Relation to Parliamentary Committees. It was issued by the Privy Council Office in December 1990 and declares most emphatically the doctrine of ministerial responsibility.
On page 6 it says as follows: "It is ministers and not officials who exercise the constitutional authority of the Crown, and it is ministers and not their officials who are responsible to Parliament."
Will the Prime Minister confirm that this is the policy of his government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I realize this occurred before the hon. member was elected, but in 1985 the McGrath committee on parliamentary reform spent a lot of time looking at the question of ministerial responsibility. It concluded in its third report, on page 21 I believe, that the doctrine of ministerial responsibility as historically practised was outdated and no longer reflected the reality of today.
It went on to recommend that the government co-operate in making officials available for appearances at committees so that members could access officials directly. That recommendation was unanimous. All parties of the House recommended it. The government accepted it. I wonder why the hon. member will not.

Mr. Speaker, I am not referring to a report of the eighties, I am referring to a document issued by the Privy Council Office in December 1990, six months ago.

June 11, 1991
Oral questions
On page 1 it says: "Ministers are responsible to the House for everything that is done under their authority". Will the Prime Minister have the integrity and backbone to accept this statement-
Just a minute. The hon. member can ask if the Prime Minister wants to do something else, but using those words imputes the honour and integrity of hon. members.

I will rephrase the question. Will the Prime Minister accept this statement and instruct his ministers involved in the Al-Mashat affair to accept ministerial responsibility for the actions of their officials?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, every single minister who was involved with this issue has been here ready to answer questions. They have appeared before committee.
In keeping with the recommendations of the McGrath committee, all of the officials who had an interest in this issue appeared before committee and answered all the questions asked by the opposition, even some of the rude and outrageous ones.
So the reality is that by being here and answering questions-even those that are out of order-for the hon. member we are showing responsibility. We are trying to comply fully with that document as well as the policy adopted by this House after the unanimous recommendation of all parties on the McGrath committee.
I think the hon. member, if he is being fair, will recognize that we fully accept responsibility.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport.
The trucking protests on Parliament Hill and in other cities in the last couple of weeks focused attention on the Canadian trucking industry. The minister mentioned at the time that there are a number of studies under way.
Can the minister advise us whether anything has been done to alleviate the concerns of the owner-operators of these trucks?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for his question and reassure him that in fact I have met with many people, including representatives of the largest transportation unions, the Canadian Trucking Association, the National Coalition of Owner-Operators Association.
I want to emphasize to the hon. member that the unions have been full participants in the task force process; indeed, they originally proposed setting up the task force in June 1990.
I also want to assure the hon. member that I will be attending the task force meetings tomorrow and Thursday in Toronto along with the Minister of State for Transport. I look forward to seeing the work of the last eight months come to fruition. I anticipate a very busy and fruitful meeting.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. For two days in a row members on this side of the House have asked ministers opposite why the government has not been actively engaged in trying to find a missing top secret memo. For two days ministers have demonstrated, in our view, a a real active lack of interest in finding that memo. Incredibly the Solicitor General today said he has not instructed the RCMP to look for it because he has not been asked.
I want to ask the Prime Minister, who described a missing budget document as a criminal act and described those who had it as criminals in advance of any court case, whether he will now instruct the Solicitor General to have the RCMP go into External Affairs to see if they can find this missing memo, or if they cannot find it, find out what happened to it? Will the Prime Minister do that, given his interest in finding missing top secret government documents?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:

June 11, 1991

John Diefenbaker?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise pursuant to the notice of a question of privilege I sent you earlier this day.
I wish to refer to the statements of the government House leader as reported in the media which I submit were intended to interfere with and impede the business of one of the standing committees of the House.
Such interference with the business of the House, which includes of course the business of committees that as you know and all hon. members know are after all creations of the House, constitutes in my view a contempt of this House.

Before the hon. member proceeds further-if it is appropriate, and it may well be, I shall certainly hear him-I listened very carefully during Question Period and I am quite sure the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond did as well. I am wondering whether the response given by the government House leader to a question on this point would make any difference to the hon. member's intervention. I bring that to the attention of the hon. member.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. As I was indicating to the Chair and to all hon. members present I refer to Erskine May, the 21st edition, page 115, which reads:
-any act or omission which obstructs or impedes either House of Parliament in the performance of its functions, or which obstructs or impedes any Member or officer of such House in the discharge of his
June 11, 1991

duty, or which has a tendency, directly or indirectly, to produce such results may be treated as a contempt even though there is no precedent of the offence.
That is on page 115 of Erskine May, the 21st edition.
It should be noted that on several occasions ministers of the Crown gave clear undertakings to the House. In fact the hon. minister opposite, the Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, stated on page 254 of Hansard, dated May 17, 1991:
-we are very anxious to get this matter before the committee as soon as possible. Then all relevant officials can be called before the committee because we are absolutely convinced that the facts we have elucidated will become obvious to those who keep an open mind.
That was on May 17. On May 23, 1991, at page 477 of Hansard the Minister of Employment and Immigration stated the following:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member and all other members of this House will have a chance in the standing committee to respond to all the issues that were raised. We have already said that we prepared a report, and that report has been released.
If there are additional matters on which further details are requested, it will be the committee's job to take care of that and I trust it will.
On May 28, 1991, on page 680 of Hansard, the present Secretary of State for External Affairs said:
Let me say as well that we have agreed there will be an open and honest inquiry-.We have said from the beginning that we would produce all of the people and all of the relevant materials to the extent that is possible.
I have given this House my commitment on that from the very beginning, and the hon. member knows it.
On May 30, 1991, at page 822 of Hansard, the Deputy Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance said:
I have no objection to that but surely it is a matter that should be properly questioned at the committee where all the witnesses they require and/or demand will be available to respond.
Mr. Speaker, in today's Ottawa Sun there is a headline, "Tories to end Probe. House leader wants Mashat inquiry dropped". In fact the minister is quoted as saying: "-the committee has already established how Iraq's former ambassador to Washington got fast-tracked into Canada".
Privilege
He is further quoted as saying: "I don't know what further facts could be adduced".
Mr. Speaker, in other words the government House leader is interfering in the committee's conduct of what was supposed to be an open and honest inquiry. He is saying to the committee that it is getting too close to the facts and that it better stop before it really uncovers the truth.
Mr. Speaker, members-

Just a moment. I have already indicated that the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond might consider carefully what the hon. government House leader did say in Question Period, but certainly that last remark is getting to be an allegation that carries with it a lot of difficulty.
I am giving the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond every opportunity, I think, to make the point, but I do not think that the point is that the statements which are reported in the House amount to interference with the committee.
The hon. minister has already, at least to some degree, responded to that. Certainly I think that the interpretation put by the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond goes farther than the argument needs.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:

I have heard, as other members have heard, some of the remarks made by the hon. member opposite. Members of my party and of that committee have made it clear that a number of further sittings and witnesses are required. They have suggested that the former cabinet secretary, Gordon Robertson, an acknowledged, non-partisan expert on ministerial responsibility, appear as a witness. They have also requested that the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of Employment and Immigration reappear in order to clarify their roles in light of information gathered since they last appeared. For the same reasons, they wish to recall Mr. David Daubney. They would also

June 11, 1991
Privilege
like to hear evidence from a former legislative assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
In conclusion, the government House leader has announced that he is, in essence, ordering the committee to shut down. His statements can only be interpreted as orders to the government majority on the committee to do what he says or else.
