speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what we have just had is an abuse of this House by debating an issue that has no right on this floor. There was no point of privilege. You will notice he did not put a motion, which is required when he raises a point of privilege. He did not demonstrate, in any way, shape or form, how he is impeded in performing his duties as a result of it. It was a bogus point of privilege and, frankly, I think it should come to an end if the hon. member is going to show the respect for this institution he frequently talks about.
Let me deal with the allegations. He suggested that I have ordered the committee to finish. To begin with, he knows that the House leader, because of parliamentary reform and the changes in the rules which this government brought in, cannot order a committee to sit or not to sit. I cannot do that.
He then quoted, a number of times, statements made in the House, where I and others have said we would welcome a committee sitting. That was not considered interference in a parliamentary committee. He also says that because outside the House I am quoted as saying I would welcome the committee terminating its sittings, that is interference. How can it be both? How can it, on the one hand, by suggesting a committee sit be perfectly appropriate, but by suggesting a committee not sit is somehow an intolerable abuse of that member's privileges? What an absurdity and what a waste of the House's time.
Again, he is abusing the House by distorting and warping what in fact was in the paper. If anybody has a privilege it is me for the deliberate distorting of what is
in the paper. What is in the paper under quotations is: "I don't know what further facts could be adduced," Andre told reporters. That is what I said. It is a breach of the privileges of this House, Mr. Speaker, for the House leader to say such an outrageous thing. My gosh, what is this place coming to that I should be so outrageous as to make this kind of suggestion?
Mr. Speaker, if you think that is a breach of the privileges of the House, I would welcome a motion and will defend myself for having so abused the hon. member's sensitivities by suggesting I do not know what further facts could be adduced. My God, I did not realize I said something so outrageous.
Come on. This is a waste of time. I suggest we get on to other business and the hon. member stop wasting time in this manner.

Mr. Speaker, I really do feel I have to provide a few observations, particularly based on the rather hysterical outburst by the government House leader.
I join with my friend, the opposition House leader, who was astonished, as most sensitive Canadians were this morning, to read the headlines in The Ottawa Sun that the House leader wants the Al-Mashat inquiry dropped. We all remember time and time again when the government House leader has indicated clearly, as other senior ministers have, in an effort to divert if you like, a discussion on the floor of the House of Commons that the committee would be the appropriate place to obtain the evidence.
I do not remember the exact quote, but I remember the statement being made that all witnesses necessary would be welcome at the committee. That suggests that if committee members had people that they believed were appropriate in order to get to the bottom of this that they ought to be heard.
Therefore, when the government House leader says that he does not know whether further facts would be adduced, that is sending a very clear signal to his colleagues on that committee that enough is enough, and the Tories plan to end the probe.
Perhaps the truth of all of this will come out in the next few days in terms of whether or not all of the appropriate witnesses are still allowed to be called. At that point we may be back again.
June 11, 1991

I simply want to join with my colleague to say that it appears to me that the government House leader is prejudging the work being done by the committee. A certain element of interference is there in his comments. After all, we are told on a regular basis by the government House leader to get off the issue in the House of Commons because the committee is where this should be dealt with. Yet now he is saying that as far as he is concerned, enough of the facts have come out and the committee, presumably, should wrap up its proceedings.
I want to simply say that it is important that we get to the bottom of this. It is important that some minister eventually accept responsibility for this dastardly sequence and the way to do that is in a committee.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the government House leader protested a bit too much in his statements. I want to cite a couple more authorities for Your Honour to assist you in consideration of this case.
The hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond has already referred to the statements in the case. I have turned to Maingot's work on Parliamentary Privilege in Canada page 193, where the learned author writes, quoting one of your distinguished predecessors, Madam Speaker Sauve. He states:
As the Speaker has said recently, ". . .the dimension of contempt of Parliament is such that the House will not be constrained in finding a breach of privileges of members, or of the House. This is precisely the reason that, while our privileges are defined, contempt of the House has no limits. When new ways are found to interfere with our proceedings, so too will the House, in appropriate cases, be able to find that a contempt of the House has occurred."
I submit what has happened here is an attempt by the government House leader to muzzle this committee. That is a breach of members' freedom of speech. That is one of our fundamental privileges in this House.
The suggestion is that there has been an attempt to muzzle our freedom of speech. If that is so, I suggest that it constitutes a breach of the privileges of the House. If it fails on that score, it is certainly a contempt of the House because it is one of our fundamental privileges.
Privilege
I refer also to Halsbury's Laws of England, fourth edition, page 608, where there is a distinction drawn between the offences of contempt and breach of privilege, citation 1500 in that work. I quote again:
The power of both Houses of Parliament to punish for contempt is a general power similar to that possessed by the superior courts of law and is not restricted to the punishment of breaches of their acknowledged privileges. Any act or commission which obstructs or impedes either House in the performance of its functions, or which obstructs or impedes any member or officer of the House in the discharge of his duty, orwhich has a tendency to produce such a result, may be treated as a contempt even if there is no precedent for the offence.
I do not need to read further, but I submit that in this case there is clearly authority. If Your Honour finds that there is a prima facie breach of privilege in this case, either myself or the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond will be pleased to move the appropriate motion to have the matter referred to the House management committee where it could be investigated fully.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel like my privileges have been abused for about 15 minutes. I tend to be busy and there are meetings that need to take place and this discussion has gone on at some length.
If, Mr. Speaker, you were to find significant members of this Chamber speaking to the press about what committees should do to be indeed a contempt and a breach of privilege of this House, I suggest that most members on the other side of this House would be guilty. On more than one occasion, I have seen an enormous amount of publicity in the last two or three weeks from members on the other side, from the Official Opposition and the third party in this House, long, long dissertations on television, lots of quotes and newspaper articles in which people are telling the Al-Mashat committee or the external affairs committee exactly what it should do.
If that is a contempt of Parliament, it would be a sad, sad day for the notion of free speech. However, this filibuster on this issue is a denial of free speech and I think it should come to a conclusion right now.

Mr. Speaker, my point of order arises from the response of the Minister of the Environment during Question Period to the question put regarding Alcan's Kemano II project.
I have provided the minister with the appropriate sections of the Federal Court ruling of May 14, 1991 by Mr. Justice Alison Walsh.
The minister suggested that perhaps only an initial environmental evaluation is what is suggested by the ruling, but I think the following two very short quotations will reveal to the minister and to the House that that is not what the court had to say and I quote from the bottom of page 36:
I conclude that the Kemano II Completion Project requires an assessment by virtue of the environmental assessment review process and that the ministers involved, and specifically the Minister of the Environment, were under an obligation to arrange for it and not frustrate this by the settlement agreement signed in 1987 finally by the order of the minister, confirmed by Order in Council that no such assessment is necessary.
A few sentences down it goes on and it says:
-deciding against an EARP assessment in connection with the present project, however, where on the facts it is evident that one is required, goes far beyond the exercise of discretion in a fair manner with which the court cannot interfere and becomes a failure to undertake a legal obligation required by law. The same is true, although perhaps to a lesser extent, with respect to the other ministers named as respondents. It is not sufficient to be satisfied with-

June 11, 1991

Mr. Speaker, I am almost finished the one sentence that I was reading.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for Skeena for having sent over to me copies of the rulings that he has just quoted from. Although I do not have page 36, it is not material to the point I want to make.
First, let me reiterate that I stand by the answer I gave in Question Period. I think what the member from Skeena and I are talking about here is a question of interpretation rather than a disagreement on what the ruling is about. Let me be clear so that there will be as little confusion as possible on what this is about in the environmental assessment process.
As far as I can tell from the pages I have in front of me, I think that when the judge refers to a process, the judge refers to this process in a generic sense of the term more than the specific sense.
The process itself is made up of two parts as they now stand under the guidelines. The first part requires that a federal government department makes what we call an initial assessment. Once the department has made that assessment, it determines whether there are or are not mitigable measures that can be taken in the case of any specific project and it can then be satisfied that those mitigable measures are taken and not ask for a public panel. There is also a public panel that can be asked for if there is what we call sufficient public interest.
In the case before us, my understanding of the ruling is that the court says that the ministers involved should do that environmental assessment process in the generic sense and that that would require the initial assessment to happen. Let me refer to page 38 of the same court ruling under the title Specific Conclusions. The last five lines of that page 38 where the justice says "with respect to paragraph 4 an order of mandamus will be issued requiring the various ministers named to comply with the
Points of Order
requirements of the EARP guidelines order and submit the proposal to an environmental screening and assessment pursuant to section 10 thereof".
That, as far as I am concerned with the information I have, is an order by mandamus to the ministers concerned, not the Minister of the Environment, but the ministers concerned, to undertake what I referred to in that initial process.
In closing my remarks, let me point out to you that as the guidelines now stand, the Minister of the Environment does not have the power to act alone in constituting a panel. To do that requires that an initiating department ask the Minister of the Environment to do that. Once that request is made to the Minister of the Environment, he or she has no choice but to order the panel. But that, mechanically, must be done first and that is why I answered the way I did during Question Period.

All Canadians should know that Hilton Works is not closing down and that people who put out this kind of rumour should not be allowed to parade it as news because it is not.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
When Bill C-ll was last before the House there were 10 minutes remaining in the question and comments period follow-
Govemment Orders
ing the speech of the hon. member for Gander-Grand Falls.
I will now recognize hon. members who wish to continue the question and comment period.

Mr. Speaker, when my colleague from Gander-Grand Falls was speaking previously on this debate I was particularly struck with his knowledge of the whole sector in Atlantic Canada.
I want to refer here to the actual purpose of that particular bill introduced in 1966. The two main purposes were to ensure that eastern Canadian ports could compete with the United States ports and to enable the ports of Halifax and Saint John to compete with Montreal and other St. Lawrence River ports.
As the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Committee contends, the budget papers that contain this measure failed to identify the full purpose and objective of the program and rationalize this decision to terminate it solely on the basis of the absence of competition between the United States and Canadian ports.
Having said that, I want to ask the member: If I were to place a phone call asking where I can get information on this or where I can get freight service-I suppose it would have to be a 1-800 number-where would I have to place that call? Who would answer?

Mr. Speaker, at this time of the year, a lot of people are planning their vacations, especially their vacations to motor to Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island or some other place.
There was a 1-800 number under that subsidiary of CN, Marine Atlantic. There was a 1-800 number until about a month ago. The 1-800 number was 1-800-565-7421. There were very catchy tunes on television and on radio advertising the 1-800 number.
The 1-800 number has now been discontinued, but if you are in the United States or in Texas, there is a 1-800 number that you can use. If you are in Alabama or any state in the United States, there is a 1-800 number: 1-800-347-19981 if you want to write it down and you are in the United States.
If you are in Canada, you cannot call a 1-800 number. You cannot call toll-free. If you want to take any of the ferry systems or any of the boats in eastern Canada that go to these islands, you just cannot call toll-free. If you

June 11, 1991
Government Orders
live in the United States, you can, and that is not the end of the story.
When you compare the rates, it is amazing. In terms of the union with Canada-I can remember when the debate was on about whether or not we were going to join Canada-there was quite a campaign on, that we should join Canada because there were advantages to it. One of the big things in the Railway Act, the act we are talking about today, was that the rates to be charged for passengers and freight moving to Newfoundland would be comparable to the rate charged if you went an equal distance on land. That is in the terms of union.
Now looking at the new rates, it is $99 for your car if you go from North Sydney to Argentia. Your cabin costs $96.25 with the GST added and no window. If you want a window, you have to pay $99.77 for your cabin. A reclining chair is $12.04 with the GST included, an adult pays $41. That is on the Argentia run. That is pretty expensive. When you add all that up, it is close to $700.
On the Port aux Basques run,-I am talking about return now with four adults in a car- it costs practically $400. You could go to Prince Edward Island 20 times on that kind of rate, down to Argentia. But in answering your question relating to competition with the United States, not only do they have a 1-800 number in the United States of America for our services to our islands in Canada, but they do not pay GST say if you phoned Bar Harbour, Maine. If you called Bar Harbor, Maine about Marine Atlantics, CN's subsidiary which operates between Bar Harbor, Maine and Yarmouth, you will notice that there is no GST on the cabins there. Also, you can get a return fare. Now you know what that means. It means you get a reduced rate if you buy a return ticket. So there you go. The 1-800 number is gone in Canada but is still in the United States. If you are in Texas or Dallas you can call free, but if you are in Canada you cannot. GST is not charged for the ferry that matches up with the state of Maine from Canada and you get special return rates which are lower than if you paid individually one rate to the other.
I believe that these rates by CN and its subsidiaries are a violation of the terms of union between Newfoundland
and Canada. They have not only taken away those subsidies, they have even taken away our railway tracks in Newfoundland. Not only are the railway tracks gone, but even the ties under the railway tracks are gone. It is pretty difficult walking down those railway lines with not even a track there or a tie. Eveiy three or four feet you drop down into a hole. That is what is left. Not only did they take up the railway tracks and the ties, they did away with the railway and took away the subsidies that we are talking about. They also sold, as I mentioned before, the telephone company that they own. They sold that last year.
We have really been sold out by the Tory government.

Mr. Speaker, I can only take it from the comments of the previous speaker that the decision to terminate this program in the budget papers, based on the absence of competition between the United States and Canadian ports, was a false assumption as were so many other items in that particular budget.
Could the member give me a comment on that, please?

Mr. Speaker, I think the entire bill that is before the House is a good indication of what the Government of Canada is doing. What the Government of Canada is doing is setting adrift the entire intent of equality in this nation, in transportation and in everything else. It is setting us adrift and it is making the decisions by cabinet. They are not even waiting for us, as parliamentarians, to pass the bill.
Why if you even look at this bill you will discover that the bill really applies, I believe, to flour and grain that was put on a railway car back in 1978 I believe. So, in other words, it would not apply unless the flour and grain has not yet arrived at its destination. The subsidy was done away with in 1988 or 1989 and the Government of Canada did not even wait to pass the bill before this Chamber. They are now bringing in that particular piece of legislation, but I would not like to use any flour that has been on a train for the last three years covered by this particular piece of legislation.
Maybe that is what is wrong every time I bake some bread and it does not work out. Maybe it is the flour that we are all using.
June 11, 1991

Mr. Speaker, I have a few words to say on Bill C-ll, but maybe you will allow me, just in passing, to make a comment which I am sure you will find relevant to the debate, at least to one of the debaters in the debate. I listened again with great interest to my friend from Gander-Grand Falls as he talked in the last few moments, answering questions from my friend from Lambton-Middlesex. I could not help but have a couple of thoughts when he mentioned that he remembered the events of the Confederation battle between the pro-confederates and the anti-confederates in Newfoundland in the pre-1949 period. Surely he does not remember it too well because he is much too young to remember a lot of it; and what a fount of wisdom this man is.
Very few people know his direct connection to the Confederation period or, after the fact, I tell my friend from Calgary Southeast, among his other many achievements he is also the publisher, the producer, of a best-selling, long-playing record called, "Oh, What a Battle It Was". This record makes available on tape to historical buffs and others some of the actual speeches of Mr. Smallwood and his protagonist during the great convention that preceded the coming together of the Dominion of Newfoundland and the Dominion of Canada in 1949.
I am not paid to do this but I believe there are still a few records somewhere available out there in somebody's cellar. If not, I have one that I would be glad to play for the member for Calgary Southeast. He would hear some great speeches by Mr. Peter Cashin, the uncle of Dr. Richard Cashin, and by Joey Smallwood and others of that particular period.
Apart from-
What's the relevance?

Ah-h, now the member for Cambridge wonders about the relevance. Apart from always wanting to throw a bouquet in the direction of my friend from Gander-Grand Falls, it is supremely relevant to revisit those debates on that particular record which my friend has seen fit to have preserved. He went to the CBC archives back in those days when he was not busy being the editor of Hansard in the Newfoundland House of Assembly, being the clerk of the Newfoundland assem-
Govemment Orders
bly, or the Editor of Debates. He has been a fairly busy fellow in his day but he found time to go to the CBC archives and have the speeches put on a record to be available to the public. Many thousands of Newfoundlanders have those records and I am sure as a result of this promotion today the requests will come flooding in again. I want him to know that my share goes to charity.
There is a relevance, I say to my friend from Cambridge. The relevance is that when those great debates were going on, apart from the rhetoric-of which we get a little bit in this House-of those days, Major Peter Cashin led the anti-confederate forces, the Newfoundland independence forces if you like, the Responsible Government League it was called, and Joey Smallwood led the other forces-by the way I was just talking on the phone to a friend of mine today who visited Joey this afternoon; he is hale and hearty, still walks around his garden three or four times a day and is in very good shape. He will be 91 this Christmas Eve, but he is in very good shape, the only living Father of Confederation.
When Joey and Major Peter Cashin and their entourages got up at the national convention in St. John's to debate the future of Newfoundland, they marshalled the various arguments which will be found on that tape to which I made reference in relation to the member for Gander-Grand Falls. Those arguments were either for confederation or against confederation. My friend from Gander-Grand Falls in his last answer made reference to one of those arguments. Joey Smallwood and others successfully sold the benefits of the two dominions, the Dominion of Newfoundland and the Dominion of Canada, coming together. Those who are about to remake the country keep in mind what Newfoundlanders did in 1949. They passed up nationhood, albeit they were only a half million souls or even fewer at that time. They deliberately, consciously in a vote-it took two votes to do it, mind you-said: "We will forfeit dominion status and nationhood, as a small country, a full-fledged member of the British Commonwealth." Do not forget that it was one of the four dominions in the Statute of Westminster back in 1931; New Zealand, Australia, Canada and Newfoundland. It was one of the original four dominions. That dominion elected by popular ballot in the period leading up to 1949 to forfeit its dominion status, to forfeit its national status, to become a province of Canada.

June 11, 1991
Government Orders
As an aside, but I believe an important aside from where I stand, I say to those who are now redrawing the map of Canada and reconfiguring what kind of Canada we are going to have, one of the many factors they have to keep in mind is that unlike every other province of this country-well, I suppose the exceptions are the original four, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Quebec and Ontario, who came in as provinces-but the only other of the ten provinces that came in as a separate entity and was not carved out of existing territory already part of the Dominion of Canada was Newfoundland and Labrador. It came in as a province, not part of a region, not a quarter of a province, to be a province. That was the trade-off.
I give notice now that when the time comes when we as Newfoundlanders have to choose between fighting for that principle and opting for some hodge-podge of regions in this country that subvert the dreams and aspirations those people had in 1949, my father and mother and the parents of my friend from Gander-Grand Falls and others, we have no doubt where we will stand in that particular debate. That is another debate for another time.
I will talk about the retroactivity of this bill in a few moments. The bill itself is an affront. It is an affront that can be traced in terms of impact right back to that great Confederation battle involving Newfoundland's decision to join Canada. Part of the package, if you like, that was put before the voters at that time when they were asked to choose between continuing dominion status or being a province of Canada, a marriage with Canada, related to matters of transportation, availability of foodstuffs at reasonable prices.
Now, 42 years later, we in Newfoundland, as in so many other provinces, but for us it is more poignant, for us it is more pointed, for us it is more focused, because we made overt decisions based on the inventory of this country as it was then, based on the advantages, based on the substantive benefits of being part of this country. I could run through them if we had the time, but just in a quick illusion, not only to do with transportation, but to do with that social safety net, the family allowance, the pensions and so on, which are now being dismantled, left, right and centre by the representatives of the confederacy to the south over there. They are just dismantling it every chance they get.
The continuance of the railway was a part of that package and that has since gone the way of the dodo bird.
It is a retreat of national government.

As my friend from Broadview-Greenwood says so well, what we are seeing is the retreat, the abdication of the national government, the shredding of the mandate of a national government. What purpose is there in having a national government if it has no raison d'etre, no reason for existing, if it works itself out of business.
Bill C-ll, which in the last House was Bill C-26, died an honourable death at third reading stage. Then the government, by the back door, got it back in here again over the opposition of we who felt it should not be here.
Mr. Speaker, if you go back to the 1200s, to 1215 I suppose, the Magna Carta, and follow through from there, the whole principle-even 1066 my friend from Regina-Lumsden says-the very beginnings, the very elemental, primitive, beginnings of parliamentary democracy and follow it through to the present day, you will find that there was always some protection for the ordinary people. This is why we call this place the House of Commons. Here we represent the common, ordinary people of Canada. That is where the name "Commons" comes from.
But we in the opposition are less able to do it when we have a government that writes its own rules every day of the week. It is equivalent to having a losing baseball team. Lord knows they have become a bunch of losers over there. Then, because they cannot win with the rules as they are, they keep changing them. So they say well, you fellows will still have nine players, but we would like to have 13. We would like to have two people at bat at the same time; we want our people only to run one base instead of three; we want to shorten the distance between bases from 90 feet to 45 feet.
It would be easy to win a game if you were allowed to write your own rules all the time. Is anybody in this Chamber surprised that this bunch of losers over here, this crowd that cannot get the support of any more than 14 per cent of the people, can still ram legislation through here? How can they do it? They can do it because they doctor the rules of the game all the time, they keep changing the rules. That is the only reason this bill is here. This bill should not even be here because it died at third reading in the last House. If they wanted to bring it back they should have had the integrity to bring it
June 11, 1991

back in the normal way instead of ramming it through as part of a package of four.
Mr. Speaker, the bill itself would undo a long-standing set of subsidies that were put here by a former government-and I will tell you, it was not the Tory government either-because it saw a need to look after the ports of Saint John and Montreal and Halifax and the other ports down the St. Lawrence.
It was done at a time when it was trying to parallel a similar circumstance which had taken place in the United States in 1959. That is why we implemented this amendment to the Railway Act in the 1960s.
It is true that that subsidy we were trying to match no longer applies in the United States. But before we throw it out, we ought to go back to the people who brought in the bill in the first place. I am glad to say it was a man by the name of Jack Pickersgill, a man who was born in Manitoba. I have always said that you do not have any control over where you were born. Not that Manitoba is a bad place to be born, but having been born in Manitoba and having worked in various parts of Canada and the United States, he had the good sense to run for and win a seat in Parliament to represent the people of Newfoundland.
My great friend and a great parliamentarian, Jack Pickersgill, represented the old seat of Bonavista-Trinity-Conception. I think it was called something different in those days, Gander-Twillingate, I guess, for a number of years.
As Minister of Transport, he introduced this legislation that this government wants to cut the guts out of. He said at the time that one of the reasons was the one I mentioned before, that it was to match the advantage of subsidy that the American ports, the eastern seaboard ports had. To put Montreal and Saint John and Halifax and those ports in a similar circumstance, he brought in the legislation. But he brought it in for another reason. It is worth reading the actual quote from that particular time.
Mr. Speaker, he said at the time: "To ensure that we will have rights which will provide some inducement and incentive to shippers to use the facilities of the Atlantic ports." To provide some incentive, some inducement.
Government Orders
I want to ask members on that side of the House who are representing those Atlantic ports, where are they now? Where are they now, that their jobs are going down the drain in Halifax and Saint John. This is not fear mongering. This has happened in the past few weeks. The elevators are closing. People are losing their jobs down there in Halifax. We have heard the stories. We have seen them in the press. Where are the people they sent here to speak up for them? Where are the members who now should be doing what Jack Pickersgill said 30 years ago needs to be done. Are those Tory members telling us and telling their constituents that there is no need now for some incentives to shippers to use those facilities?
They ought to take a look. When they go back to their ridings, if they get the nerve to go back to their ridings, they really should take a walk down around the port in Halifax or Saint John or Montreal and some of those other places and see what is happening there, see the devastation there, see the pain that this legislation is inflicting even before it has been implemented. Why can this legislation inflict pain before its time? Because this government not only has brought this bill in through the back door, it has gone and wiped out the subsidies anyway as of July 1989.
This government is now trying to get the legislative authority to do what it did two years ago. Twenty-three months ago the government wiped out this particular subsidy without any legislative debates. It is a complete shame. It is a tragedy to sit here and watch basic protections, that the people in any democracy have a right to, being eroded by a government that changes the rules of Parliament to suit its own whim. It uses its own muscle to change subsidies and laws without even the benefit of a rubber stamp in Parliament. The government has the majority to do this and if it had some good planning, maybe if it felt it important to do away with these subsidies, it would get the sequence right. This government would get the law changed first.
That is not too much for those producers to ask who are left out there twisting in the wind, nor for those farmers to ask whose prices are already, I am told, depressed as a result of this particular initiative.

June 11, 1991
Government Orders
Mr. Speaker, do you realize that export grain shipments in the ports of Halifax and Saint John have stopped? Saint John grain elevator is closed. Fifty-five people in Saint John, New Brunswick, have lost their jobs, in Halifax another 27 people. These are actual statistics which put a face, a human face, on the madness that the government is up to with this particular Bill C-ll.
There are so many more things I could say, but I see by your signal that my time is just about up.
Let's see what the present Minister of Finance had to say, the Deputy Prime Minister, a man who has a reputation for telling it like it is, about an earlier effort to do away with this particular provision, this At and East subsidy. Here is what the gentlemen who represents a farm riding in Alberta had to say when he was in opposition. At that moment back there when it was talked about that they were going to wipe out the subsidy he said that the government must not cancel the At and East subsidy. Then he went on and said:
The elimination of this subsidy could mean a loss to Canada of
something in the order of $28 million worth of value added processing
activity.
He was slightly wrong, only in the sense he was very low on the figure. It means a loss already of more millions than the $28 he mentioned at that particular time.
If there is one thing that disillusions the public, it is people who say one thing in opposition and other in government. I would have thought that the very man who would not do that is the gentlemen who is now the present Minister of Finance.
I see that you are getting ready to cut me off because my time is up. How time flies when you are having fun.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order.
There being only 10 members present I would like you to call a quorum.

Mr. Speaker, it would be a pleasure for me to participate in this debate, but I have the sinking feeling that I have already spoken at third reading, which would prohibit me from continuing. I wonder if I could see some clarification from the Chair.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: You are right.

Mr. Speaker, I want to inform my colleagues, especially on the other side, that I will do anything to get an audience. I hope you will stay to be reminded about some things for Atlantic Canada which you are participating in doing away with.
For nearly 100 years there has been a number of transportation assistance programs in place in Canada designed to keep east-west movement of goods and people going in commerce, and also designed to prevent the United States from moving in on us with their transportation systems.
Various governments at various times over the last 100 years have made wise moves, sometimes forced on them, sometimes because they did the right thing on their own. These transportation programs were designed to take into account our geography, our climate, where our people are located and how far we are from export positions.
The average grain haul in Canada is over 900 miles. In the United States it is some 700 miles. They have the advantage of a massive waterway system and much of their grain is grown closer to their seaports.
Australia and Argentina, two other main competitors are, on average, within 200 miles average of export position. It is similar in Europe. From Poland west there is not a grain haul more than 300 or 400 miles.
It means that Canada has to take extra measures to give us that so-called level playing field, although so far we have had level playing fields where the other guy has the ball on our ten yard line all the time. The reason for these programs was to give us an equal shot at the ports of Quebec, Saint John, Halifax. That was the reason for the Crowsnest Pass rates, the bridge rates and several other programs that have been done away with by the previous government and this one.

Our transportation systems are in bad, bad trouble. Our railroads, our airlines and our trucking industry, between so-called deregulation and the free trade deal have been put in an impossible position.
Somebody raised the trucking industry in the House today. The fast write-offs for the trucking industry in the United States also applies to railroads, so both the Canadian trucking industry and our railroads are at disadvantage. But we provide subsidized transportation costs for purposes I mentioned and also to equalize, to some extent, our opportunities in competition with U.S. transportation.
This measure, as others before, and I include the Crowsnest Pass freight rate, has done nothing but increase costs for grain producers. This one also affects Quebec, Ontario and the prairie provinces, particularly Manitoba and Saskatchewan.
I want to ask my hon. friends over there, where the heck are the Conservative members from the Atlantic, from Ontario, from Manitoba and Saskatchewan? We only have four left from Saskatchewan and it will not be long before there are none left. Where are they? This hurts the Canadian Wheat Board. It needs to do more effective export marketing of flour, milling wheat and feed grains. This hurts the Ontario Wheat Marketing Board.
The effect of this bill is not just a couple or 300 jobs in Atlantic Canada, in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. The effect of this sort of a measure goes away beyond those borders. In fact, I submit, there has been no net cost of this program to the Government of Canada. The maximum it ever paid in the subsidy was $40 million, and it would fluctuate from $10 to $40 million each year. But when you consider the number of people it kept working, not only in the terminals and the flour mills in Saint John and Halifax, and consider the benefit it was to livestock producers in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, who were making a buck, paying taxes, and consider the help it was to grain terminals and transporters on the Great Lakes and the upper St. Lawrence, the result was more income for the government in the form of taxes. This program did not cost the government a darned nickel.
Mr. Speaker, four grain elevators have shut down since the At and East has been cancelled: two in Midland, one in Port McNicoll and one in Prescott. The
Government Orders
terminals in Midland and Port McNicoll are in the riding of the former Minister of Transport, not the present one, the second last one. We have been through so many I think they should put a revolving door on the Minister of Transport minister's office.
It shows their level of commitment.

This is the 14th or 15th one I have been through.
Ontario flour mills have lost export contracts since they quit paying the subsidy, and require lower wheat prices to compete with mills in Quebec or with the Americans or the European community. They lower the wheat prices, that bankrupts some more grain producers in Ontario as well as in Manitoba and Saskatchewan.
I want to say, as far as I am concerned, we have a first class Speaker of this Parliament, but like all the rest of us, he is not perfect. I think the Speaker should rule with a hard hand on any government legislation that is put in effect over a year before it is even passed by Parliament.
We took the federal government to court over another bill back in the 1970s. We took it to Federal Court and the Federal Court told the federal government to pay its bills. It had to keep on paying part of the storage costs of grain in Canada. I do not know why the Atlantic provinces' governments have allowed this one. They could have taken it to court because it has to be somebody who has a direct interest in the matter. I do not know where Dover Flour Mills is. Why are they not in on this? I do not know where the management and ownership of the terminals in Halifax and Saint John are. Saint John has been shut down for over a year now. We need those grain terminals.
Canada only consumes 20 per cent of our grain production; 80 per cent of it goes to export. The Americans consume 80 per cent of their grain production; 20 per cent of it goes to export, just the opposite of our situation. So we have to do all the things we can to give us a fair shake at these markets.
When we dealt with this bill the first time in the previous Parliament, we met with and talked to the people from Halifax and Saint John. We talked to the livestock producers in Nova Scotia. You know what lengths they were feeling they had to go to? They were looking at bringing corn in from the United States or feed grains from Europe, for God's sake, and out west

June 11, 1991
Government Orders
and in Ontario we are up to our backsides in feed grain. What the heck are we doing?
This is wrong-headed, it is stupid, it flies in the face of good economic transportation sense. I know there are Conservative members from Atlantic Canada very unhappy about this. Well, you can just say the word to your Whip that you are either not going to be here for the vote or you are going to vote against it and put your action where your mouth is. With something that is bad for the country as well as bad for your own area, surely you have to persuade the government not to proceed or you have to tty to defeat it, no matter where you sit in the House.
Oh, for a minority Parliament. They would not have dared try it, they would not have dared.
The Halifax grain terminal is crucial to livestock producers because they bring in feed grain from Ontario and western Canada. They use that terminal for a surge capacity. They fill it up. They decide what space they need for the milling grains and the high-grade export grains, and they fill the rest of it up with feed grain. As and when farmers need feed grain, they truck it from that grain terminal in Halifax out to the feed lots on their farms and out to their processing plants. That is almost by the boards. The Halifax grain terminal is barely breaking even; its days are numbered.
To pursue my earlier complaint when I said I did not think the Chair was 100 per cent right on this issue of retroactive enforcement of legislation before Parliament has even dealt with it, both Houses, before it has received Royal Assent, how can you do that, Mr. Speaker? It passes all understanding as far as I am concerned.
I want to say that the subsidies paid under the Export Enhancement Program by the United States and the European Community subsidies are causing us enough trouble but we increase our troubles ourselves by doing away with this minimal program.
We should be exploring more flour and grain markets. We used to ship a lot of flour to Cuba. It was a three-way deal with the Soviet Union. It would sign a contract for two million, three million or four million tonnes of grain, specify a certain number of tonnes had to be milled into flour and the flour went to Cuba out of Halifax and Saint John.
The Cubans sent the Russians sugar, molasses and rum. That is how they paid for that flour. The Russians sent us cold cash. That arrangement was in place for about 12 or 14 years; it was a good deal. By the way, the Russians said that the Cubans make very good rum. They prefer vodka, but they will drink the stuff. It was a semi-barter deal.
Those Caribbean countries, including Cuba, badly need feed grains, and they badly need flour. What are we doing? We are shutting down the whole operation in Atlantic Canada. How dumb can the government get? Where are the Tory MPs from Atlantic Canada, from rural Ontario, from the Great Lakes ports or from the St. Lawrence ports? Where are the Tory MPs from Manitoba and Saskatchewan? We will not worry about the ones from Alberta; they have enough trouble anyway. Alberta's grain all goes pretty well to Vancouver.
Not this week, it doesn't.

Not this week, no.
Isn't it funny when there is a lockout. When there is a lockout, nobody says a word. When there is a strike: "Oh, legislate them back to work." There is a lockout. How come they do not legislate the grain companies back to work? I do not understand it.
However, nothing is moving west, so let's ship it east. The trouble is that we have lost the Crowsnest Pass rate and now we have lost the At and East rates. It makes no sense. It is of no significant use or benefit to the reduction of the deficit.
If you put that many people out of work, if you cut down on that much export out of those terminals and ports, you cut down on government revenues and you probably lose more money than what the subsidy costs.
It is not only no net cost. The livestock industry in the maritimes depends on grain. It is estimated that the abolishing of this puts the transportation costs for feed grain up by $10 a tonne. It is estimated that 5,000 jobs will be lost in the livestock industry, the feed mills, the meat packing plants and the dairies.
Surely that is not a risk worth taking over a piddling little subsidy like this.
As I said at the outset, this subsidy is what allows the Government of Canada to take into account our geography, our climate and where our people produce their goods and services. It gives us an even fight with our
June 11, 1991

competitors in the United States and the European community and these dummies want to cancel it.
I hope my hon. friend, who is a farmer in southern Saskatchewan, will get up and try to defend the abolition of these rates. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to take part in this debate and put some facts and figures on the record, not only for this House of Commons but for those who might be watching and taking a keen interest in what is happening with this debate and with this legislation.
We also have to recognize that since this At and East Program was put in place in 1967, the world shipping and economies have changed. Our grain markets have changed dramatically throughout the world, so we have to position commodities where we can best do that.
In 1967, when that act was put into place, the government of the day established the subsidy for grain and flour shipments moving for export at and east of Buffalo, New York. I sometimes wonder how well all of us understand when that was done and why it was done. Maybe my hon. colleague was here when that happened. I do not know what year he came to the House, but quite possibly he was here at that time.
The objective was to preserve jobs by encouraging the use of Canadian rail grain handling and port facilities to export Canadian grain and flour instead of shipping via the U.S. eastern seaboard ports. The At and East rail rates were frozen at the levels in effect in 1960 for grain and in 1966 for flour. The program applied to grain and flour moving from Georgian Bay, Lake Huron, Lake Ontario and the Upper St. Lawrence to the Lower St. Lawrence and maritime ports for export.
At the time the program was put in place, Canada's biggest markets for grain and flour were in Europe. Nobody can argue with that because at that time that is where the markets were. For instance, in the 1967-68 crop year, the United Kingdom was our biggest market, importing 1.8 million tonnes of wheat and flour. Canada exported 4.6 million tonnes of wheat and flour or 50 per cent of our total exports to Europe that year, compared to 3.1 million tonnes or 35 per cent to Asia.
That was 23 years ago and a lot has changed since then. Our principal grain markets are now in the Asian Pacific Rim. In 1988-89 Canada exported 4.4 million tonnes of wheat and flour, 25 per cent of our total exports, to Europe and 6.7 million tonnes or 38 per cent to Asia.

June 11, 1991
Government Orders
With that shift in markets, there has also been a shift in transportation patterns. More of our exports now move through the west coast and competition from U.S. ports is no longer considered a threat to east coast ports.
This subsidy is no longer necessary to keep Canadian grain moving through Canadian ports. The majority of the program stakeholders have recognized the subsidy is not cost effective nor needed to keep grain moving through Canadian facilities. They have expressed a willingness to explore possible alternatives.
transportation costs. The storage capacity of the elevator also ensures that there is an adequate supply of feed grain in the region at all times.
This has not changed. The Halifax elevator continues to serve the livestock, feed and flour industries. The Saint John elevator, which has closed, had been almost exclusively handling export grain from outside the region. As a result, its closure has had a minimal impact on the Atlantic agrifood sector.


The At and East only encouraged the use of high cost transport routes instead of cheaper routes dictated by the marketplace. For example, Ontario grain was shipped backward, or west, in order to transit from Georgian Bay ports and qualify for the subsidy. It also encouraged extra handling and storage at these ports. We do not have the luxury of using money to do those things. We have to be very responsible in how we spend our moneys. We have to change to alternate programs. The subsidy cost the federal government between $21 million and $48 million in the 1980s.
In 1988, 655,348 tonnes of export grain and 201,677 tonnes of export flour moved under the At and East subsidy. Over 95 per cent of the exports went through Halifax and Saint John. The subsidy for that one year was $32 million.
Export grain moved by the program represented almost the entire volume of grain handled at the port of Saint John and about 60 per cent of the volume at Halifax.
The elimination of the program was announced in the budget in April, 1989, effective July 15 of that same year. Shipments in transit, as of July 15, were eligible for the subsidy if they were exported by January 31, 1990.
As a result of the termination of the program, the Halifax elevator has lost some of the grain it previously handled and the Saint John elevator has since closed.
From the point of view of the agrifood industry, the effects have been minimal. The Halifax elevator provides an important level of competition to rail for the shipment of feed grains into the region. This competition is estimated to save about $10 per tonne on feed grain
The At and East program has been under review for a number of years. It is generally recognized that it was not cost-effective. In 1984 the program was assessed by the Canadian Transport Commission, and the Commission found that in the period from 1971 to 1981 the grain component of the subsidy created approximately 330 jobs, at an average cost of $86,780-and that is in 1981 dollars. In 1985, the Nielsen task force recommended termination of the program as a means of expenditure reduction. Since the Nielsen task force report, the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission, known as APT, has made a number of proposals mainly intended to maintain economic activity in the Atlantic provinces.
Last May the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds announced that a study of the viability of the Atlantic elevators would be conducted under Agriculture Canada's Grains 2000 program. The Grains 2000 program is operated out of the National Grains Bureau in Winnipeg, and it was chosen specifically because it was designed to allow industry participation in its projects. Industry has participated fully in this study. A consultant was chosen and a 24-member steering committee representing agriculture and transportation interests in the Atlantic region was chosen to guide the consultant's work.
The consultant selected was based in Halifax and did the study in conjunction with other consultants based in New Brunswick. The consultant met with the steering committee several times and also met with other industry groups in the region. He also examined proposals such as those submitted by the APTC and the Halifax-Dartmouth Port Development Corporation.
The study concludes that the Halifax grain elevator is viable in the short term and can be made viable in the
June 11, 1991

Private Members' Business

long term for much less than the cost of the At and East program. The report suggests that Halifax can become viable by equalizing water and grain freight rates between Halifax and the St. Lawrence ports based on a payment of about $3 per tonne on an addition of 100,000 to 200,000 tonnes of grain. The cost of implementing this recommendation would be between $300,000 to $600,000 per year.
The Saint John elevator has unique needs, and to approach long-term viability it would require a marine off-loading lake as well as additional storage capacity to accommodate an increased level of throughput. In addition, assistance of over $1 million per year would be required from the federal government to equalize water freight rates between the Saint John and St. Lawrence ports.
The study also examined the potential for a seaport elevator on Prince Edward Island. The study concluded that the volume of grain moving to and from that province is not sufficient to justify a single-use facility at this time.
The report recommended that Transport Canada consider replacing the potato handling facility at Summer-side with a multi-commodity facility.
The ministers now have the Grains 2000 report and are prepared to act on it. The government understands that the viability of the Halifax elevator is important to the local flour milling industry. The government also recognizes its importance to livestock producers and understands that the removal and the termination of the At and East has reduced the volume of grain moving through the port. For livestock and feed industries, Halifax represents a competitive alternative to rail for shipping feed grain into the maritime provinces.
['Agreed.']

He said: Mr. Speaker, my hope for this bill, Bill C-204, is that it might become the vehicle for a long overdue debate in this country about Canada's commitment to, and involvement in, the nuclear fuel cycle and all which that entails, from uranium mining through to waste disposal.
It is a debate which, when I was elected in 1979 seemed about to occur. The new Progressive Conservative government elected on May 22, 1979, was promising a parliamentary inquiry into nuclear energy. The motive for the inquiry was mixed.
The nuclear industry in Canada was a creation of successive Liberal governments. The Conservatives were open to an inquiry which, as well as raising fundamental questions as some had in mind, would uncover Liberal sins, the greatest of which, for some, was the failure to more successfully market Canadian reactors.
In any event, the government fell and with the return of the Liberals it was business as usual for government and the nuclear industry. All attempts to get any kind of public debate or input were stymied.
For instance, I tried in 1980 to get the then energy minister, Marc Lalonde, to hold hearings on the proposal to build the underground research laboratory at Lac du Bonnet, Manitoba, but to no avail. I also introduced a private members' bill at that time which called for a moratorium, an inquiry and a referendum on nuclear power. It was debated for an hour and then disappeared into history, as almost all private members' bills did at that time.
Since then, we have had the reform of private members' business which permits some private members' bills to be chosen as votable, a designation which provides for longer debates and a vote. This has meant on occasion that bills which would only have been debated once and

June 11, 1991
Private Members' Business
forgotten have actually become law, because MPs have seen fit to give a bill their support freed from the discipline of government business.
One such bill is former Bill C-204, sponsored by the former member for Broadview-Greenwood, Lynn McDonald, who I might say is also involved in the life of this bill as a leader in the campaign for nuclear phaseout. Obviously, my hopes for this bill are that it, too, might become law.
Having said that, I appeal at this point to MPs on all sides of the nuclear issue to support this bill at second reading so that it can be sent to a committee and become the context for a much needed debate.
Returning to the history of non-debate which I was recounting before, all we got from the Liberals between 1980 and 1984 was an internal departmental review which not surprisingly concluded that everything was all right.
There was some hope that the Conservatives in 1984 might return to their 1979 policy of having an inquiry, but this was not to be. Now we have the current minister of energy, the hon. member for Provencher, making speeches all over the place about the importance of nuclear power to Canada's energy future.
Just today, the minister of energy, speaking to a meeting of the Canadian Nuclear Association in Saskatoon, made an offer of federal money to the province of Saskatchewan to help bring a nuclear reactor to Saskatchewan. This is a classic case of one government with absolutely no mandate negotiating with another government with absolutely no mandate on anything, needless to say no mandate with respect to choosing to locate a nuclear reactor in that province.
Where does this strange commitment come from on the part of the minister of energy and on the part of the government as a whole? It is not from any visible, parliamentary, political or public process, that is for sure. We have had committees which looked at isolated aspects of the entire nuclear issue thanks to the freedom given to committees to study what they want.
A committee looked at food irradiation, for example, and recommended against it. The then minister of health ignored its recommendations. Who was the minister of health at that time? The member for Provencher, who is now the minister of energy and chief promoter of the nuclear option.
Another committee looked at high level radioactive waste disposal, producing a report called The Eleventh Hour, which made a number of good recommendations, most of which have been ignored by the current government. Is it just a coincidence that the research going on into high level radioactive waste disposal, not to mention the entire Whiteshell Nuclear Research establishment, is located in the riding of who? The hon. member for Provencher, who when he was the minister of health, systematically withheld information available in his department about radiation levels in Canada after the accident at Chernobyl.
I do not want to dwell too much on the hon. member for Provencher. He is simply an archetype of those whose minds are captive to the mindset of the nuclear industry, with a dash of constituency politics thrown in for good measure.
Of course, now the minister of energy and the nuclear industry have discovered the environment, particularly the greenhouse effect. Those who for years vacillated between heaping scorn on environmentalists or ignoring them now purport to have been Greenpeacers in disguise all these years and offer to lead the planet away from the dangers of greenhouse gases into the benign and beckoning embrace of increased reliance on nuclear generated electricity.
We recently had a unanimous report in this House from a committee that looked at the issue of the greenhouse effect for 18 months. That unanimous report made no recommendation whatsoever that nuclear energy ought to be regarded as Canada's response to the greenhouse effect. Yet, we have the hon. member for Provencher, the minister of energy-and I read his speeches faithfully as they come across my desk-saying time after time after time that nuclear energy is the answer to the greenhouse effect. Once again he is ignoring the unanimous views of a committee of this House as he did before with respect to food irradiation. If this is parliamentary reform, if this is giving hon. members more input into government policy, then I am
June 11, 1991

truly mystified as to what the government might mean by its rhetoric.
Not surprisingly, I find the greenhouse strategy of the nuclear industry to be reprehensible and wrong, particularly when it manifests itself in the TV ads by the Canadian Nuclear Association, an association whose major members are taxpayer funded organizations like AECL. In the absence of any real debate and/or decision by Parliament, why should public money be channelled into advocating only one side of the issue? Let us have a good debate. Let us pass this bill on second reading. Let us get it into committee and let us have a committee process in which all sides and all aspects of the debate can be aired and heard, including the issue of whether the nuclear option is the answer to the greenhouse effect.
Otherwise, if the government and/or its members defeat this bill and prevent such a process, perhaps they should provide the Campaign for Nuclear Phase-out or Energy Probe or the Concerned Citizens of Manitoba or various other environmental groups with the funds to design and broadcast ads, putting the other side of the case that is now being made on TV by the Canadian Nuclear Association.
In the time I have left, I would like to enter into the substance of the debate and give an account of why my own view is that we should discontinue the nuclear option, a view which I have held since the early 1970s when I first became active in anti-nuclear politics, long before I got to this place.
At the root of my position on this issue is not some sort of Luddite, negative reaction in principle to new technologies or progress.
My life is full of, and dependent upon, a variety of new technologies, many of which I quite enjoy and which I think greatly increase our quality of life. At the root of my opposition to the nuclear option is the quite rational judgment, which is therefore debatable, that the risk involved in nuclear energy is not acceptable, especially when we have other choices. The problem with a nuclear reactor is that when something goes wrong it really goes wrong and all the years of safe operation, all the years of pious assurances, all the years of technological hubris, are to quote an old hymn "like an evening gone". The

damage, the disruption and the other negative consequences last for lifetimes.
It is, as it has been called, an unforgiving technology, a Promethean bargain, that has only tragedy as its last result however long that result may take to occur. I have seen such consequences with my own eyes in Ukraine on the way into Kiev from the airport where older single family neighbourhoods are being bulldozed in order to facilitate the construction of high-rise apartments to house the some two and a half million people who have had to be relocated or evacuated as a result of the accident at Chernobyl.
I know that the reactor at Chernobyl is not identical to Candu reactors. I know that our system is better. I know that human error was involved at Chernobyl, but unless we are being asked to believe that our system is completely and utterly fail-safe and our people without capability for error then we have to ask ourselves whether the prospect of having to evacuate Toronto and environs, however improbable, is a risk worth taking when there are other choices.
I say that it is an unacceptable risk needlessly perpetrated by an over-all commitment to an energy policy dictated by the institutional self-interest of the energy supply industry in this country. Within this the most glaring institutional conflict of interest is the way in which AECL is asked to both market and make judgments that could affect the marketing of nuclear reactors.
A good example of this is AECL's involvement in high-level radioactive waste disposal. Being able to say that the waste disposal problem has been solved is crucial to the successful marketing of reactors abroad. For that very reason it should not be AECL that primarily determines the acceptability of disposal options. It should not be the institution which depends on a solution being perceived to have been reached and which is responsible for the judgment about whether that solution has indeed been found.
An even better example of this institutional self-interest is the way in which AECL at the Romanian reactor site in Cernavoda managed to turn a blind eye for years to the fact that it was a forced labour camp to which people were being conscripted to work, as well as to many other things in terms of structural flaws, et cetera, in the work being done there. AECL turned a blind eye

in order not to damage the prospect of further reactor sales abroad.
In any event, the rejection of risk because of the magnitude of the consequences rather than the probability of the consequences is an ordinary human judgment that we all make all the time. This is what many Canadians are doing in their rejection of nuclear power. Indeed, this is what the nuclear industry itself seems to be doing by insisting on things like the nuclear liability act which exempted it from any meaningful liability in the event of the kinds of accidents it keeps telling the Canadian public are so improbable. If these accidents are so improbable, why has the nuclear industry sought and received and now seeks to maintain this kind of protection from the consequences of accidents that it says itself are improbable? It is because it has made the same kind of ordinary rational judgment that the magnitude of the consequences make nuclear power a special case. That is what those of us who are against nuclear power are saying.
As for uranium mining and waste disposal, these for me are classic examples of inter-generational moral issues. We need to ask ourselves tough questions about whether we really have the right to bequeath to subsequent generations a world full of uranium tailings and lethal waste, not to mention the aboriginal justice issues raised by uranium mining itself in northern Saskatchewan for example.
Finally, there is the link between nuclear power and nuclear weapons which, in the final analysis, is the genesis of the special mystique attached to the nuclear industry in Canada and elsewhere ever since the Manhattan Project and the development of the atomic bomb. It is this link to the ultimate evil of planetary destruction which has provided the nuclear industry with a unique immunity from political accountability and authentic debate because it has its origins as a strategy for diverting public attention away from atoms for war to atoms for peace.
Nuclear power has been protected for years because it is the means by which nuclear technology for the purposes of global death has been morally and politically laundered. Even the Brundtland commission fudged on this issue, which is an example of the power of this issue
and its relationship to matters of national security and nuclear weaponry.
In July 1986, following the Chernobyl nuclear disaster, the federal NDP caucus launched its own public inquiry into all aspects of the nuclear fuel cycle in Canada. The inquiry was co-chaired by myself, as NDP environment critic at that time, and the former member for Vancouv-er-Kingsway, Ian Waddell, who was NDP energy critic at that time. We held hearings across Canada, received numerous briefs and presentations and conducted additional research into a variety of issues. No report was ever published because of a shuffle in critic portfolios that took both of us into other areas of concern before it was completed.
I would like, at this time, to share what I think were some of the major conclusions that were emerging from that process, all of which are in keeping with the spirit and substance of this bill.
One, the nuclear fuel chain from uranium mining to high level waste management poses unacceptable hazards to human health and the environment.
Two, nuclear power and nuclear arms are inextricably linked.
Three, nuclear power is unnecessary to meet Canadian energy needs. There are cheaper alternatives, notably demand reduction through improved energy efficiency.
Four, the Canadian nuclear industry has been a drain on the public purse. Alternative investments could create more long-term jobs and more balanced economic development.
Five, Canada's involvement in the production, manufacture, sale and use of nuclear materials and technology for all but medical purposes should be phased out.
Six, such a phase-out should be seen not in negative terms but as an opportunity to revitalize and retool the Canadian economy by reducing costly energy over-consumption in favour of a much more efficient energy use.
We could finally have an energy policy that reflected more than the narrow self-interest of the energy supply industry, an industry which, far from being interested in sustainable growth, is still committed to the infinite growth in a finite world that the Club of Rome warned us about 20 years ago.

Seven, the Nuclear Liability Act should be repealed and nuclear designers, suppliers and operators should bear full responsibility for any damage which may be caused by nuclear reactors and other nuclear facilities.
Eight, operating nuclear reactors and other nuclear facilities should be required to implement the best practicable technology for reducing risk and radiation exposure.
Nine, enforceable authorized limits for radiation exposure should be established for workers and the public from each nuclear facility, including both individual and collective limits.
Ten, the Canadian government should demand a shutdown of U.S. nuclear facilities which threaten Canadian lives and communities, including Perry, Fermi II and the Hartford Nuclear Reactor in Washington pending a public review of the facilities in consultation with Canadian nuclear regulatory officials.
Eleven, a reciprocal agreement with the U.S. should be established for continuous monitoring of all trans-boundaiy nuclear hazards. The IJC could provide a suitable mechanism for administering such an agreement.
Twelve, all aspects of visits to Canadian waters of nuclear powered and nuclear weapons capable vessels should be the object of a separate inquiry done in consultation with effective municipal and provincial governments as suggested by Gretchen Brewin, Mayor of Victoria, in 1986. In the meantime, until such inquiry reports, a moratorium on such visits should be in effect.
Thirteen-and I will be winding up soon-further construction of nuclear reactors should be halted in order to pursue other energy alternatives and in so doing to also minimize the accumulation of even more high-level radioactive waste.

Fourteen, there should be a permanent and legally enforceable ban on net imports of nuclear waste from other countries.
Fifteen, there should be a ban on reprocessing of waste from Canada and from other countries and an end to research in this technology by AECL and other government supported bodies.
Sixteen, responsibility for waste management should be removed from AECL and given to an independent commission reporting to the Department of the Environment with full public participation at every stage of the decision-making process and ample funding for the development of independent technical expertise.

Let the real costs of the nuclear product be seen and felt in the marketplace. I say this to my friends on the other side who are great fans of the marketplace.
Nineteen, Canada should be pushing for a change in the terms of reference.
With great respect, there are a number of people who want to speak in this debate. I hope he will not speak for more than another few seconds.

Nineteen, Canada should be pushing for a change in the terms of reference of the International Atomic Energy Agency so that it is no longer responsible for promoting nuclear power as well as preventing its misuse for military purposes. The IAEA's commitment to nuclear power has damaged its ability to report objectively on nuclear accidents.
A full accounting of all forms of public subsidy and support to nuclear power should be published, and a study of the impact of anticipated job losses in the nuclear industry should be conducted with a view to devising strategies for a transition to a post-nuclear energy economy.
Finally, I say to those who work in the nuclear industry that it should not be thought that there will be no more jobs in the nuclear industry if there were to be a nuclear

phase-out. There will be jobs for decades to come in decommissioning nuclear reactors, in figuring out what to do with all the high-level radioactive waste that we have to deal with already. All that a nuclear phase-out would do would be to turn the attention of the best minds in the nuclear industry to how to get ourselves out of this mess that we are in rather than how to get ourselves even deeper into the mess that we are already in.
I am soriy that my time has expired, and I am sorry that I may have treaded upon the indulgence of the House. I had even more to say, but I am anxious to hear what others have to say.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in this debate with some serious concern about the comments I have heard. Perhaps I will just refer to two very brief ones from the hon. member that I find interesting.
The hon. member talks about the government of which I am a member having no mandate to talk to another government in Saskatchewan, which he again says has no mandate. You have to understand that we are talking about a government that has a majority in this House talking to another government that has a majority in another House, and who is accusing us of not having a mandate? A person from a party which represents 22 per cent of the votes in Canada, which represents some very few seats in this House. I do not know who has the mandate and who does not.
I would suggest to the hon. member that he ought to look at who has the mandate and who has the right to make decisions on behalf of this country.
The other issue that I find rather exceptional in his comments is this. He says that we ought to be concerned about generational issues, that we ought not leave to our children and our grandchildren, et cetera, some of the legacies that we have today. I wish that party would have that attitude when it comes to spending money. I wish they would be concerned about that every time they rise in this House and say spend, spend, spend and let other generations worry about it. But that is not what this debate is about.
This debate is about nuclear energy and the benefits of nuclear energy to Canada. I want members to understand what we are talking about here. First off, my riding has one of the longest, largest operational nuclear power
plants in Canada, the Pickering nuclear generating station. It has in its capacity eight reactor units. Those reactor units provide approximately 20 per cent of the electricity that the province of Ontario consumes. So I have an interest, and I have a direct interest as a constituent and as a person who represents a constituency. That plant has operated without fail, without harm to any of its employees because of the fact that it is a nuclear plant since, I believe, 1964.
What do we have proposed here by this resolution? The resolution says that the Atomic Energy Control Board would refrain from licensing any nuclear power reactors starting in January, 1992, for 50 years. Fifty years we are talking about.
What would that do to Canada's economy and what impact would it have on the environment, short and long-term. I would like to talk about some of those, because there are some short-term impacts that would be rather dramatic to Canada, and particularly devastating to certain regions, including a region that I happen to represent. It is not just the riding of Ontario, but the province of Ontario.
Among the first victims would be the consumers living in the province that I live in and represent. Bill C-204, the one being proposed here, would prevent Ontario Hydro's Darlington nuclear power plant from having its last two reactors, reactor numbers three and four, licensed. The taxpayers of Ontario, the electricity consumers of Ontario, the NDP government of Ontario, which have invested $14 billion in building a new plant in Darlington, would be deprived by the NDP party of this House from commissioning and putting in place a reactor that will provide 10 per cent of the electricity to the province of Ontario.
It is amazing how they would stand for that. Even the NDP party of Ontario does not have the guts to do that kind of thing, yet these people over here in their glass houses sit there and say would it not be great to do so. Well, I find that rather unacceptable, particularly when these reactors are slated to come onstream in June and March of next year and the year following.
The inability to obtain operating licences for these two reactors would have a significant impact. There are some
935,000	customers in Ontario who would lose the benefits of access to this electricity that is needed a year and a year and a half from now.
June 11, 1991

Where do we go for it? I know where they would say we would go for it. They would just as soon we go to Ohio because there is no generating capacity in Ontario. We can go to Ohio and have them fire up their oil-fired generating plants so they can spew their acid rain over the province of Ontario and Quebec. That is what they prefer we do. What else would they prefer we do? Maybe go to northern Quebec and dam up a few more rivers and flood a few more terrains so that we can have the electricity. You cannot dam rivers in a year and a half, but that is what they would have us do. Or maybe it is because the member is from Winnipeg. He prefers to go to Winnipeg or the province of Manitoba and buy some electricity from one of their dams and rivers that they are talking about damming up.

It goes on from there. There is another impact of this whole resolution. We recently sold a Candu-6 unit to Korea.
