If you kill that sale, you kill an awful lot of opportunities and jobs for Canadians.
What does it mean? Well, $400 million of economic activity in Canada and 28,000 person-years of employment lost. From the party that talks about trying to create jobs in this country, by this simple resolution
28,000	man-years of work are gone with the scratch of a pen. I cannot believe that it truly-well, I can, because that is its way of doing things. I just find that the whole concept the NDP is proposing carries on this process.

technology, that maybe Canada is having second thoughts, we ought not to look at Canadian reactors.

We in Ontario have 17 reactors. There is one in New Brunswick and there is one in Quebec. I am talking about large electrical-generating reactors. They generate some 11,000 megawatts of power. speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please.

Mr. Speaker, the case has been well made by the proposer of the motion as to why this matter should go to a committee for a full-fledged debate on the matter.
I understand that this matter will stop at six o'clock p.m. and it will come up again in the fall for a continuation of this debate so that how the Liberal Party will vote is not to be determined by what is going to be basically a pro-nuclear speech here.
We have people on all sides of the issue, and we are not speaking with one voice. We are not monolithic.
To end the development and export of nuclear substances, nuclear reactors and atomic equipment and materials required to build nuclear reactors, which is ultimately the purpose of the bill as I think the member would admit, would mean a step backward in the economic development of Canada.
Regarding livelihoods of many Canadians and our international reputation, we have about 39 per cent of
the world's uranium supply and have developed a very successful and comparatively safe nuclear industry in this country. Our industry sells about $1 billion worth of uranium to domestic and foreign electrical utilities annually.
For years, Canada has been the world's largest uranium exporting country. In 1984, we became the largest producer, surpassing the United States.
After a decade of very little growth in the Canadian nuclear power industry, the 1990s looked promising for future expansion. The international markets for safe nuclear power plants are showing strong signs of revival. AECL predicts that its sales will triple over the next four years to about $660 million from $191 million in this fiscal year.
The nuclear power plant sold to South Korea will inject $400 million into the Canadian economy, creating about 7,000 jobs over a four-year period. With growing concerns about acid rain and the greenhouse effect, the Canadian nuclear industry has seized the opportunity to promote a technology that does not emit large quantities of S02 and C02 into the atmosphere.
Uranium, as members know, is largely sold to fuel nuclear reactors for electricity generation. The use of nuclear energy for that purpose is forecast to increase from the present 15 per cent to 20 per cent by 2020.
The increase in demand for nuclear energy will result in an increasing demand for uranium and create economic opportunities for Saskatchewan, which possesses vast reserves of uranium. It supplies over 20 per cent of the uranium produced in the western world.
The alternatives to nuclear energy in source provinces are running out. There is little hydro potential in Alberta, Ontario, Saskatchewan or the Atlantic provinces. Saskatchewan must have a new generating capacity in the next four or five year, and the nuclear option is a viable one.
I am the first to agree that nuclear energy must be very critically assessed. Many future scenarios indicate that meeting energy needs and environmental demands without nuclear power will be difficult. Nothing is perfectly safe, and this must apply to nuclear electrical generation as well. The tragic catastrophe in 1986 at Chernobyl brought the issue to the minds of everybody in the world.
June 11, 1991

That incident prompted the International Atomic Energy Agency to introduce two new international conventions. I will not give the details because my time is very short. We signed both of those conventions.
The incident resulted from an incredible series of human errors, incompetence, arrogance and bureaucratic squabbling in a then totalitarian system. The list of violations is extensive. It hardly needs to be said that safety precautions were nonexistent at Chernobyl.
Unfortunately, everywhere else in the world the social and political fall-out from the Chernobyl accident seems to be as long lived as the radioactivity it spewed. It provided opponents of nuclear energy with fresh ammunition. It was a tragic aberration in the history of nuclear power.
The Chernobyl type design, and this cannot be stressed too strongly, is not used anywhere except in the Soviet Union and could not be licensed to operate in our country.
Proponents of nuclear power express confidence that a new age of commercial reactor-building is already at hand, thanks to various breakthroughs in nuclear power technology. Advanced reactor designs are safer than existing models and can be built faster and for less money. A number of reactors being developed in the U.S., such as General Electric's fast-breeder PRISM reactor, Rockwell's SAFR reactor and the Department of Energy's Modular High-Temperature Gas-cooled Reactor, for example, incorporate self-shutdown mechanisms which require no mechanical, electrical or human intervention.
It remains, as we all realize, to convince a very sceptical public-I was one myself but I think the facts are beginning to change my mind-that commercial nuclear power is more reliable than ever.
The main economic disadvantage of building nuclear generating plants is their capital intensity, which makes them extraordinarily expensive. For example, in mid-1990 Ontario Hydro announced that the final price tag for Darlington would be more than $12.7 billion. It remains unknown how much it would cost to decommission a nuclear power plant once it reaches the end of its life cycle.
Private Members' Business
Yet, once in operation, nuclear generating systems produce cheaper energy per unit than thermal generating ones.
Since the Chernobyl incident, the use of nuclear energy has continued to grow around the world. In 1986, 26 nations operated 396 nuclear energy plants, which provided 15.5 per cent of the world's supply of electric power. In 1990, 25 nations operated 424 nuclear energy plants, providing about 17 per cent of the world's electricity. The steady expansion of nuclear energy world-wide since Chernobyl vindicates the safety and benefits of western style nuclear energy plants. Worldwide nuclear energy has displaced over 15 billion barrels of oil and saved $420 billion, I understand.
Our country relies on nuclear power for nearly 16 per cent of its electrical generation. Two new Candu reactors have been brought on line since the Chernobyl incident. In total, there are 20 Candu reactors operating in the country; 18 in Ontario and one each in New Brunswick and Quebec. Two others are, of course, under construction in Ontario. In 1989, four Candu reactors were included among the top 10 world reactors. The Point Lepreau station, located in New Brunswick, has been a world performance leader, producing power for more than 93 per cent of its eight-year life.
Now, what about other countries? In France, the number of nuclear energy plants increased from 49 in 1986 to 56 in 1990, supplying about 75 per cent of France's electricity, the equivalent of 68 million tons of oil. The French are proceeding with the development of a fast-breeder reactor, with the potential to deliver 50 times more energy from uranium than the standard water reactor.
In Sweden, the country that my friends in the New Democratic Party love to point at, I understand the government is moving away from its decision to phase out nuclear power by 2010. I understand that the Swedish government has concluded that it cannot afford to lose such a clean, low-cost source of electricity. In January 1991, the three political parties decided not to close two units in 1995 and 1996. Again to the member who proposed the motion, public opinion polls in Sweden showed last year that 75 per cent of the Swedish people believe nuclear energy will still be used after 2010.

Business of the House
Italy, which closed down its nuclear energy plants after Chernobyl, is now reconsidering since nuclear energy is the only valid alternative to the country's near total dependence on energy imports and oil.
What about Japan. A long-term government strategy calls for nuclear energy to supply 43 per cent of all electricity by 2010, up from 26 per cent today. To reach that goal 40 new reactors must be built.
There seem to be no insurmountable technical problems of solidifying wastes into chemically stable forms and disposing of them permanently, but political opposition has delayed the execution of specific projects in many countries. Waste disposal is therefore in hand only in the technical sense, but is well behind the schedule necessary for nuclear power to play an increasing role in the decades ahead.
Both the French and the Japanese convert their most toxic waste into a stable, glassy substance and store it in concrete bunkers at least several hundred metres below the ground. This is a temporary solution until experts determine where to dispose of the waste permanently.
There are obviously undesirable problems associated with the transportation of nuclear fuel and waste, as well as with maintenance or decommissioning of old plants at the end of their operating life. Where the equipment or building materials have become radioactive, the storage must be long-term and secure. Decommissioning costs escalate and the economics of the next generation of plants will become tougher.
However, the greenhouse effect is often a powerful argument for increasing the use of nuclear power if the safety and waste problems can be overcome.
I would ask the members: Is society better protected by dumping huge quantities of S02, NOX or C02 particulates and other contaminants into the atmosphere or by isolating relatively small quantities of radioactive waste?
A dispassionate view of the role of nuclear energy and global warming control was provided by a witness at the hearings of the Standing Committee on the Environment with impeccable environmental credentials, Dr. James Bruce. He said:
Where the nuclear option looks to be a reasonable option from
the economics of the situation, then I think it is probably better
from the point of view of the world's atmosphere than to build a
fossil fuel plant.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles A. Langlois (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have this opportunity today to address the House on Bill C-204 put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg Transcona.
I would like to take a moment, Mr. Speaker, to look at the nuclear industry in the national as well as global context. Mr. Speaker, the government of Canada actively supports the availability of a wide range of electricity supply options, including fossil fuels and nuclear power, as well as the various renewable options, such as biomass, wind, and solar power.
Conservation will also play an important and growing part in the overall future of electricity generation. Indeed, nuclear-electric generation compares favourably with other sources in terms of its overall environmental impact and does not contribute to acid rain, nor the greenhouse effect.
In sustaining a strong and viable nuclear industry, the governement of Canada continues to support the development of the uranium mining industry, as it has done for more than forty years. For decades, Canada has been the world's leading exporter of uranium and has ranked second behind the United States in terms of uranium output.
In 1984, Canada replaced the U.S. as the Western world's leading producer, and now produces more than twice as much as its nearest competitor, and one-third of the world's output. Today, the uranium industry in Canada employs almost 3,000 people, and generates revenues of close to $1 billion annually. Roughly 85 per cent of the uranium produced in Canada is destined for export, mostly to the United States, Japan and Western

June 11, 1991
Private Members' Business
Europe, where it is a major contributor to national energy programs.
Our uranium exports are critical to the electricity supply mix of our trading partners. For example, Mr. Speaker, how many realize that, in France, 70 per cent of the total electricity supply is nuclear-generated. In Belgium, the figure is 66 per cent, while in Sweden it is 47 per cent, in Switzerland 37 per cent, in Finland and Spain 36 per cent, in Japan 27 per cent, and in the United Kingdom and the United States about 20 per cent. These contributions are not insignificant, and Canada is a major source of fuel for many of these national programs.
In this latter context, Mr. Speaker, Canada's uranium producing industry is critical to our obligation under the Canada/U.S. Free Trade Agreement, which was implemented early in 1989. The FTA provides clear benefits to both Canada and the United States. It ensures that Canadian producers will have access to the U.S. market and that U.S. utilities will have access to Canadian uranium on competitive terms.
Uranium ranks sixth in terms of output value among Canada's metal commodities after copper, zinc, gold, nickel, and iron ore. However, it is much more important as an energy commodity. In 1987, Canada's uranium output was equivalent, in thermal energy terms, to the production of petroleum and natural gas combined, or almost four times Canada's production of coal. Canada has proven, untapped uranium resources which will ensure our dominant position in world markets well into the next century.
Like its competitors, however, Canada's uranium industry is currently facing an uncertain market, plagued by low and volatile spot prices, significant excess inventories and new sources of low-priced uranium from Eastern Europe.
Mr. Speaker, the proposed Bill would undermine the Canadian uranium and nuclear industries, resulting in the loss of thousands of jobs and millions of revenue dollars. Surely, Mr. Speaker, this is the time when the uranium mining industry deserves full support from governments, since uranium remains a highly valued energy resource for Canada and its principal trading partners.
Mr. Speaker, much of the increased concern about protecting the environment is focused on the uranium and nuclear industries. These concerns are shared by everyone who agrees that we should not pollute our natural environment. With regard to uranium mining, the government of Canada is confident that the monitoring processes instituted by both the federal and provincial regulatory agencies and the strict standards required by them has served to minimize environmental impacts and protect the health and safety of the mine workers and the public alike.
The uranium industry is one of the most highly regulated of all industrial activities. It should be pointed out that all Canadian uranium operations are classified as nuclear facilities. As such, they are controlled by the federal Atomic Energy Control Board (AECB) under the provisions of the Atomic Energy Control Act and the regulations derived from the Act.
The AECB issues licences for the operation of uranium mines only after ensuring that they will not have a significant effect on the health and safety of the mine workers and the public, and after reviewing measures designed to ensure adequate protection of the environment.
Mr. Speaker, Canada is committed to ensuring that the future development of uranium resources will not cause serious environmental impact. In April 1991, the AECB referred six proposals for new uranium mining projects in Saskatchewan for public review by an independent Panel pursuant to the federal government's Environmental Assessment and Review Process (EARP).
Officials of both the federal and Saskatchewan govem-menents have successfully negotiated terms of reference for a joint federal/Saskatchewan Panel, which will ensure that the environmental, health, safety and socio-economic impacts of these developments will be fully evaluated.
I am confident that this review process will demonstrate that uranium mining can be conducted in a safe, and environmentally responsible manner. I am very pleased that the two levels of government have fully co-operated in initiating this joint review process.
As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, Canada exports uranium only to those countries that have made a commitment to the international community that they will not use the uranium, or its byproducts, for nuclear

Private Members' Business
explosive purposes, and have signed a bilateral agreement with Canada to that effect.
The government of Canada remains firmly convinced that the non-proliferation precautions that have been put in place make it possible for Canada to contribute effectively to the peaceful uses of nuclear power and the resulting worldwide benefits, while ensuring that no diversion for weapons purposes occurs. Canada's safeguards are among the most stringent in the world, and the government of Canada believes that the sale of uranium from Canada contributes to our national nonproliferation objectives.
Mr. Speaker, the emerging awareness of the advantages of nuclear power bodes well for its future, and in turn for Canada's uranium producing industry.
In August 1988, Canada's Parliamentary Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources released a report entitled Nuclear Energy-Unmasking the Mystery. In its report, the Committee stated its position very clearly, and I quote:
"Maintaining the nuclear power option is vital to Canada's interests, as it is vital to the interests of society in general. There is a compelling case to be made in support of continued nuclear development, a case based upon the future inadequacy of conventional petroleum resources and upon the environmental degradation arising from burning coal in progressively greater quantities for electricity generation."
Mr. Speaker, it may be of interest to the Honourable Member for Winnipeg-Transcona to know that a November 1988 poll by Decima Research showed that eight out of ten Canadians feel that nuclear energy is a good or realistic choice for large-scale generation of electricity and that it will be an important future source of energy. This poll also revealed that six out of ten Canadians favoured nuclear energy as one of the ways to generate electricity.
So, in closing, Mr. Speaker, I will remind the hon. member for Winnipeg Transcona of the importance of the Canadian uranium and nuclear industry as both a reliable and clean source of energy for the future. Although well-intentioned, the proposed bill makes no sense in the national and global context and should therefore not be passed.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I would request that I be first on at the next sitting of the House on this particular bill.
We as Canadians have a great habit of creating something that is great for Canada and for the world, as we have with the Candu reactor and with nuclear energy. Over 50 per cent of the energy used in the province of Ontario is from nuclear energy.
As soon as we do this, there are Canadians who come forward and they want to destroy what other Canadians have created that is useful to this nation and to our competitiveness in the international market itself.
One of the great things we have going for us in this country is that we have energy. Nuclear energy is one of the cheaper forms. We would be paying about 20 per cent more for our hydro bills today if we had to pay from sources other than nuclear.
Take for example the Avro Arrow aircraft. We did that, and we destroyed it. We have to go outside our own country to find people who have confidence in our Canadian industry, in our Canadian creativity, in our Canadian scientific community.
When the Challenger space shuttle blew up in the air, they realized that it was the O ring that had caused it, that had let go. Immediately, the Americans and the international market realized that Canadians had the O ring in their Candu reactor and they never had an accident.
Let us talk about safety here. All this fear campaign about a great energy source we have in this country has got to stop. I would love a debate on it. I will fight for it any day of the week because it is one of the greatest creations of Canada.
Do not throw fear around about Chernobyl. The Russians built their energy plant first and their safety systems were non-existent. ITiey did not build them until after the accident. In Canada, we build our safety systems first, and they are built to protect us from human error. That is why they are there. We go from there, and we put our nuclear reactor in place last of all.
I just want to give a simple example of some of the fear campaign that is going on, if I may. Daughter number one comes home and she says to her mother: "Mother, I have two offers of a job for the summer. I can work at the Darlington nuclear plant or I can work in the restaurant

June 11, 1991
Government Orders
atop the CN Tower in Toronto". And mother says: "Oh, my goodness, I think you should go to the CN Tower restaurant", not knowing that that daughter working in the CN Tower restaurant in Toronto will get twice as much radiation as she will while working at the Darlington nuclear plant. Why? Because the safety devices are built into the Darlington nuclear plant, and the higher you go the more radiation you get. So wherever you go in Toronto, you will get more radiation in the CN Tower than any other place in Toronto.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, I will continue my debate later.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to conclude my remarks. We were talking about the importance of the elevator at Halifax, which is the only facility available for storage of milling wheat in that area.
The government will demonstrate a support for the Atlantic livestock and flour milling industries by taking a leadership role in ensuring the Halifax elevator remains open. We are committed to ensuring that does happen. The government has examined various options to this effect, including the proposed equalization assistance contained in the Grains 2000 report. The government is monitoring the situation in Halifax and, if needed, is
prepared to act quickly to ensure that the elevator facility continues to play an important role in the agrifood industry. The government is prepared to offer the Saint John elevator the same level of assistance as any program assistance offered to Halifax.
A number of other initiatives have been undertaken by the government to serve the interests of the Atlantic agrifood sector. Various initiatives have been put in place to help the region move toward self-sufficiency in feed grain production. We know how important it is to develop feed grain production there.
On December 14, 1989, the government announced the $6 million special Atlantic livestock initiative to provide temporary support to the Atlantic hog, beef, and sheep sectors over a period of three years.
Feed freight assistance rates were also recalculated in 1989 to take into account the storage component at the Halifax elevator. The feed freight assistance provides a fair equalization of feed grain prices with adjacent feed grain deficit areas. This is one of the programs being reviewed as part of the over-all agricultural policy review process.
Feed freight assistance has also been included in the over-all review of agriculture transportation policies being conducted as part of Growing Together, the agriculture policy review.
When the federal and provincial agriculture ministers met in Prince Albert, Saskatchewan, in August 1989, they agreed to a review of transportation policies. They decided then that the feed freight assistance, the Western Grain Transportation Act, and minimum compensatory rates on canola products should be reviewed in the light of changing economic and market conditions. The discussion paper Growing Together highlighted four pillars of reform to guide this review. The pillars include market responsiveness, increased self-reliance, a recognition of regional diversity with a national approach, and environmental sustainability. These are all very important areas.
The transportation committee of the policy review examined options for changes in the implications of such options. It presented its report to the federal-provincial agriculture ministers' meeting in Moncton in August
1990.
June 11, 1991

Subsequently, federal and provincial officials prepared a framework paper on options for using the funds currently spent on feed freight assistance and the Western Grain Transportation Act. This paper was presented to ministers in Winnipeg in November and is issued along with the committee's report as a basis for consultations.
Agriculture Canada has worked very hard to put in place a grains and oil seeds safety net program that will help farmers throughout the country, including those in the Atlantic provinces. This program has two components, the Gross Revenue Insurance Plan, or GRIP, and the Net Income Stabilization Account, or NISA. Together they provide farmers with predictable stabilization. This is probably the most comprehensive legislation that agriculture has ever had the opportunity of having in history. It is a very major piece of legislation and we feel it is a good process. The producers and stakeholders were all involved in developing that program and we feel it will be of great benefit and offer the predictability that is necessary for the long-term viability of agriculture.
Agriculture Canada is also taking a very active part in an industry-government review of the Atlantic Livestock Feed Strategy. A task group led by the Atlantic Farmers Council is examining all our programs to ensure that they contribute most effectively to the development of the Atlantic livestock sector. The task group is expected to submit a preliminary report for consideration by the federal and provincial agriculture ministers when they meet in Kananaskis in July of this year.
In conclusion, I would like to re-emphasize that this government has not forgotten the needs of agriculture producers in Atlantic Canada or, as a matter of fact, in any part of this great country.
We have been working with the provinces and with farm groups to develop new programs to better serve the industry.
We need to re-examine old programs that have been in place for years if we are going to achieve this. If we find the programs have outlived their usefulness, as At and East clearly has, we must take steps in the best interests of the industry and the country to adapt or remove them so that both farmers and the government can get better value for their money.
Government Orders
I was very pleased just a short time ago when there was an agreement in this House to see debate conclude on Friday and get on with this important piece of legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the parliamentary secretary, who is very sincerely interested in agriculture, for his contribution. I was very glad that he mentioned in his remarks the study commissioned by the minister of grains and seeds, et cetera, et cetera, which is known, I understand, as the Grains 2000 Atlantic Port Study.
I know the parliamentary secretary himself is a very successful farmer, I think in a different area of grains. I do not know if it is all in peas or not, but it is in different ingredients. What I was hoping the parliamentary secretary might say and my question to him at this stage is this: he has read, I presume, the report of the Grains 2000 Atlantic Port Study. Is he aware that the report says that unless some more export grain is channelled through that elevator, it is jeopardized.
As a farmer in his own professional life, can he see Atlantic members involved with their farm constituencies sit idly by and let a subsidy program that has been here as long as the Crowsnest Pass-not quite because that was in 1966 and it was J. F. Pickersgill, I was in the House when he mentioned why this At and East was there to enhance the delivery of grain through the ports of Halifax and Saint John.
Forget about Saint John. It is gone and it is not fighting it, although it has lost the jobs. However, as a farmer, and not necessarily as the parliamentary secretary, if he had to put his produce into an elevator, that a 25-person steering committee that he is aware of, which is the Grains 2000 Study, said that unless it gets help it is dead and gone, would he sit idly by and let our government put this bill through without any real debate and without what we have talked about for two and a half to three years, admitting there are differences in trade patterns now, admitting there are differences in so many things in the world but admitting one thing that the parliamentary secretary did not admit, that for two and a half to three years the Departments of Agriculture, Transport, seeds, et cetera, et cetera, regional development have been trying to come up with a package to offset the loss of this $28 million to $40 million subsidy which in terms of seed money, as other people have said here today, produced more income, more taxes and less unemployment insur-

June 11, 1991
Government Orders
ance and less welfare than the cancellation of this policy?
Would the parliamentary secretary sit idly by? What is his answer to my constituents who are the farmers in the Annapolis Valley who have listened for three or four years in good faith, waiting for offsets or some program to help take care of the cancellation. We all realize that subsidies in abstract are distorting, but they also are life-giving in certain situations. What is his answer to these farmers of my riding and to other good Canadians in Atlantic Canada if the recommendations of the Grains 2000 are not implemented? As I think the parliamentary secretary knows, there has not been one tittle of concrete movement or one concrete commitment to help fill the vacuum with the loss of the subsidy and put in some offsets. So what answer does the parliamentary secretary have to that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. colleague is asking me to speak as the parliamentary secretary and he is also asking me to speak as a farmer. I love to speak as both whenever I get the opportunity.
The hon. member has indicated the loss of $28 million to $42 million in the Atlantic region on the At and East program. I want to remind the hon. members that the majority of that money was used in central Canada as well as in the Atlantic region. To say that total loss took place in the Atlantic region is not correct because it happened in Ontario, and it also affected the farmers in my riding.
We do have elevators to ship out of and to receive there and we do have an inland terminal at Goderich which is quite capable of fully loading ocean vessels to full seaway depth.
And with navigation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Yes, all those things are possible. We are also committed to spending tax dollars wisely and fairly. We have indicated that we will support the Halifax elevator every way we can and we are committed to doing that. We have offered the same options to the Saint John facility if it wishes to take up some of this.
We also want to support the livestock and feed grains industry in the Atlantic region. Further development of the production of grains there is very, very important because that is job creation as well and can probably
produce, with the new varieties that are being promoted today, all kinds of opportunities in the Atlantic region for new grains and some oilseeds to be grown in those areas.
We are committed as well to working with agriculture to do that.
As I said, there are the two programs: the Atlantic Livestock Feed Initiative and the Special Atlantic Livestock Initiatives Program. We hope that we can and will continue to support agriculture across Canada, particularly in the Atlantic region.

Madam Speaker, if someone else wanted to ask a question, I would appreciate the parliamentary secretary's answer.
I was here when J.W. Pickersgill gave a statement of why the whole At and East was there. When I get on, recognized by the Speaker later on in my speech, I am not going to give him too many facts and figures about the job loss and all that. It has been covered well by those who have spoken here on the debate today, but this is such a symbolic thing that I can tell you that in terms of Atlantic Canada, this is the cut of the Gordian knot to the producers close to the land.
I have a fundamental philosophy: the closer to the land you are the more basic you are, the closer you get to the cities and the concrete canyons and that is life, things become more difficult and more artificial.
Take it easy, Pat.

I appreciate that. I do not want to get personal. That is not my speech yet.
The parliamentary secretary, the member from Calgary Southwest, is a nice, interesting young man who has got a computer mind and an interesting competent ability, but when he led off this debate he said: "The bill now before the House seeks to eliminate a subsidy which has outlived its original purpose and has become a burden on the public purse." I want to ask the parliamentary secretary what the distinction is between the At and East subsidy and the Western Grain Transportation subsidy?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I suppose they could be similar in certain ways, but we have to recognize that the markets we are supplying have changed considerably since this bill was put into place in 1967 and we recognize that.
June 11, 1991

In the first part of my speech, I gave the figures of what grain exports were to Europe at that time.
As the hon. member knows, since then we have developed major grain markets in Asia, China and in other parts. Because of other components that have come into this, the Export Enhancement Program of the United States and the programs of the European countries, many of those countries that were net importers of wheat now are exporters of wheat. All those things have changed. We have to find the best possible means of exporting our product. We have to compete in the world with what we are selling and we have to move it to a position of loading for shipment in the most economical way possible.
I believe we are being responsible in what we are doing in responding to that. I know for a fact that the withdrawal of the At and East program does not affect the people and the producers in the province of Ontario to the extent that it does in the Atlantic regions. As I said before, we are going to work with those people, with the provincial governments and with the producers to make sure that they are compensated in some way that we can work with them so that they will have a viable and good future in agriculture.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to discuss in some detail the bill before the House, Bill C-ll, an act to amend the Railway Act, insofar as it applies to grains and flour subsidies.
I must confess that I am a little bit amazed to be speaking in this House again on this very bill. At one time in the last session it died on the Order Paper.
I was sitting in my home in Thunder Bay watching television, watching the very capable and eloquent delivery on the folly of this bill by my colleague and good friend from Gander-Grand Falls. He expounded the history of the At and East bill from the development in this House in 1956 onward and it was very interesting to me.
The bill is brought on again with some surprise. I thought at one time that the government had reconsidered its position and decided not to bring forward this
Government Orders
legislation in this session, but obviously without much luck. Here we are debating it at third reading.
There is a certain amount of offensiveness in the way this legislation is brought on. Two years ago the government first brought forward its plan to do away with the At and East rates and the effects of this legislation were immediately implemented by an Order in Council. What we are doing today is in effect debating a bill which has already been operative for the last two years. We are doing some housecleaning on behalf of the government in order to implement the proper legislation which already has been operative for the last two years.
I, like some of my colleagues, have only been here for two or three years, but it has always been my understanding that any legislation in order to be operative must be passed and debated in this House, and then implemented if it is passed. How the procedure can implement the workings of this bill to cut out those subsidies and then two years later bring before us the bill for debate leaves me somewhat dumbfounded with respect to the procedures within this House.
I am told by my colleagues who have been here for a long time that the implementation of this bill was done by an Order in Council and that is the way this government has been operating in this House since 1988. That along with the closure motions and so on has taken the responsibility of government away from the people and those of us who are elected to come here, hoping to do a job. What it has done has really been an administrative form of government without due respect and due regard to the parliamentary process. I take great exception in the way this is being done.
What I will do, since it has been implemented, is talk in some detail on some historical perspectives of the bill before the House, but as I stated it really does not matter because it has been effective for the last two years.
The subsidy in question was known as the At and East rates. It really means that from Buffalo in the east to the eastern coast, a program was in effect since the mid-1960s which maintained a fixed rate level for the movement of grain and flour via rail to eastern Canada mainly for export.
Because the rail rates at that time were frozen, the cost of moving this grain from all the ports in the southern part of the Great Lakes to other areas such as Halifax and Saint John was a subsidy which was paid to

Government Orders
the railways for the movement of this grain. It was a subsidy, as my colleague behind me stated in the Question Period, which amounted to $40 million.
On this side of the House, we are not going to say that $40 million is not a lot of money, but $40 million when you talk about the grain shipments in Canada and the subsidies given to grain shipments is not a great deal of money when you consider that we spend $3.5 billion in this country on the movement of grain and on the subsidies of grain.
The At and East program evolved in response to a 1959 rate reduction by U.S. railways for grain movement. Historically the purpose of the legislation was to be competitive in the eastern part of this country with the U.S. farmers who were also producing the same commodity and offering it for sale to the same customers to whom we were trying to sell this product.
Since that time, we have been exposed to the round of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. We just cannot seem to come to grips with, or arrive at any solution or agreement in principle to, the subsidies offered to the producers of grain, not only in Canada and in the United States but offered also to our friends in the European Community.
Since that time, we have been faced with what is a common term in this House but which is growing in importance; what the Americans are doing under their Export Enhancement Program. The Export Enhancement Program as applied to the grains in this country is devastating our grain industry.
Speaking generally with respect to the growing of grain and the movement of grain, the system at one time served all Canadians very well. It served the grain producers, those who grew the product on their farms. It served the mills. It served the flour exporters, the shipping companies and the railways. It served the elevator workers in Thunder Bay, the area I represent, and in British Columbia and Prince Rupert.
I refer always to the same phrase we so often hear: the movement of grain in this country is 10 per cent protein and 90 per cent politics. In 1985, when this government took over, we saw a dwindling of the grain movement coming out of the west into the port of Thunder Bay and down to the St. Lawrence seaway where we at one time
enjoyed over 50 per cent of that export market. It dwindled to less than 35 per cent.
The drought in 1988 and the Export Enhancement Program-I talked about how the grain industry is subsidized in the United States-put all grain producers in this country and those involved in the grain industry in a great deal of jeopardy.
The farmers themselves have been placed in some difficulty. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister, and I do not want to embarrass him by these figures, at the agricultural committee this morning said that in 1983 the price of a bushel of grain was $5.80. These are the problems that we find in the grain industry today.
In 1983, the price of a bushel of grain was $5.80.
In 1991 the price of a bushel of grain is $2.75. It just so happens that in 1983 there was a different government, represented by this side of the House, when the price was $5.80. In the seven intervening years, through the mismanagement of the grain policies in this country, the price of a bushel of grain was dropped by almost half, to $2.75.
I think when we talk about the grain industry and the transportation of grain, all of the ports and all of the cities on the St. Lawrence seaway have been hampered by this problem that has been imposed by this government. All of the ports from Thunder Bay right through to Halifax, Saint John, down river ports beyond Montreal and east of Montreal have suffered because of this government's lack of concern and, I think, complete lack of knowledge of what the grain industry is all about.
The grain industiy is not just a matter of growing grain and selling it. It is a very, very intricate business that relies on timing from the time it is harvested on the prairies to the time it hits the grain cars and from the grain cars to the boats. All of that must be integrated with the sale of the commodity to our friends, usually in the eastern countries of Europe. So it is a very complicated business that needs tremendous involvement and the involvement of a government which understands and empathizes with the problems, not only of the communities, but of the people who are involved with growing this product.
June 11, 1991

At one time our only competition was in the United States. However, now we see with the advent in 1992 of the European Common Market that that may be the greatest competition we are going to have in the grain business in the world. It will be coming not from the United States, but from the European Common Market, which has in place a subsidy that really causes a serious dilemma in the Canadian wheat business.
In addition to the dilemma of the farmers and the cities involved on the St. Lawrence seaway, in the last seven years, the shippers have been having a serious problem. I can remember when there were 160 to 170 bottoms or boats that would carry that grain from the port of Thunder Bay down to the down river ports beyond Montreal. Now we are down to something like 70 or 75 bottoms or ships that are available to carry that grain down. That number is lessening because we do not use it and we do not take this business and use it for the nine months of the year. What is happening is that those who are involved with shipping grain to the down river ports are saying they just cannot afford to operate those ships.
It is another dilemma we find ourselves in. I warn this government that we are going to have bumper crops in the future and we are going to have to export this grain and we are going to have to use the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence seaway. Unfortunately, because of its actions, when it comes time to use that capacity of 22 million tonnes in Thunder Bay, and those boats that are on the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence seaway, they will not be available. They will either have been sold to other countries or torn up for scrap. That magnificent facility that we have on the St. Lawrence seaway, starting from the port of Thunder Bay, will no longer be. It has been an operative organization for so many years. It is an organization that we will not be able to replace in this country. That is one of the dilemmas because of the transportation policies of this government.
One of the other areas that causes us problems is the glut of wheat on the market. We all know what has happened with the amount of grain that we have not been able to sell, or sometimes have had to sell at distressed prices brought on by the trade agreement, brought on by the lower prices for Canadian product.
Government Orders
The low prices, again, cause such a dilemma for our Canadian producers.
The elevator workers in this country are in a terrible state. I just see on television-
