Madam Speaker, let me thank my colleague from Annapolis Valley, a former chairman of the transportation committee and a very fine chairman.

June 11, 1991
Government Orders
Getting back to the serious issue of the grain industry and the farming community of this country, what we are seeing is the over-all aspects of Canadian transportation and we see what happens to a country and to a government which operates without a policy on national transportation issues.
A country the size of Canada without a national transportation policy suffers and the farmers suffer and those involved in transportation suffer and the transportation industry suffers when there is no policy that we can follow. The country not only suffers, it bleeds and in some instances such as we are seeing today it haemorrhages and we cannot stop the haemorrhaging.
The legislation we have before us is just another example. Last week in this House we talked about another transportation issue that involved the Aeronautics Act and the changes in the piecemeal legislation, and two weeks ago the legislation was before this House with respect to airport transfer of power. Those are just some of the issues that have been hitting this side of the Chamber in piecemeal fashion.
Let us look at what has happened in this country since 1984, lacking the transportation policy it so vitally needs. Just this week in the Ottawa paper, there was a magnificent three-part article by Mark Kennedy, Ten Steps to the Dryden Disaster. One of the crucial areas there was the lack of regulation within this country, and it had a great part in the disaster. Look what happened right here in Ottawa in the last few weeks with respect to deregulation of the trucking industry. Look at what is happening to all of our seniors in this country because they cannot get on a passenger rail service and fulfil their desires to travel across and see this country because we do not have passenger rail service any longer.
Then there is the failure of this government to recognize the St. Lawrence seaway as a viable transportation route in Canada; the lack of the federal government to support a national transportation policy that uses national highways, to take an obligation to provide for the Trans-Canada Highway, which right now borders on disaster. This is what affects Canadians and it makes us wonder what Canada is all about. Without transportation this country has no unity, and without unity we have no Canada.
What this country needs and what I implore this government to do is develop a national transportation policy? that will benefit farmers, shippers and all those who are so adversely affected by what we see happening here today.

Madam Speaker, I would like to ask my friend the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon, who was a very valuable and constructive member of the transportation committee, how he, as a member from central Canada, Thunder Bay, where a lot of these grain boats start, views the cancellation of admittedly a subsidy program that certainly benefited and was supposed to benefit the Atlantic Canadian ports, even though they are sometimes in competition with the Thunder Bay port.

I thank my colleague from Annapolis Valley for that question. I will try to answer it as succinctly as possible. If we develop and operate under a national policy of transportation within this country, we must realize that we cannot just look at one area of the country and ask for its betterment at the expense of another area. When we develop and work by a policy, we have to look at Canada as a whole.
As I said, in the development of plans and procedures for the future that will take us into the 21st century with respect to rail transportation and the use of the St. Lawrence seaway, we should develop a policy that will enhance and ensure that the Great Lakes shipping fleets will stay in place and that we are able to utilize the benefits of the St. Lawrence seaway and the grain elevator systems.
I think of an article we had this past week in the Thunder Bay newspaper about Herbie Danaher, the business agent for all of the elevator workers. It gave his trials and tribulations as the business agent for that union and what he has had to do over the years. At one time we had 1,800 workers and now we have 800 workers on the waterfront. The article tells how he has had to cope with those problems and deal with those people who had such a knowledge of the shipment of grain.
Those are the areas that cause great concern to any member of Parliament that is involved in this very vital industry. We are not operating in a system; we are not
June 11, 1991

operating with an over-all plan that enhances all of the communities and all of the regions of this country.

Madam Speaker, I want to thank my hon. friend for that answer. He answered my next supplementary in part by talking about a national transportation system and trying to have a balanced plan enhancing all the different parts of the plan.
I would like again to ask my hon. friend to try to give his perspective to members of the government and to Canadians who may just happen to have stumbled upon this debate through television.
I know this member as a very fair individual, notwithstanding that he is from central Canada and we from the east sometimes feel central Canada tariff policies leave much to be desired. However, I am asking the member from Thunder Bay-Nipigon, in this balanced plan for transportation that I know he has worked for in the transportation committee, what his reaction is to an At and East subsidy that has varied between $28 million and $40 million? That is the variance over the period of years it has been in effect.
I would like to hear his reaction to the cancellation of that as well as the maintenance of the western grain transportation subsidy that helps farmers in the prairies get their grain to the western markets through the ports of Vancouver and/or Prince George, to the tune of $700 million or $800 million.
Does the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon feel that that is a type of situation that helps make Canadians in Atlantic Canada feel they are fairly treated?

Madam Speaker, I thank my colleague from Annapolis Valley-Hants for that question. Not to correct him, but the Western Grain Transportation Act is an act that enhances and assists not only the shipment of grain to the west coast ports of Vancouver and Prince Rupert, but it also enhances and assists grain that is shipped in the summertime to Port Churchill in the northern part of Manitoba. It also subsidizes the movement of grain to the ports of Thunder Bay, but does not subsidize the movement of grain from the Thunder Bay port to the down river ports.
What we have here is an industry that the government subsidizes in some form by about $3.5 billion a year. I think what we have to do-I will go back to this policy
Government Orders
that we have to develop-is take that $3.5 billion and spend it more wisely than we are doing. It must not be spent at the exclusion of areas and regions such as those represented by my friend. What we have to do is impress upon the people in this industry in Canada that we can no longer have the terrible unstable conditions on our waterfronts that I see developing in Thunder Bay, that I see developing today in Vancouver and Prince Rupert, that I see developing in Churchill.
With the kind of money that the taxpayer in this country is spending, in excess of $3.5 billion a year, what we should be able to do is assure those workers, who have dedicated their lives to this industry, that at least they would have some stability and security of employment so that they do not have to look at layoffs which may extend for 18 months. At the end of the 18 month period, even if they have been employed by Saskatchewan Wheat Pool or Manitoba Pool or Cargill or any of the others, they are no longer an employee of that company. It is just not fair and it applies to every region in this country.
We have to stabilize the labour force in those areas that are involved in the vital industry of grain, the growing of grain and the shipping of grain in Canada.

Madam Speaker, I rise to take part in the debate this evening on Bill C-ll, an act to amend the Railway Act dealing with grains and flour subsidies. I rise after listening today to many knowledgeable orators in this area, such as the hon. members for Gander-Grand Falls, for Regina-Lumsden, Halifax West, Thunder Bay-Nipigon, and Annapolis Valley-Hants, who has been part of the question and comments and a former chairman of the transportation committee, and many others. It brings home to me, and hopefully brings home to others in this great institution, that the Government of Canada, whatever government that may be, is going to have to continue to play a role in the transportation industry in this country because we are too big a country and too diversified to let the transportation industry live by the free market system.
We see this in this very bill because the results of it are already in effect today. The subsidy part of the At and East program was eliminated in July 1989. This rail subsidy has helped Atlantic Canada become more competitive in the shipping of grain by way of its ports. Along

June 11, 1991
Government Orders
with all the other cuts to transfer payments and whatever, we are going to eliminate this financial arrangement.
The effects of this have already been felt, as seen in the case of the elevator in Saint John where jobs have been eliminated. If the Halifax elevator is forced to close, this will be another devastation to this part of the country.
I agree, and the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission agree, that the rates we are talking about are inefficient and distorting but I do not agree with the government's slash and burn approach to the problem. The subsidy should not be eliminated until the effects of such a move can be offset by other programs.
The termination of this subsidy, known as the At and East, will have serious economic consequences, as I have said, for the maritime ports; not only for them but for associated activities which depend on the movement of export grain and flour through these ports. Activities at the grain elevators, port employment and railway employment will be significantly affected.
The bill will also have a negative impact on flour milling and the movement of domestic feed grains in the Atlantic region.
The importance of maintaining elevators such as the one at Halifax cannot be overstated. It is a viable operation, critical to the entire economy of the Atlantic region. As well as the activity generated by the movement of export grain through the facility, the elevator also plays a vital role in the storage and handling of domestic feed grain and milling wheat. The local poultry and egg industries and, to a lesser extent, the beef industry will be seriously affected should the Halifax elevator be unable to remain in operation.
In addition, the Halifax elevator is utilized as the only means of storage for milling wheat by the only Atlantic region flour mill.
The use of the Halifax elevator for domestic feed grains represents the only competitive alternative to the use of railways as a means of obtaining the required feed ingredients for the local livestock and poultry industry. The use of light vessels to Halifax with truck delivery beyond is the only competition facing the railways for the movement of domestic feed.
When will the government realize this? When will the government halt this brutal affront to the economy of Atlantic Canada?
As I said before about the local livestock and poultry industries, the maritimes are faced with a tremendous disadvantage in terms of feed costs versus the competition in Quebec and Ontario. Once again, the government is giving the predominant provinces priority while ignoring the Atlantic region.
This was discussed by the member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon and the member for Annapolis Valley-Hants. This is another way of playing the regions off against one another. We talk about unity in this country. As long as we play one part of the country off against the other we will not have the unity that is so greatly desired by most people in this country.
I say to the government that we must stop this. When other means are put in place and the regions of the country are able to stand on their own two feet, when the regions-whether the Atlantic region, the western region or the northern region of this country-are able to realize a standard of living that is equivalent to the other larger provinces then I believe that we are on the road to having greater Canadian unity among our people. It is not just a language problem.
The shipment of export flour through the port of Halifax also contributes significantly to employment of this port. It plays an important role for the railways in positioning boxcars in the maritimes for domestic use. Another issue that has arisen in the last couple of weeks concerns the containers moving out of the Halifax port because the railways cannot afford to move them.
The cars utilized for shipment of export flour to Halifax are then repositioned within the maritimes for the shipment of domestic cargoes. As I have been saying, the At and East program has a significant impact on the Atlantic region and particularly the Halifax-Saint John area.
Through programs over the last normal year almost 90 per cent of the total tonnage moved was exported through Atlantic ports. Export grain moving under the program represented at that time almost 100 per cent of the volume handled at the Saint John elevator and 60 per cent of the volume handled at the Halifax elevator. The discontinuation of the program already has and will
June 11, 1991

Government Orders
continue to have serious repercussions on the economic depression of the maritimes.
According to the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission, $14,5 million in economic activity has been lost in the region as a direct result of this government's strategies. The elimination of the At and East rail freight rates hurts not only workers whose jobs depend on the busy ports and righst-of-way but the Atlantic agricultural sector as well.
Already local livestock and poultry industries face a major disadvantage versus the central Canadian producers in terms of feed costs.
Prince Edward Island produces only 80 per cent of the feed grain it needs to supply the needs of its livestock and poultry industry. New Brunswick produces only 35 to 40 per cent of its requirement and Nova Scotia produces only 20 per cent. The maritime provinces depend heavily on grain shipped from western and central Canada.
Higher costs from these grains, which will certainly result from higher transportation costs, will cripple these industries, causing a further decline in the economic activity and employment in this region. The potential exists for further economic harm to Atlantic Canada should the grain elevator at Halifax be unable to continue operation.
As has been expressed by the member for Halifax West earlier in the day, we must take steps to ensure that further negative economic consequences for the Atlantic region be avoided.
This government must support Atlantic Canada on this issue. This government must support the directives to which they were elected, and it must stop ignoring the pleas of Atlantic Canada.
Again, I hate to repeat this, but this is just another emphasis on shutting down Atlantic Canada, shutting down rural Canada, pitting one part of this country against the other.
In closing, I want to say that the At and East Program may be outdated, but it is this government's responsibility to help the affected industries, whether they are western and central Canadian grain producers, railway workers, Atlantic livestock producers or eastern ports. It
must do something to protect them during the transition period and beyond.

I would just like to ask the member if in fact the cutting of the At and East Program was a direct result of the free trade agreement where it was agreed to cut subsidies. Of course, this cut came in the budget of 1989 when there was almost $400 million cut in various farm programs: crop insurance cut by $200 million, the At and East by $60 million, Rail Branch Rehabilitation Program by $48 million, grain and crop advance payments by $54 million, dairy exports by $12 million, commodity-based loans by $15 million and the Canadian Dairy Commission by $10 million.
Do you feel that the government was very naive when it made all these cuts because it is obvious the Americans have not cut theirs? Because they have not cut theirs, and our program has already been slashed, the program is in the process of being removed, or it has already been discontinued, will the Americans fill that market to the detriment of the Canadian producers?

I want to thank my colleague for his questions. A simple answer: yes, I believe this has happened. We have known that the subsidy has been a dirty word around here for some time. Subsidies to the agriculture sector, to the transportation sector, are being eliminated almost daily, as a result, yes, of the free trade agreement and as a result, also, of our neighbour to the south putting pressure on the people involved in the GATT negotiations. This is something that has been ongoing for a number of years. The elimination of this and the subsidies still being paid in the United States shows that we have got ahead of ourselves and probably are shooting ourselves in the foot by doing this.
Certainly the agriculture community and the transportation community in this country, as I said a few minutes ago, needs subsidies, it needs to be helped to keep this country strong and great. With the elimination of this particular subsidy, we will see the transportation of these goods through other parts south of us in the United States.
Yes, I believe that this is a direct result of the free trade agreement because in the negotiations, and after the signing of this agreement, it was stated that our subsidies on grains and farm commodities, on shipping

Government Orders
and on transportation must be eliminated or we could not participate in this free trade agreement.
I think we have come out second best on this deal. I believe we must go back to the table now, when they are negotiating another deal, and renegotiate these things that were mentioned in the first place by the Macdonald commission, that there were certain of these things that should be negotiated and protected for us in Canada.
I say that this has not been done, but we had better look seriously at it or we will not not only have manufacturing left in Canada, but our agriculture products will all be supplied to us from south of the border.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. You almost look surprised that I was up on debate on a bill. Perhaps it has been so long.
I would like to say at the outset that I am not pleased to debate Bill C-ll. I am not pleased because of what it does to Atlantic Canada, Quebec, Ontario, and to the prairie provinces. But it is an example of how this Conservative government does not understand Canada and why it exists as a separate country north of the United States and how it functions.
I want to work my way through that argument during my time debating this bill tonight.
This bill, which is the elimination of financial assistance to move grain and flour from one part of Canada to another will leave it to the market system, to free enterprise. It is because subsidies distort the picture, because they are no longer needed, the government says. They have outlived their usefulness.
Well, tell that to the 5,000 or so men and women, and their families, whose jobs have outlived their usefulness, thanks to the elimination two years ago of the At and East rail subsidy.
We are a country that basically built itself north of the 49th parallel in a very narrow band of people from sea to sea, with scattered settlements elsewhere up toward our other sea. Our connection is east-west, yet the normal draws in the market economy would dictate that the raw materials, in this case grain, would travel from where they are harvested to where the largest number of people are, or where export position is.
On this continent that draw is southward, to where we have a neighbour which has a population ten times our size. The economies of scale work to put pressure on that, and it is only through interventions of governments, Conservative, Liberal in the past, that has enabled us to remain separate.
We now have a Conservative government that has decided that the marketplace is something it is more concerned about than the survival of this country. It has been slowly cutting off the ties that have held this country together.
It is no irony that the same month this subsidy ended, half of the rail passenger services in this country were eliminated, a devastating blow to Atlantic Canada.
It is no surprise that a year and a half to two years into the subsidy having been removed, that we now see other freight components of the services to Atlantic Canada being undermined. The railroads are extremely worried about their competition from American rail. The port of Halifax is worried that those containers that have been coming by rail to Atlantic Canada, to Halifax, will now go by rail to New York, because of the kind of rate cutting that is happening down there, both on rail and in terms of the ports. They have already seen container traffic that originally was destined for Halifax to be picked up by foreign vessels relocated to Montreal. They are seeing rail lines removed, they are seeing their air system totally restructured in Atlantic Canada, to the point where you cannot go anywhere unless you go through Halifax. That is a boon to Halifax but it doesn't say much to a lot of the other communities which used to have a higher level of service to other parts of Canada.
So, Madam Speaker, I suggest that the elimination of the At and East subsidy is just yet another symptom of a major disease that has struck this country and it is called Conservatism and it is the implementation of the rightwing agenda.
But it hasn't just hurt Atlantic Canada. By and large, most of the grain and the flour that goes to Atlantic Canada under the At and East program goes by rail. Only one-third of that is going to Halifax by marine.
June 11, 1991

It is the rail workers in Quebec who have lost their jobs because of this move, the workers who maintain the trains, who operate them, the communities which service the trains and service the employees by providing goods and services.
In Ontario it is two-fold. Let me change that, it is three-fold. It is the rail jobs, the elevator jobs and the shipworker jobs, the men and women who ply the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence seaway who have seen yet another decline in the amount of grain available to them to move. That grain has not been redirected through another east-west link. It just does not move. That is why we have seen Ontario elevators shut down. That is why we have seen elevators in Atlantic Canada shut down.
One of the elevators in Ontario is now being considered as a storage space for used tires. Used tires in a grain elevator, can you believe that? That is their only hope for any kind of economic assistance, storing somebody's garbage in their grain elevator. Even the rats will be out of work because they will not have the feed to live on.
When my colleague the member for Regina-Lums-den was talking, he made reference to the fact that there was an estimate of 5,000 jobs being lost. Well, the annual subsidy is around $32 million a year.
Average.

I worked it out. The average subsidy is $32 million a year. Do you know what that works out to? It is $6,300 per worker.
I think I heard in this House not too long ago that one of the impacts or the realities of some of the offshore development in Atlantic Canada was a cost per job of $190,000. Here, to save money we are cutting out $6,300 per existing job. They have to pay more in income tax, they being those 5,000 men and women. They put more back into the economy than they take out through the At and East subsidy. It does not make sense. This At and East subsidy was an investment in the future of Atlantic Canada and in the men and women who work in Atlantic Canada, Quebec, Ontario and on the prairies. This is dumb economics. It is the Conservatives who do not know how to run a country, let alone a comer store.
Government Orders
Bob Rae invests in people. He does not worry about the folks on Bay Street. He knows how to work on behalf of the people of Ontario and he will continue to do a damned good job, I want to tell you.
Ask all the people who are in the construction business if they want to support this.
Madam Speaker, I think I have caught their attention.
For all the good that will do.
They are sensitive. Very sensitive.

Let us take a look at some of the specifics in this bill.
We are talking about 944,000 tonnes of grain and flour moved in 1988. About 90 per cent went to the ports of Halifax and Saint John. According to the Halifax-Dart-mouth Port Development Commission: "The economics of grain traffic at the port in 1988 amounted to $25.9 million in revenues and 263 jobs, while flour traffic resulted in $28.4 million in revenue and 220 jobs". So there are nearly 500 direct jobs in the Halifax-Dartmouth area alone. In Saint John, the port corporation says that the movement of bulk grain through its port in 1988, under the program, amounted to $8.5 million, along with 90 direct jobs. Collectively, they say that in addition to the 573 direct jobs in the two ports, another 250 indirect jobs may be lost as well, just in those two communities; that many jobs with one slice of a pen by the minister responsible for this program.
The livelihood of all those people plus all of the rail workers, the marine workers and the farmers who no longer have the ability to move or to sell their products, is on the hands of that minister.
One elevator has been closed, Saint John. We are also seeing effects on other areas. We are going to see higher freight rates for western Canada for the grains.
Let me just correct the record. The Saint John elevator is the one that is closed. Also, the transfer elevator at Port McNicoll, Ontario. I think that is in the riding of the former Minister of Transport, one of the many who have come and gone from this place under both Liberals and Conservatives, just another indication that neither party really understands the importance of transportation.
Neither party understands the importance of transportation because if they did, they would have left a minister in place long enough to learn the job. Having said that, the only one who came to the job with any knowledge was the first Conservative Minister of Transport. Although we fundamentally disagreed with him on policy,

Government Orders
at least he knew what he was talking about when he got into the ministry.
The livestock industry, the feed mills, the meat packing plants and the dairies are going to be hit by the decision of this government.
The estimate is that rail rates for domestic feed grains will go up by at least $10 a tonne. The livestock industry in the maritimes depends on grain from Ontario and western Canada, and if the transport costs do go up by that $10 a tonne, it is estimated that 5,000 jobs will be lost in the livestock industry, feed mills, meat packing plants and dairies. This is 20 per cent of the total employed in this industry and related industries in Atlantic Canada and that is from the Executive Director of the Atlantic Farmers' Council, Keith Russell.
The elevators keep closing. We have two in Midland. We have one in Port McNicoll and one in Prescott. I\vo of those are in the former Ministers of Transport's riding.
Ontario flour mills have lost export contracts and require lower wheat prices to compete with Quebec mills for CIDA contracts. At the same time, Ontario farmers are already receiving record low prices and cannot afford to see prices drop.
For the Ontario Wheat Marketing Board, the At and East allowed it the flexibility to store wheat longer before shipping it which allowed it to get a better price. The elimination of the At and East Program forced the storage facilities in Georgian Bay to close and made shipping wheat to maritime ports during the winter more expensive.
I want to touch on another point. The existence of the At and East provided some flexibility for the Port of Thunder Bay. As you know, Thunder Bay is closed in terms of the marine side for two to three months each winter. It varies, but somewhere between the middle of December and the middle of January we shut down and we are open again when the ice goes.
During the late fall after the Welland Canal closes, we can still move grain by water to the bay ports and store it
there for inclusion in the At and East. That allows more grain to come off the prairies during the winter months and to fill up the elevators in Thunder Bay, while at the same time providing for the possibility of a winter rail program.
By eliminating the At and East Program and by eliminating those elevators which I talked about in the Great Lakes, we have lost some more flexibility.
In addition, thanks to this policy and the lack of concrete action by this government dealing with the inequities of the Western Grain Transportation Act, we have seen hull after hull after hull either flagged out to be used elsewhere in the world instead of the Great Lakes or cut up for scrap so that our Great lakes fleet has lost the ability to move a bumper crop for this country.
Decisions like this put forward because of a desire to conform to market economics have really undermined a part of the fabric of this country: our ability to grow excellent grains, the best in the world on our prairies, and get them to markets, through our eastern ports or through our western or northern ports. It is one more knife in the coffin of the grain industry in this country.
I say to you that the government has made a fundamental mistake, both in philosophy and in terms of practice. This has got to be changed and it will be changed by another government because it is too important to leave in the hands of the market.
Madam Speaker, I thank you for your indulgence. I want to conclude by saying that I am not happy to be speaking on this bill. I do not think it should be before us and that is why we will be voting against it.

Mr. Speaker, like other members who have participated in this debate, I have fundamental mixed emotions for a variety of reasons. I am not going to waste much of my limited time tonight to talk about those reasons. I am going to come down to the basics of the bill.
The bill is now C-ll. It used to be C-26. The hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan, who gave a very constructive contribution to the debate and is also one of the more active, constructive members of the transporta-

tion committee of which I had the honour at one time to be the chairman, knows fully the ramifications of the bill as does his colleague for Thunder Bay-Nipigon, another member of the transport committee. He gave a very balanced approach. I did not agree obviously with the full extension of some of the thoughts, but I understand why he and his House leader and others who have spoken initially have said they were not happy to speak because this bill, as the hon. member for Regina-Lumsden said earlier, which is absolutely right, is that this is a retroactive bill that is putting into law what a budget did back in 1989.
Mr. Speaker, I do not know what law school you went to, but I know you went to a venerable one and I certainly went to an honourable one. One of the most invidious, odious pieces of legislation was a retroactive piece of legislation that was put into law after the event and changed the rules half way through midstream.
On retroactivity, this bill should never have been before the House, I am not going to waste much time on the procedural aspect of the mutation, the interesting parliamentary mutation from an aberration of prorogation, when things were dead; but of course aberration and abortions are not to be treated lightly here. Prorogation used to mean that everything was cut off at the pass. If you did not get the legislation through, it died on the Order Paper.
This, Mr. Speaker, as you and I well know, was a great motivational inspiration to make some deals. As you got into June, July or August, as I used to sit here in the earlier days of my tenure, the George Mcllraiths, the Davie Fultons and men who understood Parliament got together and said: "Hey, we have debated this too dam long". That was of course before television which even makes it longer now because it cuts through to the core and cuts through to the sham. Even Carol Burnett could not stay longer than 10 years, and yet a lot of these debates seem to go on 10 years. But unfortunately-and I say it sadly-my former colleagues in the government, all of whom are honourable souls, have an Achilles' heel and that is the fact that they do not understand the parliamentary process.
I could go on to a whole speech on that. I am not even going to mention the Prime Minister who never had any parliamentary experience before he came here. That could be part of the problem too.
Government Orders
Some of us earned our spurs in the trenches and did not come from the corporate boardrooms to the cabinet room. I say that is part of the problem of this parliamentary system. That is part of the parliamentary system and the problem that we have today as, Mr. Speaker, you and I well know.
We talk about the mother of battles and we talk about that horrible charade that we just went through in the Persian Gulf. I will not get into that tonight. But we have at least something serene, something stable, something basic, and that is the Mother of Parliaments that we are all supposed to have taken something from and/or adopted and adapted to our own particular geographic, historical and traditional and/or social mores and ways.
One of the basics of Parliament was that at a prorogation the Order Paper was dead. Government, get your house in order and renegotiate the new bills because something happened in the last session and they did not get through.
With that invidious notice of motion given approval by the Speaker I have to say sadly, Mr. Speaker,-I am almost prepared to predict that the slippery slope of the present Chair is going to be defined by his ruling on that invidious notice of motion-that with one stroke of the pen, Mandrake the Magician resurrected five dead bills that were in voodoo land.
With a little parliamentary imprimatur and the persuasion of the government House leader, they came to life again. The resurrection of Lazarus was never more supreme than those five bills that came out of that invidious notice of motion.
That is what we are dealing with here tonight. We have one of them on our platter. It should have been through negotiation. It could have been done through consent.
Perhaps this bill need not have taken the time it is taking in Parliament now because I agree with some of the comments, from the members opposite, especially those of my friend from Halifax West. I better not touch him too much because this gets too close to home.
I agree that the de facto input of subsidy under the At and East, Bill C-26 which is now Bill C-ll, has been dead since July 16, 1989. Of course, as the hon. member for Regina-Lumsden said, once you cut out the subsidy, then it is kind of silly to talk about shipments of grain to the east.

I never thought I would ever be doing this in my life, but I happen to be sitting here in the opposition. That is part of the problem of this House. There are a lot of government members who never sat in opposition. They forgot from whence they came.
I agree with some of the comments made by my former colleagues who have spoken tonight. We cannot attune hypocrisy to any one individual, but the generic term applies to the hypocrisy in opposition. You say: "A, B, C and D," and then you get in government and it is "X, Y, Z".
You know something, Mr. Speaker, the fellow called Preston Manning is down the hill in a place called the Civic Centre. I am told by my colleague from Beaver River that there are 2,000 people there tonight to hear the new messiah on the political field. He has a lot of things to say.
One of the things he has to say is that this institution which used to be the highest court of the land should no longer be the biggest hypocrite forum in the land. With television we can no longer get away with saying one thing in opposition and then getting in government and doing just the opposite. That has happened so often.
In fact, there is an interesting contribution of the member for Burin-St. George's in quoting-I see the Minister of Grains and Oilseeds here; he is a very good friend of mine-the remarks of the present Deputy Prime Minister in his contribution to the debate on the At and East when he was in opposition. He said nothing different than I am saying tonight because what he said then was true. What I am saying tonight is true.
Coming to the reality of this debate, it was the then Minister of Transport who then set up-I think he said this under the National Transportation Act debate, and I happened to be a member in 1966- the transportation commission and he became the first chairman of the National Transportation Agency, which was an interesting thing to do in those days. Now Eric Nielsen is, so things haven't changed that much.
However, Mr. Pickersgill said many things. I am going to cut through all the wheat and the chaff, even though this is what this bill is about, because my friends on the
opposite side who say it is dead, it is over, it is history, they forget the histoiy from whence they came. The whole reason for the At and East was that little part of Canada which is trying to sustain itself. Mr. Pickersgill, my adversary at the time, was a lowly backbencher. I was about three rows up here to the right, so I have really come full circle. I watched him in the front row make his inimitable speech. I won't get into the mannerisms that he sometimes used, but the important thing he said about At and East is that it "was to ensure that we will have rates which will provide some inducement and incentive to shippers to use the facilities of the Atlantic ports". There are many more things he said.
When I hear friends of mine opposite say that the At and East is histoiy because the de facto implementation under cabinet order was July 16, 1989, I start to ask myself the question: "Is the elevator left in Halifax history?" That is the crux of this debate.
I cannot think of another individual item that affects Atlantic Canada so adversely, even though no one understands it, as the cutting of the At and East. In fact, I believe that in the proverbial bowels of the bureaucracy some bureaucrat was picking at bottom line reduction in spending and said to a confrere: "We have got to cut certain moneys out and we've got to cut certain payments out. What's this At and East?" Quite understandably I can almost believe that he could not have got an explanation. Someone looking at this escalating subsidy of $28 to $40 million-and that's approximate because it changed from year to year, but between $28 and $40 million-could easily say: "Hey, in our deficit reduction program let's slice this down".
Madam Speaker, do you know what we found out when the bureaucrats came before the transportation committee? I think my hon. friend from Thunder Bay-Atikokan was there and my hon. friend from Thunder Bay-Nipigon was there, as well as other members. We had officials from the Departments of Finance and Transport and whatever. I almost have the name of one, but I am not in the habit of mentioning names of public servants when they cannot defend themselves, but this is all a matter of the public record. In effect, we found out through the hearings of the transport committee on the At and East two years ago that someone inferred-now I am paraphrasing but I could get the absolute minute of the transport evidence to support what I am about to

say-that: "Whoops, we slipped. We cut out the subsidy and now because of GATT and the international implications of a subsidy for export, we cannot reimpose it".
That is one of the messages received by the transport committee that had some hearings on this issue.
Madam Speaker, I don't know how much more time I have. Can you give me a little hand signal? Good-five minutes, that is great.
I am glad to see the minister here because I have a very real respect for the minister. I know he is anguished over this. However, Mr. Minister, do you really believe the statement of your parliamentary secretary, the computer whiz from Calgary Southeast, with a great competent mind but no heart and no compassion? He hasn't learned compassion. The Reform Party is like a wildfire in Alberta because a lot of competent members do a good job mechanically but they do not have any compassion for the people. If the parliamentary secretary was a member from Atlantic Canada he could not have made the speech he made to lead off this debate on Thursday, June 6. His first sentence was: "Mr. Speaker, the bill now before the House seeks to eliminate a subsidy which has outlived its original purpose and has become a burden on the public purse".
I ask the parliamentary secretary to stand up in this House, this open forum, to admit that the Western Grain Transportation Act is a subsidy for grain movement which distorts the market and has outlived its usefulness. I do not think the parliamentary secretary even understood the beginnings of the At and East, as illustrated with the quote I gave from Mr. Pickersgill, then Minister of Transport, that it was there for a very designated purpose. The hon. member for Regina-Lumsden and others have said that, in terms of the stupidity of eliminating this subsidy, it is more than offset with the cost to the government in increased welfare, in increased unemployment insurance payments, and the loss of the economic activity and the tax that could have been raised by that economic activity. We know the jobs are lost. The Saint John elevator is gone. We are not even trying to resurrect it.
The misleading thing about this debate that makes me most irritated of all is that when everyone talks about cutting out the old history no one mentions what the
Government Orders
minister did then. It was this minister in the House tonight, I think, who was responsible for setting up the Grains 2000 port study. The minister received the report in November 1990 and it was finally released to the public in February 1991. Let us not say what that young little youthful computer parliamentary secretary from Calgary Southeast said: "Well, we are going to monitor the situation", and I quote from page 1289 of Hansard:
And if needed, the government is prepared to ensure that the
Halifax elevator remains in operation for the benefit of the Atlantic
livestock and flour milling industries.
What the heck does the young computer member for Calgary Southeast and the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture think the Grains 2000 ports study said? It said that unless there is help, unless export grain is enhanced, that elevator goes down the drain the same as the elevator in Saint John goes down the drain. When that elevator goes down the drain, we cannot resurrect it. It is the same fallacy as Preston Manning, coming back to Reform, says: "Hey, we do not want Quebec unless Quebec says it is in". When do you ever have a divorce and then ask to get the terms of living? I could put that another way but in effect it is the same for this elevator.
Kill it off.

You do not have the elevator killed off and then suggest that a munificent government-we know there is not that much money around-is going to resurrect it. I mentioned the resurrection of Lazarus earlier, but it is not going to happen to a sterile elevator when world trade has gone by. Of course, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture is right about trade changes in the movement of grain. However, what he did not say is that we have already lost sales to some of our traditional customers because the At and East subsidy is not there. That helps to distort the trade of grain.
I do not know if the minister is going to contribute before this debate ends but the Grains 2000 report, and I give him credit for setting it up, says, as he knows from his bureaucrats, and my point and every Atlantic Canadian members' point has to be that you cannot support Bill C-ll unless there is something more than the wistful thinking of the Parliamentary Secretary to the

Minister of Transport, who says: "Well, we will monitor, and if the need arises we may do A, B, C and D".
I was the chairman of the transport committee for two or three years or more-that is a past date and I do not mind trading on it at all-and we had hearings on this issue and tried to use the lever of not passing the bill to get the bureaucracy to come up with something called "set-offs".
Offsets.
Offsets. The same thing, but twisted around. It had the same impact.
Spin-offs.

Spinoffs, offsets, setoffs, we have had three years of discussion and there is nothing except this wistful pious hope that, if needed, we may be prepared to ensure that the elevator may stay for the benefit of the agriculture industry, of the flour industry, of jobs.
If this was a bill castrating the Western Grain Transportation Act, there is not a member in the western caucus even of a government who would have allowed this to come this far. My sadness is that there are not more Atlantic Canadian members up here in this House of Commons on all sides in a collective issue that has no partisan stripe, or should not have, but it is going to have unless members exercise. I know good members try within the government caucus to get the offsets, but there are no offsets today. We then waited and marked time until we heard the grain study report.
I appreciate, Madam Speaker, you have been very kind and generous, more so than usual, but I understand that because I know my time is just about up on this particular situation. I am not going to trespass further.
I really say that, without anything firm in offsets, we have talked for three years in the House and the committee, delegations, the Atlantic Transportation Commission, suggesting certain proposals that have not been accepted. In fact, in talking to the Atlantic Transportation Commission today, there have been letters from the Atlantic Farmers' Council of May 31, the Canadian Feed Industry, the Co-op Atlantic of May 17 and Maritime Advisory Council on June 3, others who
have written to the minister asking: "what are you going to do with the offset program?"
What do they get? They get a slap on the face, no answer to the letters, but this bill on the floor of the House. I conclude with this. One of my colleagues on the opposite side of the House, who is a friend of mine says that it is all history. It does not matter because it was all dead because, in effect, July 16, payments stopped and the railways did not do it. If it was dead, why-

Madam Speaker, I listened with interest to the intervention in this debate of my colleague, the member for Annapolis Valley-Hants. Perhaps we should have let him talk a little bit more on the transport committee. He makes eminent sense in his opposition to this bill.
I wonder whether the member would care to react to the following statement. If we are to survive as a nation, if we are to ensure that the items that we export, particularly grain products like wheat, like flour, rf we should as a country be neutralizing transport. In other words, it should not cost anything to get it to our ports so that once we get there, then the marketplace, the international marketplace, would begin to click in. In that way, there would be no internal distortions in terms of east-west direction, and we would ensure that the value added could be accomplished throughout the country rather than just at key points. I wonder if he would care to comment on that.

Madam Speaker, I think if I understand my hon. friend's question, it is a nice leading question and I would agree with that. That is in effect what the At and East was trying to do.
He mentioned the country. We all can make compassionate speeches on the country. I cannot emphasize enough that in Atlantic Canada, even though people do not understand it, those who do-and they are the farmers, they are the producers, they are the people in the marine and the transportation industry-this is a cut of the Gordian, another slice of the Gordian knot that keeps us all together.
June 11, 1991

As we have all said here in this debate, it was relatively peanuts when you put the $28 million to $40 million to little old Atlantic Canada against the $700 million or $800 million for western grain transportation. Madam Speaker, I would like to ask my good friend from Annapolis Valley-Hants whether he would care to comment on a matter in terms of equalizing opportunity between Atlantic Canada, Quebec, Ontario, St. Lawrence and Great Lakes ports, the matter of ice-breaking. You do not have to break ice in Halifax and Saint John.
I and my colleagues are not complaining that the taxpayer pays for the cost of ice-breaking. We are not too worried about that. Does my hon. friend have any estimate as to whether or not the ice-breaking services in Quebec, in Montreal, in the upper St. Lawrence and the Great Lakes, exceed the costs of the At and East rates?

Madam Speaker, my hon. friend from Regina-Lumsden has asked a beautiful question. I must say that in all the debate I have been involved with over several years, I frankly do not know the answer. Most people do not understand that the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission for
Government Orders
several years suggested different modes and different ways to move that grain.
It is a good question. This is something that, frankly, I think government should have done. What is that thing called in Washington, the office of financial management or budget control? That is a question that I think deserves an answer, and I agree. I am not against the ports of Montreal, Quebec and the St. Lawrence, but those are extra costs that you do not have when you go to Halifax, which is one of the world's great open, natural all-year ports.
The other thing they do not have is the offset of cutting the subsidy: How much because of the loss of jobs-and other people have touched on this-the increase in unemployment insurance, the increased welfare, the loss of tax dollars from depreciated economic activity? I would say that on both counts, in terms of the offset of navigational aids and the ice-breaking work, that that would be veiy close to the subsidy we pay to Atlantic ports.
It is a lot more.

Or more. Well, we all can play with figures, depending on how you start to calculate the base calculations.
Second, and I think almost as important, the absolute cut in the subsidy is not a net benefit to the government. It is going to be a net deficit to the government.
Madam Speaker, I am glad to have a chance to say a few words on Bill C-ll, the At and East rate bill. I want to compliment the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants because-

speechtext: Before the hon. member gets into his comments, may I assume that the hon. member is splitting the 20 minute period with another member? It will make it easier for the Chair to advise the hon. member.

Madam Speaker, I assume we may have to get unanimous consent for each of us to get 40 minutes but we will try our best.
The bill that is before the House tonight is Bill C-ll, which replaces the old Bill C-26, and I believe that the

June 11, 1991
Government Orders
debate tonight is really about the government bringing back a bill at third reading without unanimous consent.
There is a very fundamental aspect about this whole debate that is fundamental to the survival of Atlantic Canada. I think the hon. member for Annapolis Valley- Hants brings to this debate two valuable perspectives. One, he has been a distinguished chairman of the transport committee for many years so he has been through all the briefs and presentations by grain producers, shippers and so on, but also, he comes from one of prime agriculture areas of Nova Scotia. His perspective is, perhaps, very well founded. He really touches the kernel of what we have to do in this countiy if we want to have a broadly-based agriculture industry that is diversified.
During the free trade debate our caucus had public hearings in Fredericton and we heard presentations mostly opposing the free trade deal, but some were relatively in favour of it. The statement which really caught my idea of how devastating the free trade deal would be to Atlantic Canada, to much of Ontario, and to many other parts of Canada; was the comment by somebody after a long afternoon and all kinds of presentations when it was said that if you want to see what free trade can do for New Brunswick, go across the border into Maine and see what free trade has done for Maine. They have had free trade with the rest of the United States for 50 years, 100 years.
When you stop and think about agriculture in Atlantic Canada, they have their specialties like potatoes in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island and those commodities. They have a special climate and soil base and all the rest of it. They also have a dairy industry which they do not have much of in Maine. They have a pork industry which they do not have much of in Maine. Yet, they have the same resource base generally.
Look at companies like Irving, and McCain's, especially, which was a world-wide food processing industry started in New Brunswick. They do not have any McCain's company that has a world-wide base in Maine that I know of. That is because we have organized our agriculture on the basis that we want medium-sized units, very efficient, and we want to produce milk and
cheese and these other commodities of the dairy industry all over the country.
If you go to the United States, you can go to Wisconsin, Minnesota, Florida, or California. Those are the main dairy producing areas. Our concept, which the Tories are rapidly trying to destroy, and God help them if they serve for another two and a half years, they will have gone a long way towards doing that, is based on trying to have a broadly diverse industry through the use of marketing boards, supply management, and marketing mechanisms like that. To some extent the Wheat Board is another mechanism which tries to diversify and help the industry.
The debate tonight is not so much about whether the At and East rate will be effectively killed, as the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants said. It was effectively killed on July 16, 1989, when payment of the subsidy was stopped. There are a lot of people in this House, including the hon. member who just spoke who has a stake in his constituency, who want to see this kind of agriculture continue in this country.
The Tories are hell bent on another scheme of market economy. They think they will solve all the problems. It will be a disaster. It will be a disaster for Canada because the kind of diversified agriculture we see in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island will be destroyed, if we destroy those special instruments we have put in place, including the At and East rate.
It has already been described that it is going to cost our agriculture producers down there some $21 a tonne for their feed grains. It may not sound like very much, until you talk to hog producers in Prince Edward Island, as we did a couple of weeks ago when we visited there with the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings. They are teetering as to whether they are making a go of it or not.
Removing this subsidy, throwing the whole marketing board system into question, may not show up in the big macro-economics of the countiy, but it has a profound influence on the individual producers. Hundreds and thousands of those individual producers making a go of it with a medium-sized, very efficient operation is what gives rural Canada the vitality we want to maintain.
I am surprised when I hear and see columns by one of the Tory members for Halifax where he says: "We do not need these subsidies down here. We will make it on our
June 11, 1991

Government Orders
own". That is one aspect of the whole agriculture side of it.
Then there are the industrial jobs. Already the Saint John terminal has closed, throwing 55 people from the maritimes out of work, a very substantial number of people in that community. The Halifax terminal may eventually close. It involves another 27 jobs I am told and, perhaps, several hundred if one considers the stevedores and the rail people and so on. Therefore, there is a very, very profound impact of the At and East rate.
What we were trying to do when this was put in place, was to try to balance the cost of shipping from Buffalo to the Atlantic ports, which are two or three times more than the cost of shipping and the distance involved from Buffalo to New York City.
This is an important debate because it talks about the viability of Atlantic Canada, the viability of our agriculture industry, the diversification of our economy and it is very important that the government not be able to get away lightly with removing support programs to our most vital industry, the agriculture industry.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wish to make three points with regard to this debate on Bill C-ll.
The first point deals with the procedural aspects, the second with the substance of the bill itself and third, the measure of fairness or, indeed, lack of fairness with regard to the bill.
The hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants made reference in his remarks to the fact that this was a previous bill known as Bill C-26. Thereafter, the bill had been reinstated by a government omnibus motion, which made members of my party express great frustration and anger that the government would attempt to reinstate a bill which was basically, in procedural terms, dead on the Order Paper as a result of the government's decision to prorogue the House.
Many members in our caucus have spoken out against this particular bill, some with great emotion, all based on factual information provided to us by various interest groups in our respective regions, whether we come from the west or from the Atlantic region.
I think it can be said that most members of Parliament on this side of the House, and I can only speak for those in my caucus and in the Liberal Party, disagree wholeheartedly with the government on the measure to reinstate the bill. In doing so, we do not just do it for political gains.
I just want to review the substance of that bill. It implements an April 1989 budget decision to eliminate what is commonly referred to as the At and East rates effective July 15, 1989. That was almost two years ago. 'These At and East rates are really specified under section 272 of the Railway Act. Under this section of the Railway Act, shippers in Atlantic Canada for instance paid 1960 rail rates for export of grain and 1966 rates for export of flour. Those rates have not been frozen at the levels they were at on those two dates.
The Government of Canada subsidizes the balance of these rates to amounts of between $20 million and $40 million or so in recent years. Perhaps a more precise figure is about $37.3 million for the fiscal year 1988-89. That is the substance of Bill C-26 and now Bill C-ll. It is a subsidy. It is a subsidy paid by the Government of Canada to individuals who happen to reside in the regions of our country.
I see across the way the minister who has some responsibility for regional economic development in this country. I have to ask myself why a government would, at this time with the economic situation being the way it is, want to rid itself of this particular subsidy affecting primarily a smaller region in this country. Thirty-two million dollars to the Government of Canada is not a large expenditure in terms of its total expenditures.
The third point that I had raised at the beginning of my remarks, because I know I have limited time, is the fairness. We subsidize western grain transportation. I think it has been referred to as $700 million or $800 million, whereas in the Atlantic it is roughly $32 million. I have not heard any member on this side of the House, in the years in which I have been elected to this Parliament, question the authenticity, the need and the

June 11, 1991
Government Orders
importance which the subsidy for western grain transportation does for that region of the country.
I think most members, if not all, would support and support enthusiastically that kind of subsidy to that region of the country. The reason why is because it is just, it is appropriate and it is fair.
What we find particularly disturbing in Atlantic Canada is there is $700 million and $32 million.
I ask the Chair, where is the fairness? The fact of the matter is, there is no fairness. This is a deliberate act to inflict economic pain on those of us who happen to reside in Atlantic Canada. If it were otherwise, it would not proceed.
We have heard the catch-all phrases: "We are going to review the prospects of trying to save the grain elevators in the port of Elalifax. We are going to review that at some point in the future". That is a code word which this government has used time and time again to do nothing. For those of us who have been the victims of this government's policy in Atlantic Canada, we are disheartened to learn that a $32 million subsidy is being cut off when a $700 million plus subsidy for another region of the country is going to proceed.
When I say $32 million, what do I mean by that? I said $32 million, $37.3 million, $30 million and $40 million, average it off if you will. The economic impact of the termination of the At and East program for grain elevators in dollars is $3,735,000. The flour mill in Halifax is $3,200,000. It includes wages and benefits paid by flour mills at Halifax and also goods and services purchased.
With regard to the grain elevators, it includes wages and benefits paid to elevator employees at Saint John and Halifax, and also goods and services purchased by elevators.
The additional cost of livestock and poultry feed is $18 million on an annual basis. This has been calculated with the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission, using tonnage of feed grain handled under the Livestock Feed Program of Canada and rail freight rates, which in the absence of the Halifax elevator, would apply in lieu of present water compelled rail rates.
Local grain production, $950,000; port and railway employment, $8,280,000 adding up to approximately, on a yearly basis, anywhere between $32 and $37.3 million. That is the extent of the subsidy and that is where it goes.
For those of us in Atlantic Canada, we just call out, not for a special rate or a preferential rate but just for due process, fairness and some semblance of dignity for the people who live in that particular region. It is no wonder that residents of Atlantic Canada say: "Hey, we have to re-examine those national institutions which impact so negatively on our economy and on our people".
In closing, let me put this brief amendment on the record. I move:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the
word "that" and substituting the following therefor:
Bill C-ll, an Act to amend the Railway Act (grain and flour subsidies), be not now read a third time but that it be read a third time this day six months hence.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first of all I want to thank my colleague from Gander-Grand Falls for such an intelligent, thought provoking question at this hour of the evening.
Succinctly put, I think the measure the government has put before us tonight ought to be addressed from a number of perspectives. Specifically, with regard to the question as raised by the hon. member who has now brought to the attention of the House that there will be large quantities of imports from the European Economic Community, I think it fits quite nicely with the government's over-all economic thrust, which is clearly the following.
We have a large geographical map of Canada. We have a small population base dispersed over this large geographical mass. We are going to deny the role of the national government in terms of bringing people and geography together with regard to our transportation system.
The government does not want to be involved in that any more. It wants to let the so-called free market enterprise operate, but the fact and the truth of the matter is that when it says that and when you check the record of where this particular quantity of goods will come from, it is being massively subsidized by the foreign country that is exporting into Canada.
That has been the economic philosophy and thesis of this government; to deny Canadians in the poorer regions of this country an opportunity to place their trust and their faith in other regions and in other people throughout Canada domestically and hinge their bet on some foreign power whether it be Third World, the European Economic Community or our economic neighbours to the south.
In response to the hon. member, I find it rather frightful that we in Canada as national legislators would allow this kind of behaviour and conduct to continue. We know, because of fact after fact, that we as Canadians are being robbed of our economic livelihood domestically and creating a dependency, not domestically but internationally, on markets abroad and on foreign economies to provide Canadians and in this particular instance, Atlantic Canadians, with a product which is both reasonably priced and appropriate under the circumstances.
