Madam Speaker, I was listening as the hon. House leader for Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition was speaking and moved this motion. He represents an area of our country called Cape Breton Island. Thinking about the railway, it was not that long ago, it was in the last year, that the federal government decided that there would no longer be rail passenger service from the riding of the hon. member who moved this motion, extending right down to Truro, Nova Scotia.
The trans-Canada link of CN ended. Passenger service from coast to coast ended because there was no longer a connection from Newfoundland to British Columbia. It ended. It stopped with that decision in the past year involving Cape Breton Island.
Just think of it. The federal government subsidizes a bus operation in Newfoundland. When you get on the bus and go to the ferry boat in Port-aux-Basques, if that bus does not make that ferry boat, you have to spend the night in Port-aux-Basques. If the ferry boat does not meet Acadia Bus Lines in North Sydney, you have to spend another night in North Sydney, and if the private bus company does not meet the train in Truro, Nova Scotia, you have to spend another night there. You can see what change has taken place in the past year. That is why I support the motion put forward by the opposition House leader.
When you think about it, it is rather interesting. The presence of the federal government in rural areas like Cape Breton Island and Newfoundland has practically disappeared. The post offices are being closed one after the other. That job is gone to that community, never again to be returned. Never again will you see a flag pole with a Canadian flag on it in a lot of these small

June 11, 1991
Government Orders
communities because that was the one building that had it.
No more will you see a train move down the track, because CN has closed and laid off the people. There have been great plans to give them pensions and the golden handshake, but the jobs are gone and the federal presence is gone.
The federal presence on land with your trains and with your post office, which was usually the one place you could identify the federal government, is gone.
Then by air. Air Canada, a Crown corporation, was cut back and no longer do you have that presence in the rural areas. You have air traffic controllers today in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland. In the name of saving person-years, the Government of Canada embarked on a policy of hiring Americans. Bring them up on contracts to work in Toronto in our air traffic control centres so that they would not count as federal employees. I think that is what was behind it, because we have young Canadians today who are anxious to get into air traffic control, very highly paid positions in the federal government, perhaps some of the highest.
Last year, we were hiring Americans on contract. Now we have a bill before the Elouse to move the airports to local authorities. Federal employees again will completely disappear from some communities in this country, never again to be treated as federal public servants, but as employees of a corporation operating an airport.
Some of us received letters lately. I received one today, and I went back over my files to discover that back in 1989 I had received a similar letter talking about the rumour of closing the Burnt Point lighthouse. This fellow says: "We have no meaningful land mass between us and the European and African continents and many times in years past the fact that contact could be made to the lighthouse keeper by means of a citizen's band radio has meant the probable difference between being rescued or lost."
Today the contract has been awarded to close the Burnt Point lighthouse in Newfoundland and to close another 11 lighthouses. The cost to the federal treasury
is $1 million apiece. One million dollars to do away with one person-year which is absolutely necessary. There are another 22 being closed. The contracts are going. I will put it on the record that a member from the Government of Canada, from St. John's East, interfered politically and got a lighthouse in Belle Island, Newfoundland, lifted from the list. A political interference by the member for St. John's East on behalf of politics.
We have the Government of Canada saying to us in eastern Canada that we are not even allowed in Coast Guard again to use our ice-breakers. They are tied up. You see the new policy is that you tie it up. There are seven tied up today in Quebec City. Five are tied up in Dartmouth, Nova Scotia. There are another two tied up for engine repairs in St. John's, Newfoundland. Meanwhile, there is ice everywhere around the coast up there. The policy is: "Well, you know, we are looking at the Arctic transportation system and when one of those large ships gets stuck, we are going to send up an ice-breaker from Dartmouth, Nova Scotia, up to Greenland." To save money. It is cheaper to tie them up than it is to have them operating.
That is the policy of the federal government. No matter where you look, it has had a small presence in Atlantic Canada. That is why the six-month hoist is so important. We must put an end to this bill which stops the subsidy on the movement of grain into eastern Canada. It is another point in a long list of actions by the Government of Canada which has seen the removal of federal presence in the air, on the land and on the sea. The House here today should vote with the hon. member, the House leader for the Official Opposition, in the motion to put a six-month hoist on this bill. Every member of the government who votes for it will be congratulated in the next election.

Mr. Speaker, this is not a debate that I am pleased to take part in. In fact, I have already spoken twice on the At and East legislation, the first time on February 12, 1990.
At that time I pointed out that there were 400,000 to
500,000	tonnes of wheat sent under the At and East regulations by the Canadian Wheat Board. The Ontario Wheat Board alone moved between 150,000 to 200,000 tonnes under this legislation on an annual basis.
June 11, 1991

I want to commend our opposition House leader for his amendment. I recall placing a similar amendment back on June 5, 1990, to delay the implementation of this legislation until 1995.
Had the government listened to what we were saying, not only in the Official Opposition, but listened to what the witnesses in front of the legislative committee dealing with this piece of legislation were saying, it would have realized that it was making a grievous error.
When it looked at the Grains 2000 study of November 1990-and a delay such as we proposed at that time would have allowed it to take a look at the impact of this-it would have realized the error of its ways and withdrawn this legislation and put Atlantic Canada back on a competitive basis in terms of its livestock and poultry industries and saved all those jobs connected to the flour mills and the elevators in Atlantic Canada.
This government moves very, very slowly. I recall April 12, 1989, when we asked the government to do something about the no-rolled beef that was coming into Canada at the time, a million pounds a week. Since that was tabled at that time, those imports have tripled. As a result we have six packing plants that have closed in Ontario since that time. This low-grade beef has devastated the beef industry in eastern Canada.
Finally, the former Minister of Agriculture acknowledged the crisis and told the Canadian Cattlemen's Association that he has instructed his officials to require that United States beef, whether graded or ungraded, be identified as such to consumers.
Two years and two months after the problem was drawn to his attention, the government is finally going to look and see what is going on.
I have to suggest tonight that I strongly suspect that I had some of this cheap ungraded imported United States beef in the cafeteria in the Confederation Building at lunch time, tough as nails. It stays with you. You have to chew on it for a long time.
When this government cut back this subsidy, as I mentioned earlier tonight, I suspect part of the reason was that it was trying to do away with subsidies to adhere to the provisions of the Free Trade Agreement. It thought that this is a transportation subsidy, it would be a
Government Orders
good one to do away with. The government completely ignored the fact that the maintenance of the Mississippi waterway is done by the United States Department of Defense. That, in effect, is a subsidy to the United States grain industry.
Let us examine the other subsidies the U.S. is giving. I will use one as an example, the Export Enhancement Program. For the year 1989 it was $777 million, in 1990 it was $556 million, and in 1991 it was $900 million, a total of $5,033 million since it was first introduced in May 1985.
This government is very naive to have entered into such an agreement without having the United States lower its subsidies at the same time as ours are being lowered.
It is kind of amusing that this government stands idly by and does not do anything about these subsidies. In fact, there is a provision in the free trade agreement to call for consultations if the other country keeps its subsidies. There is also a provision to ask for compensation. The government has done neither. Instead, it has opened up the borders to United States grain and grain products. We all know what is going to happen in Atlantic Canada when those subsidies on United States grain look so attractive to the grain buyers. That market will not be supplied by Canadian grains, it will be supplied by grains from other countries.
One of the interesting things I found the other day was that one of the very major grain companies in North America, American-based, has really taken advantage of these subsidies, both coming and going. It uses the export enhancement subsidy to transport grain out of the United States. Then, in turn, it took a subsidy from the European Common Market to transport barley-that is the original product it exported-from Sweden back into the United States. It has it both coming and going and this government sits idly by and cuts back our transportation subsidies, which were put in place in 1966 in order to ensure an adequate supply of grain to Atlantic Canada when the seaway is frozen up, grain that would travel by rail from western Canada or from Ontario into the areas of Atlantic Canada where it is used, or from where it is exported.

June 11, 1991
Government Orders
I also have to take this government to task and ask it to retaliate concerning another issue that has been brought to my attention just these last few days. The Chicago Board of Trade has passed a resolution just recently to ensure that its Export Enhancement Programs only handle American product. Therefore, this resolution would not allow those companies to buy Canadian grains because they might turn around and export them.
This is another abrogation of the free trade agreement, if this government stands idly by and lets this happen. Our Ontario soybean industry is hit hard, as the United States is the largest export market, with 70,000 tonnes shipped this year.
With what is happening here, in terms of the pressures that are being brought to bear on the Canadian producers, there were over 70 food processing plants closed in Canada last year, 32 of those in the province of Ontario. I know the minister likes to brag about the 50 new plants that have opened. However, I should remind him that on the list his department gave to me one of those plants was in Arizona, an irradiation plant, and another one in Butte, Montana, a canola-crushing plant. Those are hardly Canadian plants. Two were water-bottling plants, some were warehouses, some were plants that had previously closed and reopened.
The fact of the matter is that the food processing industry in Canada is hard pressed. By removing the At and East subsidy, by opening up the borders to American wheat, flour and other products that market will be lost to Canadian producers, who produce the highest quality grain in the world as efficiently as any of our counterparts in the United States. The government has failed to recognize that their input costs, input costs that are under direct control in many instances-I speak here of interest rates and fuel costs-have placed them out of competition.
I ask this government to reconsider the error of its ways and reinstate this legislation which is so badly needed in Canada at this time.

Mr. Speaker, Atlantic Canadians are wondering what it is that the federal government has against them. We have seen a relentless attack on Atlantic Canada and we have seen nothing to assist the fishing industry, which we
all know is in a crisis and has been for some time. We have seen unemployment insurance cuts having a drastic impact on the region and cuts to transfer payments to the provinces making it ever more difficult for the provincial governments in that region to fund health care and post-secondary education. We have seen cuts to VIA Rail which have had a major impact on the ability of people within the region to move about that region. We have seen the closing of post offices. We have seen a major attack on the region of Atlantic Canada and, as I say, Atlantic Canadians are wondering why this is. What is it that the federal government has against them?
At this time all these things took place when Atlantic Canadians were and are suffering from severe economic conditions and totally unacceptable levels of unemployment.
The situation in Atlantic Canada is indicative, of course, of decades of neglect by successive federal governments and by provincial governments which refused to take matters in hand.
Last weekend, some 1,200 New Democrats were in Halifax for our annual convention, and I have had many opportunities also to visit Atlantic Canada on other occasions. What Atlantic Canadians are saying is that they have had enough of these policies which attack them, which undermine their ability to create jobs and to function in Canada as a viable region.
They demand some attention to their legitimate concerns from the federal government, and surely they have a right for the federal government to pay attention to those demands.
Coming from a province like Saskatchewan, it is easy for me to understand the concern and the anger that exists in Atlantic Canada. In fact, all of the regions of this country have been neglected by the government's obsession with its free enterprise market-driven agenda. This bill that we have before us now, Bill C-ll, which will cut a further $35-or-so million from the Atlantic Canadian economy is another example of this government's obsession with market oriented policy, and in this particular case with transportation policy.

They also proposed to maintain the movement of export grain and flour through these Atlantic ports to maintain the commercial viability of those two ports of Halifax and Saint John. They proposed that the frozen rates to the St. Lawrence ports be allowed to rise to a compensatory level and be held at a compensatory level on an annual basis by the National Transportation Agency, and that rates to the ports of Halifax and Saint John be set at a fixed differential above those rates to maintain the current competitive relationship between the St. Lawrence ports and the Atlantic ports.

I am very concerned in particular about the effect it will have on the ports of Saint John and Halifax since I know both the ports and the cities very well. speak with him frequently, and I know he is very interested in this debate this evening.
Although it has been done many times this evening, as much for myself as anybody else, I want to recall what At and East means. I had heard the term many times and, quite frankly, I did not quite know what it meant.
It was developed in 1959 and it is a grain and flour subsidy program administered by the National Transportation Agency. It does two things. It gives a subsidy on grain moving essentially from the Great Lakes to ports east of Montreal: Halifax and Saint John, New Brunswick; and for flour moving from points east of Thunder Bay and transported by rail to ports east of Montreal again transported to Halifax and Saint John.
The reason this was developed in 1959 was that in the United States the U.S. railway systems reduce their rates at and east of Buffalo, New York. So the "at" was Buffalo for the United States. The "at" was essentially Montreal for us. Their reduction of rates made it very difficult for Canadians to compete and the fear was that we would use the U.S. route to transport our grains and flours, so in 1959 the At and East, which we are discussing here this evening, was implemented.
It worked quite well until the budget of April 27, 1989, when the announcement was made that the 1959 At and East rate was going to be cancelled. It gave the reason for it initially as I just gave, but then it said the competitive concern no longer existed because the cost of shipping by rail to the United States ports was now considerably higher than the cost of shipping by water through the Great Lakes and St. Lawrence seaway.
As many people have said during this debate today, that was only one of the reasons this policy was developed. Again, to use the words of the then Minister of Transport, the Hon. Jack Pickersgill, another reason the legislation was under consideration was to ensure that we have rates that would provide some inducement and incentive to shippers to use the facilities of Atlantic ports. In other words, the major reason was for ensuring that the eastern Canadian ports could compete with the U.S. ports. I ask the government to stop and take account of what it has done, take account of what it is about to continue to do, and take account of one case in particular in which we in the opposition told the government it was doing the wrong thing when it came to the handling of grain, and that was a few months ago on the Advance Payments for Crops Program. We pleaded with the government at that time. It can do nothing more than come back to us at this time and say to the opposition, if it is being honest with itself and honest with Canadians: "You told us the right thing, opposition members." It did reinstate the advance payment. I am asking the government, I am pleading with it on behalf of primary producers and every one in the system; the employees, the workers, the elevator operators, the port workers, those who want to purchase grain from Canada at that time of year. It opens another market, it gives another avenue to ship, and heaven forbid we need all of those eveiy chance we get.
June 11, 1991

The government talks about being competitive and that we have to stay that way, and every time we turn around it takes away one of our competitive edges, one of our management tools and one of our operative tools in marketing of grains and crops. The government speaks one thing out of one side of its mouth and another thing out of the other side of its mouth. It really begs the question.
In closing, I ask the government to reconsider. The amendment before the House tonight is giving it the chance to reconsider what it has done and what it wants to make official by the passing of this bill. When government members vote with their conscience, I hope they stop to think that what they are doing is to the detriment of so many in so many different ways. I ask them to support the amendment before the House put forward by the House leader of the Opposition here this evening.

Madam Speaker, it is a privilege, although I was not intending to speak on this debate. I must admit that, I would not call it coerced, but I was motivated to speak. Now that I have spent the last three hours here, I think it is very appropriate. It again proves a lesson to me that if you stay in this House and listen to the debate there is so very, very much to learn. I am sure the Canadian people know that there are not many more than 20 people out here and I hope there are more of them out there who have also learned a great deal about a topic which is of extreme importance to eastern Canada.
As I listened to the ribbon of thought, I said: "Now how can I relate that to my constituency?" The longer I spend here the more I feel that I can relate it because I was in eastern Canada this past weekend and I am in my own constituency a great deal and the two are very similar. We are all like voices in the wilderness saying: "Please pay attention. Please do not do any more economic injustice to us."
When I think of the $35 million subsidy that goes toward the At and East I relate that to my community and I relate it to transportation. Sault Ste. Marie is at the confluence of the Great Lakes. We had a proud Sault Ste. Marie lock. It has been closed for three years. It would cost $35 million to replace that entire lock. We have implored the transport ministers, all of them, to put some money into the canal because it is a Canadian link
Government Orders
between the Great Lakes. The answer from our government is that there is no necessity for a Canadian link and we can rely on the American locks. Thirty-five million dollars would make a tremendous investment in our community. The lock is on the very flag of our city. Does it want us to tear it off the face of the community? That is why it is so very, very easy to relate to what is happening here with At and East.
I now realize the extreme importance of the funding of this subsidy to eastern Canada. The amount is perhaps insignificant to the amount of money when you compare it with the dislocation of people and the social programs which have to come into place to fund, I understand,
5,000	people whose jobs will be lost because of this action. I am sure the cost will be much more than the $32 million.
My reading tells me that the revenues into Halifax and Saint John are beyond the $32 million subsidy. It is a net gain. Therefore, why the action?
I think all of the members from eastern Canada have suggested that. We cannot understand the rationale. The rationale from the government, as it said on April 21, 1989, was that the subsidy has the effect of diverting traffic away from the seaway in favour of subsidized rail movements and is inconsistent with the government's market-oriented transportation policy. There is the bottom line. It is for market oriented transportation policy, as in VIA Rail, and beyond transportation policy we get into Canada Post and PetroCan. We are talking about a federal presence in eastern Canada, in northern Ontario, that we are beginning to miss. We are losing that federal presence. This is a disavowal of the government's obligation to be in these outlying areas, the extremities of Canada. It is extremely, extremely unfortunate, and it is a euphemism to say unfortunate.
From time to time it has been attempted, I do not think intentionally, to pit region against region. The figure of the western subsidy amounts to $700 million and certainly the $32 or $35 million pales in comparison. Should we be pitting west versus east? From time to time it involves central Canada. People say: "This is done at the expense of eastern Canada to support rich central Canada". I resent that attitude, because central Canada, Ontario and Quebec namely, is suffering economic hardship, probably beyond just about everyone else. Because of the loss of manufacturing jobs people can no

Government Orders
longer look to central Canada with envy. We are in similar circumstances with eastern Canada.
Subsidy is a difficult concept to define, certainly as shown by the free trade agreement. There was a purpose and there is a purpose for subsidies. If regional subsidies are used strategically and appropriately, they can help the areas of Canada that require that help. We just cannot disband all subsidies because of a bottom-line, budgetary decision. We cannot allow that to happen.
Take a look at the irony of this situation. We are competing with the Europeans, who are heavily subsidized in agriculture, and the Americans, who are heavily subsidized, and we are the good people, the fair traders who once again bow to everybody and say: "We will lower our subsidies or we will cut them completely out".
Again I can relate the same experience to my constituency in terms of steel. The steel industry in the United States is subsidized to the tune of $30 million. In Canada if there is a very small intent to subsidize steel the Americans countervail and harass us with rulings that are actually frivolous. However, when it comes to the agreement and the dispute settlement they are not so frivolous because the panel rules against us.
Therefore, this subsidy issue is a very delicate one and very, very difficult to define. Our Canadian government always acts very sheepishly and non-aggressively in its dealings with the American government.
Dislocation of people is what we are talking about. The dislocation and the costs associated with the dislocation are nothing. They pale in comparison to what this At and East had accomplished since 1966.
Various people have mentioned the retroactivity of the bill. I have only been here two and half years and I only recall one other bill that was made retroactive. It is hard to imagine legislation that can be implemented retroactively. There is a great deal of legislation we would like to absolve or get rid of, take off the books retroactively, if only we could do that.
In closing, I apologize for my perhaps total lack of comprehension of this At and East subsidy and all the ramifications of cutting out this subsidy for eastern Canada.
I am beginning to comprehend it and I do understand the philosophy and the theories of this government that I know are detrimental not only to eastern Canada but to all of Canada.

Madam Speaker, I was not intending to speak on this bill but I have sat here for the last four hours listening patiently, together with my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood, to all the arguments against this bill.
I have not seen any Tories with the courage to stand up to defend Bill C-ll. If it is such a good piece of legislation, where are the Tories? Canadians have a right to know. If it is good legislation and if it is defensible then why are they not standing up and doing their job? They are getting paid big bucks to come to this Parliament to speak out on behalf of their constituents.
A good question is where are the Tories? Where are the ministers? We have two lousy Tories in the House.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for York South-Weston has been in this House as long as I have been in this House. He very well knows that it is not parliamentary, and should not be done in a speech especially when it is done as wilfully as it is now, to mention the presence or absence of members or ministers in the House. The hon. member is very well aware of that.
As he has been in the House for the last few hours, I am sure he could find some other way to talk about the bill which is now in front of the House, or the amendment which his House leader has put on the table.

Madam Speaker, I was not commenting on their presence or absence in the House. I was commenting on their absence from the debate.
There is a distinction. There is a very clear distinction. I could pretend they are in the House but I cannot pretend that they have participated in the debate, which they have not. That is the point I am making, and that point is parliamentary.
I will speak to the merits of Bill C-ll. I will make some very brief comments and I would hope that some cabinet ministers will stand up on behalf of the Government of Canada to indicate the reasons so many people must lose their jobs as a result of the end of the At and East subsidy.
Perhaps they can explain to the people of Canada why the government has chosen to pass the bill retroactively. As other speakers have indicated, the subsidy in fact terminated some two years ago. The government, in the last Parliament, introduced Bill C-26. Then it decided to prorogue Parliament.
When a government prorogues Parliament, legislation that is on the Order Paper dies. Bill C-26 ought to have died. It was down. It was out, and the government tried to resurrect it. In fact, it did resurrect it through some type of parliamentary boondoggle or mouth to mouth resuscitation. It brought the bill back to life.
Here we are debating the bill now known as Bill C-ll at third reading stage. Not only has this bill been resurrected but in effect it will be retroactive to terminate a subsidy that has been in place from the mid-1960s until two years ago.
The government has not provided a reasonable rationale for terminating a subsidy that amounts to anywhere from $33 million to $35 million annually. Now, to some people that is a lot of money. Indeed, it is a lot of money. But it makes absolutely no economic sense as to why this government has chosen to terminate that particular subsidy, again, as part of a systematic plan to destroy Atlantic Canada.
Does the government not realize the impact that this bill will have on the economy in Atlantic Canada? My colleagues have very eloquently pointed out the negative
Government Orders
economic impact that this bill will have in Halifax, for example, and in Saint John. Export grain shipments to Halifax and Saint John, as you know, have been stopped, and as a direct result the Saint John grain elevator has closed, putting 55 people out of work.
Surely the 55 people at the Port of Saint John, the grain elevator employees, have a right to hear from their representatives on the government side the reasons why they are out of a job today. The government does not have the courage to stand up and tell those people. The continued viability of the elevator at Halifax is in question as a result of this particular bill as well.
Will the government explain to the 27 employees at the port of Halifax who have already lost their jobs why it is that they are out of work today? This particular bill will suck out of the Atlantic economy not $35 million, but maybe five times that amount, perhaps ten times that amount, in terms of the economic spin-offs as a result of that particular activity.
It makes no sense at all to put some 500 or 750 people out of work when the Government of Canada will end up paying much more in terms of unemployment insurance, much more in terms of other types of subsidies, to Atlantic Canada, the parts of Atlantic Canada that are affected by this regressive and unconscionable piece of legislation. Those people, if they are working, will pay taxes. That is why this bill makes no sense at all, it puts people out of work. And when you are out of work, you cannot pay taxes. So the government says: we want to save $35 million and so we are going to end this subsidy that has been in place, that subsidizes the transportation of grain to ports at and east of Buffalo, as I understand it.
The amendment posed by my House leader, the House leader for the Official Opposition, makes eminent good sense. What does that amendment do? It would put on hold this piece of legislation for six months. I am convinced that if government members thought about this a bit, if they reviewed some of the documentation that I have reviewed over the last number of hours, if they listened to the opposition members who have spoken, they, too, will become convinced that it is the wrong thing to do, and certainly at the wrong time. Canada is in the midst of a recession and here the government is simply compounding the problem in an

June 11, 1991
Government Orders
area of the country that needs as much assistance as possible.
As I indicated, this is not the first action of this government which has shoved a further nail into the coffin of the economy off Atlantic Canada. There have been others. My colleagues from the Halifax area, for example, and other parts of Atlantic Canada, have stood up time and time again to defend their constituents, indeed the constituents of Conservative members who do not have the courage to stand up and defend this piece of legislation, if in fact it is defensible.
Here it is, Bill C-ll. It is but two or three pages. What it does, the impact of these two or three pages of legislation, is significant, to say the least, in terms of the economy of two ports in particular and in all of Atlantic Canada.
I would ask, in closing, that the government reconsider this bill, to simply hoist it from the Order Paper for a six-month period as requested by my House leader, and in that period I am convinced that we on the opposition side will be able to convince government members that it is the wrong thing to do.

Madam Speaker, I sat here and listened to the excellent speech of the hon. member for York South-Weston and I note that the government introduced a motion yesterday to change the hours of sitting in this House to extend them to 10 p.m. throughout the bulk of the next two-week period.
The point of order, as the parliamentary secretary must know, is that there is not a single minister of the Crown in this House. While the rest of the members are forced to sit here until ten o'clock debating government legislation, the ministers go and tuck up in bed.
I resent that. The ministers have an obligation to be here. At least two of them should be here. They should not be home tucked up in bed while we are debating their crummy legislation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member does know that this is not a point of order and I must say that I am amazed that he would even consider thinking where ministers are or could be.

Madam Speaker, I, too, would like to join the debate at this late hour and wish as well, like my colleague, that the ministers from the government side would be here and listening to
our points. What is raised in this debate is about the Canadian value of caring, about the Canadian value of fairness and equality for regions.
Bill C-ll, an act to amend the Railway Act (grain and flour subsidies), also known as the At and East bill, is indeed an indictment, an indictment of our set of Canadian values.
Let me just tell the government opposite, the few members who are here, that to me, Bill C-ll poses hazards to people's lives, poses hazards to the citizens of the Atlantic region in particular, and indicates to me that this bill is an index of contempt by the government in this great institution, Parliament.
Why is that? Bill C-ll was introduced during the previous Parliament, as we know, as Bill C-26. It died on the Order Paper at third reading. Showing contempt for Parliament, showing contempt for Canadian citizens represented here in Parliament, the Tory government resurrected Bill C-26 following the commencement of the new session. The bill was resurrected at the same stage, trying to bypass the series of readings and debates so that Canadians may know more of the ills of this particular bill.
The government, I also submit, is showing contempt for Parliament as the rail subsidy for grain shipments was terminated in July 1989 and today, two years later, they are trying to pass legislation to legitimize what then was not legitimate.
I recall a fundamental teaching in high school that one of the principles in law-making is you do not pass a law that makes an act punishable that at the time was not. In other words, you do not pass a retroactive law.
What will prevent government in the future if we allow this bill to dictate on the events of the past by usurping the power and authority of law-making.
Export grain shipments to Halifax and Saint John have stopped and as a direct result the Saint John grain elevator is closed, putting 55 people out of work.
Perhaps 55 people in the eyes and minds and hearts of this government are not many but every citizen that suffers a job loss has to be taken care of by the government. There is no excuse. That person has a family to support, that person has a family to feed.
June 11, 1991

Truly, the economic impact on that part of our country will be devastating if we allow this to proceed.
Moreover, this bill in a sense reflects the mismanagement of agriculture by this government of agriculture. In a sense, it also tells of this government's undermining of orderly marketing in the country. It removes the storage option for grain, forcing the producer to sell at harvest time, producing a glut in pricing. We know the consequence of that.
It also will have a very serious effect, a negative effect, on our export capacity to export grains and flour.
When we recall that three government studies have seriously questioned the wisdom of removing the At and East bill, how can we tell Canadians that this government is listening to experts in the country? I think it shows the arrogance of this government.
As I said in the beginning, this bill is an indictment of the Canadian values of caring for our citizens wherever they are, of ensuring that there is fairness from east to west to north in Canada. We should really entrench in our thinking as parliamentarians the principle of equality of regions, the equality of provinces irrespective of their size. They are Canadians.
About a couple of weeks ago I had the privilege of visiting Saint John's and I was impressed by the beauty of that area. I was impressed by the sense of belonging and community in that part of the country. Let us continue to preserve that. Let us give hope for the citizens of the Atlantic region. I from the west, from the province of Manitoba, also a have not province, truly feel the pains of the citizens from the Atlantic region.
In conclusion, the Liberal Party wants to give Atlantic Canadians fairness. As a result, we have proposed an amendment that the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "that" and substituting the following therefore:
Bill C-U, an act to amend the Railway Act (grain and flour
subsidies) be not now read a third time but that it be read a third
time this day six months hence.
Why is that? Why have we proposed this amendment? It is because we would like to give this government a last chance, a time to reflect and avoid regrets in the future, a time to repent and avoid remorse in the future, a time to retreat for this government so that Canadians may preserve their Canadian values.

It is disgusting.

Despicable.

June 11, 1991
Government Orders
last session because it knew there would be a protracted debate and probably a very vigorous debate, mounted particularly by those members who are from eastern Canada. It is not to be forgotten that the electors of eastern Canada saw fit to throw out most of the Tory hacks who were representing them in this House for the years from 1984 to 1988 during the 1988 election.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception, my hon. and gallant colleague, is living proof. Rather than introduce it in the normal way, it decided to do something completely unprecedented in the history of our Parliament.
The hon. Minister of Supply and Services wags his head. I tell him this was completely unprecedented. If he would take the time to look at the precedents, he would agree with me. Never ever before has a government moved unilaterally to bring bills back into the House at a stage and ignoring all previous stages.
Tell us about the bill and not the procedure.

The hon. member says: "Tell us about the bill and not the procedure". Never mind the procedure, he says. I remind the hon. member that procedure is a very important thing in this country. Arthur Meighen lost an election because of procedure. He called it constitutional froth and was defeated at the polls, and I remind the hon. member of that. It is a remembrance that might serve the hon. member well come 1992 or 1993. He may find that the procedures that he and the
government he supports have adopted have resulted in such an abuse of the privileges of the members of this House that the Canadian people are sick to death of that kind of abuse and will throw this government out. The government will be lucky to hold as many seats after the next election as the Bloc Quebecois now has.
I do not want to get on to the next election. I would rather deal with the present, and I want to deal with the procedural aspect of the present. That is the argument that this bill has been brought before us in a way that is clandestine and wrong. The government has never ever before proceeded to introduce a motion to reinstate bills at any stage in the proceedings of the House without the unanimous consent of the House.
See how reasonable we were when we were in opposition.

Always, on previous occasions, unanimous consent was given.
The hon. member says: "See how reasonable we were when we were in opposition". Consent was very rarely given because it was very rarely asked for.
In the days when the hon. member was in opposition, we had a government in Canada that knew how to run the House of Commons. It organized its affairs. It organized its affairs so that when a session was prorogued the business was done and it started a new session with a new agenda and a new program, completely contrary to the situation we are witnessing today in this House.
There is no new agenda. There are no new programs. We are debating these old bills and they are being reintroduced by a short-circuit method to avoid legitimate debate and legitimate criticism in this House and in the country. That is what is going on in this case and that is what has gone on in several other cases. Five bills were introduced by this outrageous technique, a totally unprecedented technique.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to discuss a matter I raised the other day here in the House. Canada is now experiencing one of the worst recessions in its history, further aggravated by the fact that it was created by the same Toiy government that was elected to protect and enhance the well-being of Canadians. It is clear this government has failed miserably, Madam Speaker.
I rise in the House this evening to draw the attention of government members to the fact that some regions in Canada are worse off than others in these difficult times, and the Liberals are not alone in feeling this is so. The Conference Board of Canada also believes that Quebec has been affected more severely by the recession than other provinces.
On June 4, the Liberals spent a whole day drawing the attention of the government to the disastrous economic situation in the Montreal region which has been severely hit by the recession. One example is the manufacturing sector, where plant after plant is closing its doors. I am thinking of General Motors in Boisbriand, and Henkel in Ville d'Anjou, my former riding, right next door to Saint-Leonard. Pascal, one of the oldest hardware chains in Montreal, has closed its doors, and I could go on with a whole list of companies and plants where jobs have been lost, Madam Speaker. It is particularly ironic that we should be talking about employment today, considering that this government was elected in 1984 on a promise to create jobs.

Jobs, jobs, jobs. That was the slogan of the 1984 Tory campaign and look what happened today.

Montreal's hotel industry is also suffering the negative impact of this recession. In Montreal, more than 4,000 jobs have been lost in this sector since 1988. Last April, the unemployment rate in the Montreal region, a densely populated area, was 4 per cent higher than the unemployment rate in the Toronto region. Madam Speaker, this government has created a recession, and that is intolerable.
Perhaps we should also consider the Gaspe and the Magdalen Islands, one of the most beautiful regions in Canada, which now has an unemployment rate of over 27 per cent. What hope do young people have for the future in an area which offers no opportunities for durable employment? We can't expect to revive the hope and confidence of these young people with the kind of empty shell offered by the Minister of National Health and Welfare at the end of last month.
The Tory member from Gaspe is well aware of the problems in this region. Unfortunately, he didn't have the courage to defend the interests of his constituents. I am referring to an article that appeared in the Quebec City newspaper Le Soleil on March 7.
The privatization of bait plants by Fisheries and Oceans and Public Works seems to work in favour of producers, at the expense of fishermen. Nevertheless, this industry forms the basis of the region's economy.
Madam Speaker, how can the Minister of National Health and Welfare expect to convince the residents of this area that his recent announcement will help them, when he is doing nothing to support the economic base of this region?
I would also like to know what the government intends to do to prevent an exodus of young people looking for durable jobs because there are no opportunities in this region.
Madam Speaker, you are signalling that my time is up. Thank you very much.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to take a few moments again to tell the government's involvement in regard to regions of Canada and the objectives in reducing regional disparities throughout the territory.

Adjournment Debate
In order to reach our goal, we have created different ways and means, including the financial assistance program. It was within a concept of the Canadian government to announce nearly two weeks ago a series of measures which we intend to implement in order to lead support to economic development in the Gaspe-Magdalen Island regions and promote job creation.
I would like to tell once again the nature of the endeavours. The measures are related to the setting up of Gaspe-Magdalen Island Economic Development Corporation. This corporation, besides promoting economic development in the area will also be involved in prospective activities, investment and promotion of the fields of industry and tourism, not only in Canada but internationally:
Our government will assume the operational costs of the corporation during the next five years through contributions totalling $1.7 million. The government even goes one step further in offering a grant of $2 million to the same corporation, enabling it to sponsor a newly created organization known as Gaspe and Magdalen Island Investment Registration.
This limited partnership will invest blocks of capital between $50,000 and $400,000 to develop into expanding companies. Occasionally it may invest in a start-up stage of a corporation operating in the manufacturing or service sector. This investment will ensure healthy capitalization in most of the promising enterprises.
A new loan insurance program will also be announced. It will be an acceptable organization of the Gaspe-Magdalen Island region. This new program will allow the carrying out of many important projects which will be named and drawing the boards of inadequate funding.
The government will have a loan guarantee of $6.4 million between now and March 31, 1993.

Madam Speaker, as you know, I have had the opportunity to ask the government a number of questions concerning the case of Mohamed Al-Mashat. He is the former Iraqi Ambassador to Washington who was fast-tracked into Canada.
We were in the process of investigating this particular matter when the government decided today to shut down the process. We had the opportunity to invite a number of witnesses before the committee. We had the opportunity to ask questions, and obviously we were getting close to the truth. The result is the government today decided that it has heard enough and it no longer wishes the inquiry to carry on, notwithstanding the very explicit promises of the government that it was calling the inquiry in order to get to the truth of what happened, to understand how it was possible for a former ambassador of a country with which we were at war, to gain access to Canada as a landed immigrant, within a matter of weeks, when it takes others months and at times years to enter Canada.
We embarked on the inquiry. A number of cabinet ministers were embarrassed as a result of some of the evidence that was heard. I guess the government is no longer interested in understanding completely what happened in the Al-Mashat matter.
We do know that the government has presented several versions of what happened. We had version A, then version B, then version C and then version D and we really do not know how many other versions are out there. We do know that on the evening of May 13, the former Secretary of State for External Affairs, the former Minister of Immigration, and several other ministers were present at a meeting with officials. At that particular meeting they decided to blame the nephew of the leader of the Official Opposition, Raymond Chretien, who happens to be the second in command at the Department of External Affairs.
They also decided at that particular meeting to blame Mr. David Daubney, a former Conservative member of Parliament and the Chief of Staff to the former Secretary of State for External Affairs. Mr. Daubney himself gave evidence at the committee that he was blamed for reasons of symmetry. In fact, that was the terminology that was used at that particular meeting. The government has not, in any way, allowed the opposition to understand completely what happened at that meeting on May 13. We do know that a report was rewritten by individuals in the Privy Council Office with apologies already in the report that a fellow by the name of Shortcliff was sent to visit Mr. Daubney and Mr. Raymond Chretien to tell them that they had apologized. In
June 11, 1991

fact, Mr. Chretien indicated very clearly to the committee that he had nothing to apologize for and that he did not apologize.
Madam Speaker, I note that my time is up. Perhaps, the hon. member opposite can explain to the people of Canada why the government is shutting down the inquiry when it promised we would have a full inquiry into this matter.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Richardson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it has been a long day and I appreciate your patience in the chair, particularly in re-answering questions that have been so often answered in this House.
I am responding now to questions raised in the House on May 30 by the hon. member for York South-Weston on the Al-Mashat case.
In an exchange with the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the member asked about differences in the chronologies released on May 14 and on May 30. Since the parliamentary committee first began hearings on the Al-Mashat case, this question has been answered on several occasions by both ministers and officials.
I should emphasize that the government has responded to requests from the committee for documents on this case. I understand there is still a standing offer to Privy Councillors from both the Liberal and New Democratic parties which would allow them to pursue Mr. Al-Mashat's immigration file.
For the benefit of the hon. member, let me briefly summarize the facts. Auditors from both the Department of External Affairs and the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission were appointed as soon as minister Valcourt stated that an investigation would take place into this matter. This audit was completed on the basis of corroborated evidence and facts which could be confirmed at that time.
Following the release of the first chronology on May 14, new information became available as a result of public statements, some factual inaccuracies also were found in that document. This was acknowledged by the Secretary of State for External Affairs before the parliamentary committee on May 30.
Adjournment Debate
As a consequence of these acknowledged inaccuracies, ministers requested additional information and further interviews were carried out by auditors, including with persons outside of government. This resulted in a fuller chronology released on May 30, which provided a more detailed account of the handling of Mr. Al-Mashat's case and noted inaccuracies contained in the earlier chronology.
In a supplementary question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, also on May 30, the member for York South-Weston had pointed out one such factual error between the two chronologies. He asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs on which date the defectors committee decided Mr. Al-Mashat was not a defector.
Again this question has come up before the parliamentary committee, but I would answer the question as follows:
The chronology released on May 14 unfortunately left out a key word. The defectors committee had determined on March 1 that Mr. Al-Mashat probably was not a defector. A final determination could be made by the defectors committee only after Mr. Al-Mashat had been interviewed by officials at our embassy in Vienna. This interview took place on March 5.
Vienna sent its assessment of Mr. Al-Mashat by telex, which was received in Ottawa on March 7. On that day, the defectors committee met to consider the report and concluded that there was insufficient intelligence value present to consider Mr. Al-Mashat as a defector.

Madam Speaker, last week I asked the minister of health if the government would be willing to accelerate the phase-out of chlorofluorocarbons and other ozone-depleting chemicals from the present schedule of 1997, instead to the year 1995.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment replied and said, "no". Perhaps, if reasons are provided this evening, the government might agree to 1995 instead of 1997.
According to medical forecasts, more than 46,000 Canadians are likely to develop skin cancer this year. The incidence of melanoma, the most dangerous form of

June 11, 1991
Adjournment Debate
skin cancer presently known, has, in addition to that, more than doubled in the last 20 years.
The Canadian Dermatology Association says that these figures do not yet reflect the impacts of a thinning ozone layer, and that the risks of skin cancer will continue to rise into the 21st century. Our young people are particularly at risk.
In April of this year, scientists with the National Aeronautics and Space Administration in the United States released new data showing that ozone depletion was occurring at twice the rate previously predicted. This has allowed the United States Environmental Protection Agency to conclude that ozone depletion over the United States will result in approximately an additional 6 million cases of skin cancer and 200,000 deaths over the next 50 years.
Compared to 10 years ago, there is now on average, according to the scientific community, 5 per cent less ozone in the stratosphere over southern Canada.
These findings therefore have veiy serious public health implications. The ozone layer is the earth's only natural protective shield against the sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation. Increased exposure to such radiation will increase the incidence of skin cancer and eye disease, weaken our immune systems and also decrease the yields of certain important agricultural crops.
Now, to return to the cause, which is chlorofluorocar-bons. The Canadian government currently plans to phase out chlorofluorocarbons in 1997. Other countries are moving faster than Canada.
Germany will end its chlorofluorocarbon production in 1995. Australia, Norway and Sweden will all have eliminated 95 per cent of their chlorofluorocarbons by 1995.
In the light of these developments, the question is will the Minister of the Environment or the minister of health and welfare or someone on their behalf phase out by the year 1995 ozone depleting chemicals, specifically chlorofluorocarbons, halons and methyl chloroforms, to protect the health of present and future generations of Canadians?

speakeroldname: Mr. John A. MacDougall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the satellite data on ozone layer definition and the agreement with the data from Canadian stations do
not significantly change our understanding of the state of the ozone layer but reinforce the need for strong international action.
Canada's consumption of ozone depleting substances is decreasing faster than required by the Montreal protocol. The 1990 Canadian consumption of CFCs was 33 per cent below that of the 1986 level used as the benchmark for the Montreal protocol.
We are committed to zero consumption of CFCs by the year 1997, three years ahead of the international schedule.
The objective is the ozone consumption by the year 2000, five years ahead of the international schedule. From the ozone depletion substance in general, we are now more than two years ahead of the international schedule.
Large decreases are occurring in several other industrialized countries as well. As a commitment in the green plan Canada will continue to work on the domestic reduction and recycling initiatives of CFCs and partnerships with the provinces.
The National Research Council is working with the industry to evaluate CFC alternatives. Our regulation program eliminates specific use of ozone depleting substances as adequate replacements become available.

Madam Speaker, I want to tell you about a constituent of mine named Hyacinth Vernon.
Ms. Vernon is a single mother, she has four children and she goes to work. Until recently, she and her children lived in an apartment near my constituency office on O'Connor Drive but she had to move because, quite legitimately, her landlord wanted to move relatives into her apartment.
There are very few places for a Canadian who is a single mother of four children and who is a member of the working poor to go to live these days. The vacancy rate until recently in metropolitan Toronto was less than 1 per cent. In fact, it was about .3 per cent. She had been on the waiting list for public housing in the metropolitan Toronto area since 1986, some five years. She was forced to move in with her cousin, the husband of her cousin and her cousin's two children in one bedroom.

There you are, we had three adults and we had six children in a one bedroom apartment. We know that that could not go not go on very much longer. She had to move out. Where could she go then? There was still nothing available in the rental apartment market, there was still no public housing available. Now she is in a one-room motel room in the Americana Motel on Kingston Road in Toronto with her four kids.
She continues to work every day. She hands her weekly cheque of some $283 net over to the social and community services department, the welfare department. They pay the rent on the motel, then hand her back enough bus tickets to get her back and forth to work every day and they give her $26 a day to feed, clothe and look after herself and her four children.
Now I am told by the welfare department in metropolitan Toronto that Ms. Vernon is only one of about 100 similar cases in metropolitan Tbronto right now. Why in heaven's name Ms. Vernon does not just throw in the towel I do not know, but obviously she is made of pretty good stuff.
Ms. Vernon cannot get into public housing because she is one of some 17,000 Canadian citizens and landed immigrants who are now on a waiting list for public housing in metropolitan Toronto. On top of that, the Ontario Minister of Housing, because of a decision of the Supreme Court of Canada, has now said that he is going to admit refugee claimants to public housing as well. There are some 90,000 refugee claimants in Canada at the present time, 60,000 of those are in Ontario. They are now available for public housing.
Where in heaven's name are we going to put these people? Refugee claimants are the responsibility of the federal government. CMHC has no money. Employment and Immigration has no money. Where in heaven's name, Mr. Minister, are we going to put these people when refugees are a federal responsibility?

speakeroldname: Mr. John A. MacDougall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to respond to my colleague on the question of refugees benefiting from the security of government-assisted housing.
Adjournment Debate
The hon. member is aware that the federal government, through the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, shares responsibility with the provinces in the delivery and support of low-cost housing.
The National Housing Act in no way restricts these benefits to Canadian citizens or landed immigrants. In fact, putting restrictions in place would contravene human rights legislation.
The hon. member is quite correct in noting that demand for government-subsidized housing is great, especially in the Toronto area where so many refugee claimants reside. I am pleased to advise the hon. member that officials of CMHC, the Ontario Ministry of Housing and Canada Employment and Immigration are already working together to identify the extent of the demand and its impact on the availability of subsidized housing.
Throughout Canada, family members, church groups, multicultural societies and other non-profit organizations are working to improve the living conditions of recent arrivals to the country. We have seen remarkable examples of communities rallying to the aid of those driven from their own homelands by war or oppression.
The hon. member may recall the dramatic footage of a boat load of Ihmils who had arrived on the rocky coast of Nova Scotia. The people of the nearby villages found them. They were sheltered, clothed, fed and given every possible form of aid and help.
These are genuine expressions of kindness and concern. It is a very direct and personal response to the need.
As the minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation mentioned in his earlier response, when the Vietnamese boat people arrived in this country a number of years ago, they were desperate for housing. At the time, CMHC had some vacant apartments in housing administrations. Mortgage insurance operations with refugees are settled there.
It is interesting to note that very quickly they became established in the community and were able to find their own housing. In fact, it has been reported that some of the people who were helped in this way treated their assistance as a temporary loan and paid the government back.
